| 5 | Every port implementation the module touches runs its conformance suite | QR-15 |
| 6 | Layer 1: every existing TypeScript test and scoreboard for the function passes against the Rust implementation, with every pinned number identical and no expectation edited | QR-19, QR-21 |
| 7 | Layer 2: the property differential runs with exact equality, and was shown to fail on a planted one-ulp change | QR-21 |
| 8 | Layer 3: the shared fixtures and goldens are byte-identical natively and on wasm | QR-20, QR-21 |
| 9 | Every tolerated difference is a both-sided ledger entry naming one case and its reason | QR-21 |
| 10 | `differential` mode has run in CI and in dogfooding with no unexplained mismatch | QR-21 |
| 11 | `cargo mutants --in-diff` is clean or ledgered; line and region coverage are at or above the crate's floor | QR-17, QR-18 |
| 12 | Its exports are called once per user operation, and the boundary cost was measured on browser, Node and workerd against the TypeScript it replaces, with the result in the PR body | QR-22b |
| 13 | The wasm artifact's size is within its ledger, its peak memory reported, and its Workers budgets measured | QR-22c, QR-22d, QR-23 |
| 14 | Every untrusted-input entry it exposes has declared caps and a fuzz target, seeded and run, with no open crash | QR-28b, QR-29a–QR-29d |
| 15 | Logging goes through the `log` facade; errors follow the `thiserror` convention with generated codes; the poison-and-recover scenario covers the state the module holds | QR-25a, QR-26a–QR-26c |
| 16 | The `PORTED_FUNCTIONS` ledger lists the function, and once the switch is `rust` the TypeScript export is a re-export of the shim | ADR-0054 |
| 17 | Any Unicode table it uses comes from a pinned crate with a version-asserting test | QR-20b |
| 18 | Its exit criteria (QR-33b) are recorded in the PR | QR-33b |
| 19 | Docs reflect the shipped state | QR-30 |

**QR-33b. Per-module exit criteria.** The PR that moves a module's first
switch to `rust` MUST record, for that module:

| Criterion | What is recorded |
|---|---|
| Port shape | **Structure-preserving** (the Rust follows the TypeScript's structure, so a reviewer can read them side by side) or **redesigned** (with the reason; a redesign leans harder on layers 2 and 3 of QR-21, since layer 1's tests no longer map one to one) |
| TypeScript deletion deadline | By default, the TypeScript implementation is deleted in the release AFTER the one in which the module's switch first defaults to `rust` — one release of differential data. A later deadline is allowed per module only with a recorded reason |
| Rollback | Flipping the switch back to `ts` or `differential` in the composition root; no other step. While the TypeScript exists, rollback MUST stay that cheap |
| Freeze lift | The freeze on the module's feature work lifts when its switch is `rust` AND its TypeScript is deleted; from then on its new features go to Rust only (ADR-0054 decision 23) |

When the last function of a TypeScript package reaches `rust`, the package is
deleted, its tests are kept and pointed at the shim, and only then are they
moved to Rust.

# Release Publishing Guide

Operator runbook for publishing `@kamiazya/whiteboard-mcp` to npm and GHCR.

---

## Required GitHub Environments

Three protected environments must exist before a release run reaches its publish and deploy jobs:

| Environment | Job | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| `production-npm` | `publish-mcp` | npm OIDC Trusted Publishing (no token required) |
| `production-docker` | `docker-publish-sign` | GHCR push + cosign keyless signing |
| `production-web` | `deploy-web` | Cloudflare Pages production deploy; holds `CLOUDFLARE_API_TOKEN` and `CLOUDFLARE_ACCOUNT_ID` |

The two publish environments should require at least one reviewer before the job runs.
Without the environment protection, the `release.yml` publish guard is incomplete.
A forced re-publish runs the tag's own copy of `release.yml`, so a tag ruleset restricting
`mcp-server-v*` tags to maintainers (creation, update and deletion) is required too; see
**Docker SBOM and Provenance** for what it protects. Until that ruleset exists, do not
trust a signature or provenance naming the `refs/tags/<tag>` identity: trust only the
`refs/heads/main` identity.
`production-web` carries the Cloudflare secrets, so protect it the same way.
`release-please` and `advance-stable` bind no environment: neither holds a registry or
deploy credential. The PR-preview deploys use a separate `preview-web` environment, which
is not part of a release (see [cloudflare-pages.md](deployment/cloudflare-pages.md)).

---

## Required Tag Shape

All publish runs — automated and manual — require a `mcp-server-v<semver>` tag.

Valid examples:

```
mcp-server-v0.1.0
mcp-server-v1.2.3-rc.1
```

Invalid examples (rejected by SemVer preflight step before any credential is used):

```
mcp-server-v-typo        # not a SemVer
mcp-server-vrc1          # not a SemVer
v0.1.0                   # wrong prefix
mcp-server-v0.1          # missing patch segment
```

The SemVer validation step runs _before_ checkout in `build-mcp` and `build-docker`,
the jobs that check the tag out, and first in `docker-publish-sign`, which pushes under
it. Invalid tags are rejected before any code is checked out or credentials are
requested.

---

## Automated Publish (`release.yml`)

`release.yml` is the single production publish path for both npm and Docker.

### How a release flows

1. Merge a Conventional Commit (`feat:`, `fix:`, etc.) to `main`.
2. release-please opens a Release PR titled `chore: release main`. The `linked-versions`
   plugin groups the plugin and `mcp-server` components into one PR, so the title names
   neither a component nor a version.
3. A maintainer reviews and merges the Release PR.
4. `release.yml`'s `release-please` job reports what the merge released, and the jobs below
   it run from those outputs:

   | Job | Runs when | Does |
   |---|---|---|
   | `release-please` | every push to `main` | opens or updates the Release PR; creates the tags and GitHub Releases when it is merged |
   | `advance-stable` | the root (plugin) component was released | fast-forwards the `stable` branch to the release tag |
   | `build-mcp` | `mcp-server` was released, or a forced re-publish with `publish_npm` | runs the publish gate and packs the npm tarball, with read-only permissions |
   | `build-docker` | `mcp-server` was released, or a forced re-publish with `publish_docker` | runs the publish gate and container smokes and builds the image into an OCI archive, with read-only permissions |
   | `publish-mcp` | `build-mcp` succeeded | npm publish of the tarball `build-mcp` packed |
   | `docker-publish-sign` | `build-docker` succeeded | image push and cosign signature of the archive `build-docker` built |
   | `build-web` | any component was released | installs and builds `apps/web` and archives `dist/`, with read-only permissions and no secret |
   | `deploy-web` | `build-web` succeeded | Cloudflare Pages production deploy of the site `build-web` archived; skips its deploy step while the Cloudflare secrets are absent |

   Apart from each publish or deploy job waiting on its build job, the jobs after `release-please` are
   independent of one another: one failing does not stop the others, so a failed
   `advance-stable` leaves the npm package, the image and the web deploy published.
5. `force_publish_tag` input: can re-publish a specific tag (e.g. after a transient
   OIDC failure). Must match `mcp-server-v<semver>`; rejected before checkout otherwise.
   The `publish_npm` and `publish_docker` inputs (both default on) choose which halves run.

### Publish gate scope: publishability, not correctness

`build-mcp` runs the **publish** tier of `tests/e2e/distribution/release-gate-matrix.json`
via `pnpm publish-gate` (`tools/checks/src/publish-gate.mjs`, a matrix-driven runner that
mirrors `pages-release.mjs`). That tier is scoped to **publishability**: does the tarball
build correctly, contain the required files, carry an SBOM, and actually start when
unpacked (the `test:distribution` vitest suite — the packed tarball, plain and under
`WHITEBOARD_DEV=1`, the Codex config and the packaged entry — then `smoke:packaged` and the
packaged-daemon/server-mode node smokes)? It also carries a fast, deterministic **correctness floor**
(`pnpm typecheck` + `pnpm test:mcp-node`) so an obviously broken tag never publishes.

It deliberately does **not** re-run the full browser/jsdom test matrix
(`pnpm test` = every vitest project, listed in `CONTRIBUTING.md`). That correctness is
already proven by **verify CI (`ci.yml`) at the identical tag SHA**: a release tag always
points at a commit that was pushed to `main`, and `ci.yml`'s `verify` job (gated on
`test-unit`, `test-jsdom`, `test-browser`) already ran against that exact commit before a
human merged the release PR. Re-running the same suite a second time inside `build-mcp`
produced no new correctness signal — it only re-exposed an already-green commit to
environment flakes (three consecutive releases failed publish this way, each on a
different flake inside the re-run, while npm sat stuck at an older version). See
`ci-verify-coverage.test.ts` and `publish-gate-runner.test.ts` in
`tools/arch-lint/src/` for the automated guards that keep this
boundary from drifting.

A blocking cross-workflow dependency on verify's *reported* conclusion (rather than on
branch-protection having already required it) was considered and rejected: `build-mcp`
only depends on `release-please`, not on `verify`, so querying verify's conclusion at
publish time races a same-push `ci.yml` run that may still be in progress, and would
require granting `actions: read` that the workflow does not otherwise need. If a stronger,
machine-checked guarantee is wanted later, add it as a non-blocking advisory annotation
first.

### Build and publish are separate jobs

Each half is a **build** job and a **publish** job. The build job checks out the tag,
installs dependencies and runs every gate with `contents: read` and nothing else; its
checkout sets `persist-credentials: false`, so the job token is not left in `.git/config`
either. The publish job holds the credential — `id-token: write`, and `packages: write`
for the image — and checks out nothing and runs no repository or dependency code. It
downloads the artifact its build job uploaded, checks it against the sha256 that job
reported, and publishes it.

The split exists because any lifecycle script, test or smoke in the tree could otherwise
mint the OIDC token npm and Sigstore accept, or read the GHCR push token.
`ci-policy.test.ts` in `tools/arch-lint/src/` fails on a job that holds either permission
and checks out the repository, runs a repository action, or runs `pnpm`, `npx`, `node` or
a script-running `npm` verb, and on a release checkout that keeps the token where the job
does not push with it (only `advance-stable` does).

Every build job upstream of a publish or deploy installs into a cold pnpm store
(`cache-store: 'false'` on `setup-pnpm`): the store cache is keyed by the lockfile alone
and written by default-branch jobs that run every dev and test dependency, and a store
poisoned there would be packed into the output that the reported sha256 then certifies.
`workflow-credentials.test.ts` fails on any job a publishing job `needs` that restores a
cache.

### `build-mcp` and `publish-mcp` jobs (npm OIDC provenance)

`build-mcp` steps (in order):

1. Validate `mcp-server-v<semver>` tag shape via `TAG` env var (not inline expression —
   prevents shell injection).
2. Checkout the release tag, with `persist-credentials: false`.
3. On a forced re-publish, refuse when the checked-out tag is not `GITHUB_SHA` or the run
   was not dispatched from the tag (see **Force-publish via release.yml**).
4. Install dependencies (Node 24 pinned).
5. `pnpm audit --prod --audit-level=high`: a high or critical advisory in a production
   dependency stops the publish.
6. `pnpm publish-gate`: runs the publish tier (typecheck, mcp-node floor, build,
   artifact checks, SBOM generation, tarball/packaged smokes) — see "Publish gate
   scope" above.
7. `verify-pack-contents`: the packed tarball carries the README and LICENSE and no test
   artifacts or internal `_artifacts`.
8. Upload SBOM as GitHub Actions artifact `npm-sbom-<run_id>` (retained 90 days,
   `if-no-files-found: error`).
9. `pnpm pack`, which resolves the `catalog:` protocol to concrete ranges.
10. `pnpm audit:published --tarball <it>`: npm installs that tarball into an empty
    directory — with none of `pnpm-workspace.yaml`'s overrides, which are not published —
    and `npm audit --omit=dev --audit-level=high` runs there. Step 5 reads the lockfile,
    where an override can clear a floor a consumer's install never gets; this reads what
    `npx @kamiazya/whiteboard-mcp` resolves. The scheduled `audit.yml` runs the same check
    daily.
11. Upload the tarball as `npm-tarball-<run_id>` (retained 7 days) and report its sha256
    as a job output.

Permissions: `contents: read`. No environment.

`publish-mcp` steps (in order):

1. `actions/setup-node` with Node 24 and the npm registry (npm 11.x meets the Trusted
   Publishing requirement).
2. Download `npm-tarball-<run_id>` and check it with `sha256sum -c` against
   `build-mcp`'s output.
3. `npm publish <tarball> --access public --provenance --ignore-scripts` (OIDC Trusted
   Publishing, no NPM_TOKEN). The provenance names the same workflow, commit and ref as
   before the split: the job runs in `release.yml`, in the same run.

Permissions: `contents: read`, `id-token: write` (job-scoped, not workflow-root).
Environment: `production-npm`.

### `build-docker` and `docker-publish-sign` jobs (keyless signing)

`build-docker` steps (in order):

1. Validate `mcp-server-v<semver>` tag shape via `TAG` env var (same guard as npm job).
2. Checkout the release tag, with `persist-credentials: false`.
3. On a forced re-publish, refuse when the checked-out tag is not `GITHUB_SHA`, the commit
   the dispatch ran from, which the image's provenance and the cosign certificate name.
4. Install dependencies.
5. `pnpm publish-gate`, the same publishability tier the npm job runs (see "Publish gate
   scope" above), then `pnpm smoke:docker` and `pnpm smoke:docker-backup-restore`, the
   checks only a container can answer. It does **not** run `check:release-candidate:docker`:
   that aggregate chains `pnpm test`, the full matrix verify CI already ran at this SHA.
   Re-run on one runner at the tag, it failed the 0.0.20 image three times on three
   different load-dependent tests, and a re-run checks out the same tag, so a flake there
   blocks the image for that whole release. `check:release-candidate:docker` stays the
   local, full pre-release pass.
6. `docker/build-push-action` with `sbom: true` and `provenance: true` (OCI attestations),
   exporting an OCI archive instead of pushing; the attestations travel inside the archive.
7. Upload the archive as `docker-image-<run_id>` (retained 7 days) and report its sha256
   as a job output.

Permissions: `contents: read`. No environment.

`docker-publish-sign` steps (in order):

1. Validate the tag shape again: the tag names the pushed reference.
2. Download `docker-image-<run_id>` and check it with `sha256sum -c` against
   `build-docker`'s output.
3. Log in to GHCR, then `skopeo copy --all --preserve-digests` the archive to
   `ghcr.io/kamiazya/whiteboard:<tag>` and `:latest`. `--all` pushes the whole image
   index, attestation manifests included, and `--preserve-digests` refuses to rewrite
   anything, so the digest pushed is the one `build-docker` built. A `docker load` would
   drop the attestations.
4. `cosign sign --yes` of that digest, using `DIGEST` and `IMAGE_REPO` env vars (not
   inline shell expansion); keyless signing via Sigstore OIDC, no private key material.

Permissions: `contents: read`, `id-token: write`, `packages: write` (job-scoped).
Environment: `production-docker`.

### `advance-stable` job (plugin channel)

Git-based plugin consumers (the Claude Code marketplace source ref, Codex `@stable`
marketplaces) resolve the `stable` branch, so plugin content ships when the Release PR
merges rather than on every push to `main`.

Steps (in order):

1. Check out with full history and tags.
2. Fetch the root release tag (`root_tag_name`) and verify it resolves to a commit.
3. `git push origin <tag-commit>:refs/heads/stable`, with **no force flag**.

Permissions: `contents: write`. No environment.

**It fails on a non-fast-forward.** If `stable` holds a commit that is not an ancestor of
the release tag (someone pushed to `stable` directly, or history on `main` was rewritten),
git refuses the push and the job goes red; the workflow never rewrites `stable` itself.
Plugin consumers stay on the previous `stable` until it is resolved. To recover:

1. Compare the branches: `git fetch origin && git log --oneline origin/stable ^<tag>` lists
   what `stable` has that the tag does not.
2. Decide what those commits are. If they belong, land them on `main` through a normal PR
   (a later release carries them); if they are stray, a maintainer resets `stable` to the
   tag deliberately, outside the workflow.
3. Re-run the failed job (`gh run rerun <run-id> --failed`): it re-reads the same tag and
   pushes again.

### `build-web` and `deploy-web` jobs (hosted app)

The hosted app is split the way the publish halves are, because a secret bound to one
step is no boundary inside one job: the install and build run dependency code, which
could rewrite the wrangler a later step runs with the token.

`build-web` checks out the release commit with `persist-credentials: false`, installs
dependencies, builds `apps/web`, archives `dist/` as `site.tar`, and reports its sha256 as
the job output `site_sha256`. It has `contents: read` and no secret.

`deploy-web` holds the Cloudflare secrets and runs no repository or dependency code:

1. A sparse checkout of `.github/deploy` alone, with `persist-credentials: false`.
2. `npm ci --ignore-scripts` there, which installs the wrangler pinned in that directory's
   `package-lock.json` (integrity-checked, no lifecycle scripts). This tooling lives outside
   the pnpm workspace on purpose, so the install pulls in nothing else.
3. Downloads `site.tar`, checks it with `sha256sum -c` against `build-web`'s `site_sha256`,
   and unpacks it.
4. Runs `wrangler pages deploy … --project-name=kamiazya-whiteboard` against production,
   through `cloudflare/wrangler-action` with `wranglerVersion` set to the same pinned
   version, so the action uses the installed wrangler and runs no install of its own. The
   deploy step skips itself when the Cloudflare secrets are not configured in
   `production-web`.

`tools/arch-lint/src/workflow-credentials.test.ts` holds every job in every workflow that
references a deploy or publish secret to this shape. To move wrangler, bump the exact version
in `.github/deploy/package.json` and regenerate its lockfile (`npm install --ignore-scripts`
in that directory); the deploy jobs read `wranglerVersion` from the lockfile, so no workflow
changes. The other deploy paths for the same project are in
[cloudflare-pages.md](deployment/cloudflare-pages.md).

Permissions: `contents: read` for both. Environment: `production-web` (`deploy-web` only).

## Dry-Run Verification (`ci.yml`)

Every PR and push to `main` runs non-destructive dry-run checks in `ci.yml`.
No `id-token: write`, no registry push, no cosign — safe to run on any branch.

```bash
# Local dry-run (no publish, no id-token):
pnpm publish:dry-run

# Or run individual steps:
pnpm publish:dry-run:npm    # pnpm pack + SHA-512 + SBOM placeholder
pnpm publish:dry-run:docker # docker build (no push)
```

`ci.yml` jobs:

- `verify`: after its build, runs `pnpm publish:dry-run:npm` and uploads tarball
  artifacts to `npm-tarball-dry-run` (`if-no-files-found: error`).
- `dry-run-docker`: installs, runs `pnpm publish:dry-run:docker`, uploads metadata to
  `docker-image-dry-run` (`if-no-files-found: warn` — Docker daemon may be unavailable).
- `packaged-smoke`: installs, builds, then runs `pnpm smoke:distribution:packaged:node` — the
  same **publish**-tier packaged-distribution smoke that `pnpm publish-gate` runs at
  release time — on every PR, so that gate cannot go stale between release tags without
  a PR-side failure.

## npm SBOM Artifact

SBOM generation for npm uses `@cyclonedx/cyclonedx-npm` (workspace devDependency,
lockfile-pinned at v4.x):

- **Why CycloneDX over syft**: pure Node.js package (no binary install), CycloneDX
  format aligns with the `signingStrategy: "npm-provenance"` in
  `supply-chain-policy.json`, version fixed via pnpm lockfile for deterministic CI output.

- **Lockfile binding**: the script uses `pnpm deploy --legacy --prod` from the workspace
  root, which reads `pnpm-lock.yaml` to install production dependencies at exact pinned
  versions — the same graph validated by `check:release-candidate`. The `--legacy` flag
  is required by pnpm v10. This avoids re-resolving `^` / `~` ranges independently at
  SBOM generation time. `cyclonedx-npm` is then run against the deployed directory with
  `--ignore-npm-errors` (suppresses `ELSPROBLEMS` for absent devDependencies, which are
  intentionally excluded from the prod-only deploy).

- **Output**: `packages/mcp-server/_artifacts/npm-sbom.cdx.json`
  Uploaded as GitHub Actions artifact `npm-sbom-<tag>` with 90-day retention.

- **Safe stdout contract** (`generate-npm-sbom.mjs`):
  Emits a JSON summary with: `sbomFile` (basename), `sbomBytes`, `checksum` (SHA-512),
  `tool`, `toolVersion`, `sbomFormat`, `specVersion`.
  Never emits: SBOM contents, dependency names, package paths, registry auth,
  OIDC material, or full build logs.

- **Script**: `packages/mcp-server/scripts/release/generate-npm-sbom.mjs`
  (a package script — `pnpm --filter @kamiazya/whiteboard-mcp generate:sbom:npm`,
  which is how `check:release-candidate` calls it; there is no root script of
  that name)

- **When it runs in CI**: `pnpm publish-gate` (used in the `build-mcp` job) runs
  `generate-npm-sbom.mjs` as one of the publish-tier gates, before `npm publish`. This
  ensures the SBOM content regression tests in `sbom-policy.test.ts` always execute on
  the release path.

- **Staleness guard**: `generate-npm-sbom.mjs` also writes a sidecar fingerprint file,
  `packages/mcp-server/_artifacts/npm-sbom.inputs.json` (SHA-256 of `pnpm-lock.yaml`
  and `packages/mcp-server/package.json`, plus a SHA-512 of the SBOM file itself).
  `sbom-policy.test.ts` recomputes the current fingerprint before running its
  content-policy assertions, so a locally generated SBOM that predates a dependency
  change fails with an actionable "stale, run `pnpm --filter @kamiazya/whiteboard-mcp
  generate:sbom:npm`" message instead of reading as a false dependency-policy
  regression. See `packages/mcp-server/src/server/release/release-signing-provenance-sbom.md`
  for the full contract (current/stale/absent states).

## Docker SBOM and Provenance

Docker SBOM and provenance attestations are produced by `docker/build-push-action`
with `sbom: true` and `provenance: true` in `build-docker`. These flags cause Buildkit
to generate OCI attestation manifests into the image index of the OCI archive that job
builds, and `docker-publish-sign` pushes them alongside the image layers. No custom
signing keys or bespoke signing formats are used.

The Docker image is keyless-signed by cosign via Sigstore OIDC. The signing
identity is tied to the GitHub Actions OIDC token of the `production-docker`
environment, not to any stored private key.

The certificate identity is the signing workflow's URL at the ref it ran
from, and the certificate also records the event that started the run. A
release has exactly two shapes, so verify against the one the image came
from rather than a pattern that accepts both:

- a release-please release signs as `release.yml` on `refs/heads/main`,
  triggered by `push`;
- a forced re-publish signs as `release.yml` on `refs/tags/<tag>`, triggered
  by `workflow_dispatch`. `build-docker` refuses a forced run whose
  checked-out tag is not the commit the run was dispatched from, or that was
  dispatched from any ref but `refs/tags/<tag>` itself, and `docker-publish-sign`
  signs only after it succeeds, so a forced
  re-publish is always dispatched with `--ref <tag>` (see
  **Force-publish via release.yml** below) and never signs a tag under
  `main`'s identity.

Pin the whole identity, the trigger and the repository. An unanchored
`--certificate-identity-regexp` accepts any workflow whose URL merely contains
the repository path, such as one in a fork on a branch named after it.

Verification of a release-please release:
```bash
cosign verify ghcr.io/kamiazya/whiteboard:<tag> \
  --certificate-identity 'https://github.com/kamiazya/whiteboard/.github/workflows/release.yml@refs/heads/main' \
  --certificate-github-workflow-trigger push \
  --certificate-github-workflow-repository kamiazya/whiteboard \
  --certificate-oidc-issuer "https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com"
```

Verification of a forced re-publish, with `<tag>` the same tag in both places:
```bash
cosign verify ghcr.io/kamiazya/whiteboard:<tag> \
  --certificate-identity 'https://github.com/kamiazya/whiteboard/.github/workflows/release.yml@refs/tags/<tag>' \
  --certificate-github-workflow-trigger workflow_dispatch \
  --certificate-github-workflow-repository kamiazya/whiteboard \
  --certificate-oidc-issuer "https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com"
```

The tag identity is only as strong as control over who can create the tag. A
dispatch from a tag runs **that tag's** copy of `release.yml`, so anyone who
can push `mcp-server-v9.9.9` at a commit carrying an edited workflow can drop
the `environment:` binding, sign, and produce a certificate this second check
accepts. A tag ruleset restricting creation, update and deletion of
`mcp-server-v*` tags to maintainers is therefore **required** for the forced
re-publish identity to mean anything; without one, trust only the
`refs/heads/main` identity.

## Docker Release Candidate Verification

Run the Docker-specific gates before tagging a release that includes a new
image. These run in addition to — not instead of — the CI gates:

```sh
# Full Docker release verification (CI gates + Docker gates).
pnpm check:release-candidate:docker

# Or run the Docker-specific gates individually after check:release-candidate:
pnpm smoke:docker              # Docker image boots, serves MCP, auth smoke
pnpm smoke:docker-backup-restore  # backup → restore round-trip via volume mounts
```

The non-Docker release gates (unit tests, typecheck, distribution smokes,
etc.) are bundled in `pnpm check:release-candidate`. The Docker aggregate
runs CI gates first, then the two Docker-specific smokes:

```sh
pnpm check:release-candidate           # CI-equivalent gates (no Docker)
pnpm check:release-candidate:local     # above + mutation:contracts
pnpm check:release-candidate:docker    # CI gates + Docker gates (full docker release)
```

The machine-readable gate manifest lives at
`tests/e2e/distribution/release-gate-matrix.json`.

## Rollback and Retry

**npm**: npm does not support unpublish after 24 hours for scoped public packages.
Use `npm deprecate @kamiazya/whiteboard-mcp@<version> "use <next-version>"` to
mark a broken release deprecated rather than removing it.

To re-publish a corrected tarball for the same version, you must bump the version
(create a new Release PR via release-please). For hotfixes, use a patch bump
(`mcp-server-v0.1.1`).

**Docker**: GHCR images can be deleted or retracted via the GitHub Package management
UI or the GitHub API. Coordinate with any downstream users before removing an image.

**Force-publish via release.yml**: Use `force_publish_tag` input to re-run publishing
for an existing tag (e.g., after a transient OIDC failure or a failed image push). The
`publish_npm` and `publish_docker` booleans (both default on) choose which halves run, so
either can be retried alone: `npm publish` fails on a version npm already has, so retry
only a failed image push with `publish_npm` off, and `docker-publish-sign` re-tags
`latest` when it runs. A dispatch with no tag runs neither. The tag must match
`mcp-server-v<semver>` and the `production-npm` and `production-docker` environments
must approve.

Dispatch a forced publish **from the tag itself**:
`gh workflow run release.yml --ref <tag> -f force_publish_tag=<tag>`. npm provenance,
the image's provenance and the cosign certificate all name the commit and ref the run
was dispatched from, so both `build-mcp` and `build-docker` fail right after
checkout when the checked-out tag is a different commit, or when the run was dispatched
from any ref but `refs/tags/<tag>`, and neither publish job starts — a dispatch from `main` would otherwise publish the
tag's tarball and image under `main`'s identity, even at the tag's own commit.

## Placeholder Gate Policy

Two root scripts remain fail-closed placeholders:

```
publish:npm-provenance  →  exits 1 with "[publish:npm-provenance] not implemented"
publish:docker-sign     →  exits 1 with "[publish:docker-sign] not implemented"
```

These scripts exist in `package.json` as reservations for future locally-runnable
publish gates. They are referenced as `futureGateId` values in
`tests/e2e/distribution/supply-chain-policy.json`.

**Why they remain placeholders**: A publish gate that exits 1 unconditionally
cannot be used in the release gate matrix. Adding a failing script to the matrix
would block every `pnpm check:release-candidate` run. The gate will be promoted
to a real entry in `release-gate-matrix.json` only when the script becomes a
deterministic, non-destructive runnable gate (e.g., a dry-run validator that
checks credentials are present and reports readiness without actually publishing).

---

## Why `implementedNow` Remains `false`

`tests/e2e/distribution/supply-chain-policy.json` has `implementedNow: false` for
`npm-tarball` and `docker-image` artifacts.

`implementedNow: true` would imply that a runnable gate script exists in
`release-gate-matrix.json` for the publish step. It does not — the actual publish
runs inside GitHub Actions with OIDC tokens that are unavailable locally. Setting
`implementedNow: true` before a locally-runnable, fail-safe gate script exists
would create a false policy signal and cause drift tests to fail (the gate would
be expected in the matrix but the placeholder script would break it).

The flag will be flipped to `true` when:
- A non-destructive, locally-runnable `publish:npm-provenance` script exists
  (e.g., it validates publish prerequisites and reports readiness without publishing),
- AND that script is added to `release-gate-matrix.json` under the `publish` tier.

# Pull Request Review Checklist

Use this checklist when reviewing or self-reviewing a pull request in this repository.

## Correctness

- [ ] The change does what the PR description says it does.
- [ ] Edge cases and error paths are handled.
- [ ] No regression against existing tests; all CI checks pass.

## Tests

- [ ] At least one nearest-layer test covers the root cause or new behavior.
- [ ] Tests follow the red-first TDD loop (written before the implementation).
- [ ] The correct test layer is used (`mcp-node` / apps/web jsdom / `web-browser` / E2E).
- [ ] No test has been weakened or deleted to make the build pass.

## Schema and contracts

- [ ] Any cross-boundary contract (MCP tool, HTTP route, persisted JSON, SSE sync frame) is backed by a Zod schema.
- [ ] Types are derived via `z.infer<>` — no hand-written parallel interfaces.
- [ ] If a new MCP tool is added, `pnpm smoke:e2e` is extended to call it at least once.

## Code quality

- [ ] Server code uses `getLogger(...)` — no `console.*` calls in `src/server/**`.
- [ ] Updates are immutable — no in-place mutation of inputs.
- [ ] Files stay under 800 lines — source and test alike, each held by its own shrink-only grandfather list in `tools/arch-lint/src/file-size-budget.test.ts`. Test files get the same budget rather than a higher one, because measured across this repo they run only 1.09-1.17x the size of source files at every percentile; the guard's own header carries the table. Functions stay under 50 lines, held the same way by `tools/arch-lint/src/function-size-budget.test.ts` beside it — a separate guard because a function's boundaries need an AST, and a separate CLASS of debt because a file budget is satisfied by moving mass between files while the long function survives whole. In both, an entry is a ceiling the subject must stay under, and a ceiling may stand at most a tenth (or 25 lines, whichever is more) above the current reading — `tools/arch-lint/src/size-ledger-headroom.ts` says why — so paying debt off lowers the number on the record rather than leaving room for it to grow back unseen.
- [ ] Comments explain the enduring *why*, not the narrative of how the PR came about.

## Documentation

- [ ] User-visible changes are documented in `docs/` (Diataxis quadrants).
- [ ] Developer-facing changes are reflected in root OSS files or `docs/contributing/`.
- [ ] No aspirational documentation — docs describe the shipped state only.

## Security

- [ ] No secrets or credentials are hardcoded.
- [ ] User input is validated at system boundaries.
- [ ] Auth paths are reviewed if touched.

## Commit hygiene

- [ ] Commits are logically split by concern (not one monolithic squash).
- [ ] Commit messages follow Conventional Commits (`feat:`, `fix:`, `chore:`, etc.).
- [ ] PR title is a valid Conventional Commit title (used as the squash-merge commit message).

# Security baseline: the OpenSSF control matrix

This page records, control by control, where Whiteboard stands against the
OpenSSF supply-chain guidance and the standards it builds on: what is met and
where the evidence is, what is a gap the repository itself can close, and what
only the repository owner can do because it lives in GitHub settings, in an
account or in a decision about the project.

It is a record of the current state, not an aspiration. A row says **met**
only where a file, a workflow or a guard test shows it; a control whose
evidence sits in a setting nobody could read is marked as such.

Statuses:

| status | meaning |
|---|---|
| **met** | satisfied today; the evidence column says where |
| **gap-technical** | not satisfied, and closable by a change to this repository |
| **gap-owner** | not satisfied, and closable only by the owner (a setting, an account, an application or a project decision) |
| **planned** | arrives with the Rust core ([ADR-0054](adr/0054-rust-core.md); requirements QR-27 to QR-29 in the [development quality requirements](quality-requirements.md)) |
| **n/a** | does not apply, with the reason |

## Sources

Each standard was read at its current version on 2026-11-06.

| standard | version read | what it is used for here |
|---|---|---|
| [OpenSSF Scorecard checks](https://github.com/ossf/scorecard/blob/main/docs/checks.md) | v5.6.0 | the automated score; measured locally below |
| [OpenSSF Security Baseline (OSPS Baseline)](https://baseline.openssf.org/versions/2026-08-28) | 2026-08-28 | the control set, levels 1 to 3 |
| [OpenSSF Best Practices Badge criteria](https://www.bestpractices.dev/en/criteria) | criteria as of 2026-11 | passing in full; silver and gold summarised |
| [Concise Guide for Developing More Secure Software](https://best.openssf.org/Concise-Guide-for-Developing-More-Secure-Software) | 2023-06-14 edition | the 29-item checklist the other guides refine |
| [npm Best Practices Guide](https://github.com/ossf/package-manager-best-practices/blob/main/published/npm.md) | main branch | lockfile, install, publishing and provenance practice |
| [SCM Platform Configuration Best Practices](https://best.openssf.org/SCM-BestPractices/) | main branch | branch protection, access and CI settings |
| [SLSA](https://slsa.dev/spec/v1.2/) | v1.2 | the Build track levels |
| [NIST SP 800-218 (SSDF)](https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/sp/800/218/final) | v1.1 (Feb 2022); [Rev. 1 draft, v1.2](https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/sp/800/218/r1/ipd) (Dec 2025) | the practice groups worth tracking |
| [CISA Secure by Design pledge](https://www.cisa.gov/securebydesign/pledge) | May 2024 | the seven goals, read for a single-maintainer open-source project |
| [ANSSI secure Rust guide](https://anssi-fr.github.io/rust-guide/) | current web edition | the Rust rules the core will follow |

## Measured: OpenSSF Scorecard, local run

The repository had never been scored: `api.scorecard.dev` answered 404.
`.github/workflows/scorecard.yml` now runs Scorecard weekly and publishes the
result. Before that, Scorecard v5.6.0 was run locally over this tree
(`scorecard --local=. --format=json`); the checks that need the GitHub API
(Branch-Protection, CI-Tests, CII-Best-Practices, Code-Review, Contributors,
Maintained, SBOM's release half, Signed-Releases, Webhooks) cannot run that way
and are judged from the REST API and the workflows instead.

| check | local score | status | evidence / fix / owner action |
|---|---|---|---|
| Binary-Artifacts | 10 | met | no binaries in the tree |
| Branch-Protection | API only | gap-owner | the REST API shows `main` protected with four required status checks (`build`, `pr-title`, `ci-gate`, `CodeQL`) enforced for everyone; the review settings were not readable (HTTP 403). Owner: confirm or enable a ruleset on `main` requiring a pull request, blocking force pushes and deletion, dismissing stale approvals, and applying to administrators |
| CI-Tests | API only | met | `ci.yml` runs on every pull request; `ci-gate` is required |
| CII-Best-Practices | API only | gap-owner | no badge yet. The application data is prepared [below](#best-practices-badge-application-data); applying is the owner's |
| Code-Review | API only | gap-owner | merges are by the single maintainer; AI review is not a human approval. Closes only with a second human reviewer |
| Contributors | API only | n/a | counts contributors from distinct organisations; nothing in the repository can change it |
| Dangerous-Workflow | 10 | met | no `pull_request_target` checkout of PR code; untrusted values read through `env:`; held by `preview-pr-deploy-label.test.ts` and `workflow-credentials.test.ts`, and by zizmor on every PR (below) |
| Dependency-Update-Tool | 10 | met | `.github/dependabot.yml` (npm and GitHub Actions, with cooldowns) |
| Fuzzing | 10 | met, partly | Scorecard credits the fast-check property suites. A coverage-guided fuzzer exists — cargo-fuzz in `crates/fuzz`, run on pull requests and nightly — with one template target so far; every untrusted-input entry gets a target as it is ported (QR-29a to QR-29e) |
| License | 9 | met | `LICENSE` is Apache-2.0, which the GitHub API reports. The local 9 is an artefact of local mode, which cannot ask the API for the licence identifier |
| Maintained | API only | met | commits weekly; the repository is older than the 90 days the check requires |
| Packaging | 10 | met | `release.yml` publishes to npm and GHCR |
| Pinned-Dependencies | 8 | gap-technical | every action is SHA-pinned (`workflow-supply-chain.test.ts`, repo-wide). `Dockerfile.server`'s two `FROM node:${NODE_VERSION}-slim` base images are not pinned by digest (Scorecard reports four lines, counting the two stages built on them). Fix: pin by digest through a build argument the release resolves from `.node-version`, and add the `docker` ecosystem to Dependabot so the digest is refreshed rather than frozen |
| SAST | 0 locally | met | CodeQL (default setup) is a required check on `main`; local mode cannot see check runs, which is the whole 0 |
| SBOM | API only | gap-technical | a CycloneDX SBOM is generated in CI (`sbom-npm`) and in every release run, and the container image carries an SBOM attestation, but no SBOM is attached to the GitHub release, which is where Scorecard awards the second half. Fix: attach `npm-sbom.cdx.json` to the release (see Signed-Releases) |
| Security-Policy | 10 | met | `SECURITY.md` |
| Signed-Releases | API only | gap-technical | the npm package is published with provenance and the image is cosign-signed, but the GitHub releases carry no assets (0 on each of the last three), and Scorecard reads only those. Fix: a release job that uploads the SBOM, a `SHA256SUMS` file and the provenance bundle to the GitHub release; it is the same job QR-27b requires for the native binaries |
| Token-Permissions | 8 | met | every workflow declares a root `permissions:` block granting no write, writes are per job (`workflow-supply-chain.test.ts`). The 8 was `release.yml` (no root block) and `preview-cleanup.yml` (root `deployments: write`), both fixed. The job-level writes left are the ones a job exists for: release-please and the stable-tag push (`contents: write`), the preview deployment records (`deployments: write`) |
| Vulnerabilities | 10 | met | no open OSV advisory; the two suppressed ones are published as VEX (below) |
| Webhooks | API only | gap-owner | needs admin read. Owner: any webhook should use a secret |

## Workflow static analysis: zizmor

`ci.yml`'s `zizmor` job runs [zizmor](https://docs.zizmor.sh) 1.32.0 at
its `regular` persona on every pull request and push to `main`, and fails the
job on a finding (template injection, credential persistence, dangerous
triggers, excessive permissions, and impostor commits behind a pinned SHA).
Locally: `uvx zizmor@1.32.0 .github/`. The configuration is
`.github/zizmor.yml`; `workflow-supply-chain.test.ts` holds that the job fails
rather than uploading, at a pinned version, with a read-only token.

Measured over `.github/` on 2026-11-06, the `regular` persona raised three
findings outside `ci.yml`, all deliberate and now suppressed with the reason
beside each: the stable-tag job's persisted checkout token, the privileged
`workflow_run` half of the preview build/deploy split, and the setup action's
exact-pinned corepack install. Its `self-repository` suggestion (24 sites, 13
of them in `ci.yml`) is disabled in the config, because the guards name the
local action by its `./` path. Status: **met**, and a gate: the job is one of
`ci-gate`'s `needs`, the one required check, so a finding blocks the merge.

The stricter `auditor` persona, which gates nothing here, adds what is worth
knowing: `RELEASE_PLEASE_TOKEN` and `SONAR_TOKEN` are repository secrets used
outside a deployment environment (gap-owner: move each into an environment
bound to its one job), and constant-valued expressions such as
`${{ matrix.shard }}` are expanded inline in `run:` blocks, eight lines in
`ci.yml` and one in `sonarqube.yml` — not exploitable, since none carries
attacker-controlled text, but passing them through `env:` would make the
auditor persona clean too.

## OSPS Baseline (2026-08-28)

### Level 1

| control | requirement, in short | status | evidence / fix / owner action |
|---|---|---|---|
| OSPS-AC-01.01 | MFA for access to sensitive resources | gap-owner | Owner: require 2FA on the account (and on any organisation that later owns the repository) and on npm |
| OSPS-AC-02.01 | new collaborators get least privilege by default | gap-owner | a GitHub setting; owner to confirm the base permission is read |
| OSPS-AC-03.01 | direct commits to the primary branch are prevented | gap-owner | required status checks block a direct push today; owner to confirm "require a pull request" is on (see Branch-Protection) |
| OSPS-AC-03.02 | deleting the primary branch requires confirmation | gap-owner | owner to confirm deletion is restricted in the ruleset |
| OSPS-BR-01.01 | untrusted CI metadata is sanitised | met | branch names and PR fields read through `env:` and normalised (`preview_label()`); `preview-pr-deploy-label.test.ts` |
| OSPS-BR-01.03 | untrusted code cannot reach privileged credentials | met | preview build and deploy are split across `pull_request` and `workflow_run`; the deploy job fetches nothing unlocked (`workflow-hygiene.test.ts`, `workflow-credentials.test.ts`) |
| OSPS-BR-03.01 | official channels are encrypted | met | GitHub, npm, GHCR and the hosted app are HTTPS only |
| OSPS-BR-03.02 | distribution channels are authenticated | met | npm and GHCR over TLS, with provenance and signatures |
| OSPS-BR-07.01 | secrets are kept out of version control | met, partly | `secretlint` blocks a staged secret at pre-commit (`lefthook.yml`). Fix: run it in CI too, since a hook can be skipped (an integrator item for `ci.yml`). Owner: enable GitHub secret scanning push protection |
| OSPS-DO-01.01 | user guides for basic functionality | met | `docs/tutorials`, `docs/how-to` |
| OSPS-DO-02.01 | a guide for reporting defects | met | `.github/ISSUE_TEMPLATE/bug_report.yml` |
| OSPS-GV-02.01 | a public discussion mechanism | met | GitHub issues and pull requests |
| OSPS-GV-03.01 | the contribution process is documented | met | `CONTRIBUTING.md` |
| OSPS-LE-02.01 | source licence is OSI-approved | met | Apache-2.0 |
| OSPS-LE-02.02 | released-asset licence is OSI-approved | met | the same licence; the npm tarball's `license` field |
| OSPS-LE-03.01 | licence file in the repository | met | `LICENSE` |
| OSPS-LE-03.02 | licence shipped with released assets | met | `packages/mcp-server/LICENSE`, checked into the tarball by `verify-pack-contents` |
| OSPS-QA-01.01 | repository publicly readable at a static URL | met | `https://github.com/kamiazya/whiteboard` |
| OSPS-QA-01.02 | public record of changes, authors and times | met | git history |
| OSPS-QA-02.01 | dependency list for direct dependencies | met | each `package.json` and `pnpm-lock.yaml` |
| OSPS-QA-04.01 | list of codebases when there are several | n/a | one repository |
| OSPS-QA-05.01 | no generated executables in version control | met | Scorecard Binary-Artifacts 10 |
| OSPS-QA-05.02 | no unreviewable binaries in version control | met | the binaries tracked are PNG images (documentation and screenshot fixtures) and TTF font files; none is a build output |
| OSPS-VM-02.01 | security contacts documented | met | `SECURITY.md` (private vulnerability reporting) and `.github/CODEOWNERS` |

### Level 2

| control | requirement, in short | status | evidence / fix / owner action |
|---|---|---|---|
| OSPS-AC-04.01 | a task with no permissions specified gets the lowest | met | every workflow declares a root block, and none grants a write there (`workflow-supply-chain.test.ts`) |
| OSPS-BR-02.01 | each release has a unique version | met | release-please, semver tags |
| OSPS-BR-04.01 | each release has a log of functional and security changes | met | `CHANGELOG.md`, `packages/mcp-server/CHANGELOG.md`; advisories linked from the fixing release (`SECURITY.md`) |
| OSPS-BR-05.01 | standard tooling to ingest dependencies | met | pnpm with `--frozen-lockfile`, `npm ci` for the deploy tooling |
| OSPS-BR-06.01 | releases signed or in a signed manifest | met | npm provenance (Sigstore), cosign keyless signature and attestations on the image |
| OSPS-DO-06.01 | how dependencies are selected, obtained and tracked | met | [Dependencies](#dependencies-how-they-are-selected-obtained-and-tracked) below |
| OSPS-DO-07.01 | build instructions | met | `CONTRIBUTING.md` quick start, [development](development.md) |
| OSPS-GV-01.01 | list of members with access to sensitive resources | gap-owner | drafted in [Project members](#project-members-and-roles) from `CODEOWNERS`; collaborators were not readable here, so the owner confirms the list |
| OSPS-GV-01.02 | roles and responsibilities | gap-owner | drafted in the same section; the owner confirms it |
| OSPS-GV-03.02 | contributor guide with acceptance requirements | met | `CONTRIBUTING.md` (pull request checklist, commit rules), [review-checklist](review-checklist.md) |
| OSPS-LE-01.01 | contributors assert authorisation on every commit | gap-owner | no DCO or CLA. A decision first (DCO sign-off is the usual choice); enforcement is then the DCO GitHub App or a check over `Signed-off-by` trailers |
| OSPS-QA-03.01 | status checks pass before merging to the primary branch | met | four required checks, enforced for everyone |
| OSPS-QA-06.01 | CI runs automated tests before a change is accepted | met | `ci.yml`, aggregated in the required `ci-gate` |
| OSPS-SA-01.01 | design documentation of actions and actors | met | [explanation/architecture](../explanation/architecture.md), [explanation/security-model](../explanation/security-model.md) |
| OSPS-SA-02.01 | external software interfaces described | met | `docs/reference/` (configuration, export formats, the `x-whiteboard` schema), [architecture/wire-protocol](architecture/wire-protocol.md) |
| OSPS-SA-03.01 | a security assessment | met | [explanation/security-model](../explanation/security-model.md), with its "Current limitations" |
| OSPS-VM-01.01 | CVD policy with a response timeframe | met | `SECURITY.md` (72-hour acknowledgement, 14-day high-severity target, coordinated disclosure) |
| OSPS-VM-03.01 | private vulnerability reporting | met | GitHub private vulnerability reporting is enabled (REST API: `enabled: true`) |
| OSPS-VM-04.01 | discovered vulnerabilities published | met | the GitHub Security Advisory process in `SECURITY.md`; no advisory has been needed yet |

### Level 3

| control | requirement, in short | status | evidence / fix / owner action |
|---|---|---|---|
| OSPS-AC-04.02 | jobs get only the privileges they need | met | per-job grants; `ci-policy.test.ts` scopes `packages: write` to one job, `workflow-supply-chain.test.ts` scopes `id-token: write` in the Scorecard workflow |
| OSPS-BR-01.04 | trusted collaborator input is validated | met | `release.yml`'s `force_publish_tag` is read through `env:` and checked against the checked-out tag and the dispatched ref before anything publishes |
| OSPS-BR-02.02 | assets associated with the release identifier | met | the npm version and the image tag are the release tag's version |
| OSPS-BR-07.02 | a policy for managing secrets | gap-owner | the practice is written down in [Secrets](#secrets) below; a rotation cadence is the owner's to set |
| OSPS-DO-03.01 | instructions to verify integrity and authenticity | met | `SECURITY.md` "Verifying a release"; the cosign verification commands in [releasing](releasing.md) |
| OSPS-DO-03.02 | instructions to verify the release author's identity | met | the cosign certificate identity and the npm provenance's workflow identity, in the same places |
| OSPS-DO-04.01 | scope and duration of support per release | met | `SECURITY.md` "Supported Versions" |
| OSPS-DO-05.01 | when releases stop receiving security updates | met | the same table: a version stops when a newer one is published |
| OSPS-GV-04.01 | collaborators reviewed before escalated permissions | gap-owner | a policy only the owner can adopt; suggested text in [Project members](#project-members-and-roles) |
| OSPS-QA-02.02 | compiled released assets ship with an SBOM | met, planned | the image carries an SBOM attestation; the npm package is not compiled. The native binaries get `cargo auditable` plus a CycloneDX SBOM (QR-27a) |
| OSPS-QA-04.02 | subprojects as strict as the primary codebase | n/a | one repository |
| OSPS-QA-06.02 | when and how tests run is documented | met | [testing](testing.md), `CONTRIBUTING.md` |
| OSPS-QA-06.03 | a policy that major changes add or update tests | met | test-first workflow in `AGENTS.md`, [testing](testing.md) |
| OSPS-QA-07.01 | one non-author human approval before merging | gap-owner | needs a second human maintainer |
| OSPS-SA-03.02 | threat model and attack surface analysis | met | [explanation/security-model](../explanation/security-model.md) — trust boundaries and protections per runtime |
| OSPS-VM-04.02 | non-affecting vulnerabilities in a VEX document | met | `.github/security/whiteboard.openvex.json`, held equal to the audit suppressions by `vex-audit-ignores.test.ts` |
| OSPS-VM-05.01 | threshold for remediating SCA findings | gap-technical | `SECURITY.md` "Remediation thresholds" sets the vulnerability threshold; no license-finding threshold is stated yet |
| OSPS-VM-05.02 | SCA violations addressed before any release | gap-technical | `release.yml` audits the lockfile and the packed tarball before the npm package publishes; the container image (`docker-publish-sign` needs `build-docker`, not the audit) and the web deploy are not gated on an audit |
| OSPS-VM-05.03 | every change checked for vulnerable or malicious dependencies, and blocked | met | `pnpm audit:prod` in CI, `ci.yml`'s `dependency-review` job on every PR (one of `ci-gate`'s `needs`, so it blocks; it skips on push to main, which `ci-gate` declares), and `minimumReleaseAge` (seven days) in `pnpm-workspace.yaml` against a freshly published malicious version |
| OSPS-VM-06.01 | threshold for remediating SAST findings | met | `SECURITY.md` "Remediation thresholds" |
| OSPS-VM-06.02 | every change checked for weaknesses, and blocked | met | CodeQL is a required check |

## Best Practices Badge

### Passing

The passing level has 67 active criteria. "attest" means the criterion is a
statement the owner makes on the application form; the evidence is what to
point it at.

| criterion | status | evidence |
|---|---|---|
| description_good, interact, contribution, contribution_requirements | met | `README.md`, `CONTRIBUTING.md` |
| floss_license, floss_license_osi, license_location | met | Apache-2.0, `LICENSE` |
| documentation_basics, documentation_interface | met | `docs/`, `docs/reference/` |
| sites_https, english | met | GitHub, npm, the hosted app; all docs in English |
| discussion, maintained | met | issues and pull requests; weekly commits |
| repo_public, repo_track, repo_interim, repo_distributed | met | public git repository; pull requests carry interim work |
| version_unique, version_semver, version_tags | met | release-please, semver tags |
| release_notes, release_notes_vulns | met | the changelogs; advisories linked from the fixing release (`SECURITY.md`) |
| report_process, report_tracker, report_responses, enhancement_responses, report_archive | met, attest | issue templates; the public issue tracker is the archive. The owner attests response practice |
| vulnerability_report_process, vulnerability_report_private, vulnerability_report_response | met | `SECURITY.md`; private reporting enabled; 72-hour acknowledgement |
| build, build_common_tools, build_floss_tools | met | pnpm, TypeScript, Vite, tsdown |
| test, test_invocation, test_most, test_continuous_integration | met | vitest, `pnpm test`, CI on every PR |
| test_policy, tests_are_added, tests_documented_added | met | `AGENTS.md`, `CONTRIBUTING.md`, [testing](testing.md) |
| warnings, warnings_fixed, warnings_strict | met | `tsc` strict, Biome with `--error-on-warnings` |
| know_secure_design, know_common_errors | attest | owner attests; [explanation/security-model](../explanation/security-model.md) is the evidence of applied knowledge |
| crypto_published, crypto_call, crypto_floss, crypto_keylength, crypto_working, crypto_weaknesses, crypto_pfs, crypto_random | met, attest | platform crypto only (WebCrypto, `node:crypto`, WebAuthn passkeys, TLS left to the platform or the operator); nothing hand-rolled |
| crypto_password_storage | n/a | no passwords are stored; authentication is by passkey and bearer credential (security model) |
| delivery_mitm, delivery_unsigned | met | HTTPS delivery; npm provenance, cosign signatures |
| vulnerabilities_fixed_60_days, vulnerabilities_critical_fixed | met | no open advisory; audits gate merges and releases |
| no_leaked_credentials | met | `secretlint` pre-commit; publishing uses OIDC with no stored npm token |
| static_analysis, static_analysis_common_vulnerabilities, static_analysis_fixed, static_analysis_often | met | CodeQL on every PR, Biome |
| dynamic_analysis, dynamic_analysis_unsafe, dynamic_analysis_enable_assertions, dynamic_analysis_fixed | met | property-based tests with fast-check, browser and end-to-end suites; the memory-unsafe half is n/a for TypeScript, and for Rust is the nightly fuzz run under AddressSanitizer with `--careful` (QR-28f) |

Nothing at the passing level is a technical gap; the only remaining step is
the application itself.

### Silver and gold

Of the criteria above passing, these do not hold today:

- **Owner decisions or people**: `dco` (silver; see OSPS-LE-01.01),
  `governance` and `roles_responsibilities` (silver; see Project members),
  `access_continuity` and `bus_factor` (silver; gold requires two people who
  could carry the project on), `two_person_review` and `require_2FA` (gold),
  `contributors_unassociated` (gold), `security_review` (gold).
- **Technical**: `documentation_roadmap` (silver; no public roadmap page),
  `signed_releases` in the GitHub-release sense (silver; the Signed-Releases
  fix above), `test_statement_coverage80` (silver) and
  `test_statement_coverage90`/`test_branch_coverage80` (gold; `pnpm coverage`
  measures but sets no floor — the Rust side gets floors in QR-18),
  `build_reproducible` (gold; planned for the binaries, QR-28e),
  `copyright_per_file`/`license_per_file` (gold; no SPDX headers), and
  `hardening`/`hardened_site` (gold; not yet assessed against the criteria).

## Best Practices badge application data

The application at <https://www.bestpractices.dev/en/projects/new> asks for
the following. Everything here can be pasted as it stands.

| field | value |
|---|---|
| project name | Whiteboard |
| description | A local-first whiteboard and document workspace, with an MCP server (`@kamiazya/whiteboard-mcp`) that lets AI assistants read and edit it |
| homepage / repository | `https://github.com/kamiazya/whiteboard` |
| licence | Apache-2.0 |
| contribution | `https://github.com/kamiazya/whiteboard/blob/main/CONTRIBUTING.md` |
| vulnerability report process | `https://github.com/kamiazya/whiteboard/blob/main/SECURITY.md` |
| build | `pnpm install --frozen-lockfile && pnpm build` |
| tests | `pnpm test`; CI: `https://github.com/kamiazya/whiteboard/actions/workflows/ci.yml` |
| static analysis | CodeQL (required check), Biome |
| release notes | `CHANGELOG.md`, `packages/mcp-server/CHANGELOG.md` |

Once the project has an id, the README badge is
`[![OpenSSF Best Practices](https://www.bestpractices.dev/projects/<id>/badge)](https://www.bestpractices.dev/projects/<id>)`.
The Scorecard badge,

## CISA Secure by Design pledge

Read for an open-source project with a single maintainer, the seven goals map
as follows: **MFA** is OSPS-AC-01.01 (gap-owner). **Default passwords** do not
exist: the daemon is reached over an owner-only socket and server mode defers
to the operator's identity provider. **Reducing classes of vulnerability** is
the move to a memory-safe Rust core ([ADR-0054](adr/0054-rust-core.md)) with
`unsafe` forbidden. **Security patches** reach users through the npm `latest`
tag and the image's `latest`. **A vulnerability disclosure policy** is
`SECURITY.md`. **CVE transparency** is the advisory process, with a CWE in each
advisory. **Evidence of intrusions** is out of scope for a local-first tool;
server mode logs through the daemon's structured logger, which the operator
collects.

# Testing Strategy

This document is the canonical reference for testing philosophy, layer selection,
property-based testing, mutation testing, and quality gates in this repo.

- [CONTRIBUTING.md](../../CONTRIBUTING.md) — contributor workflow (quick-start, commits, lint, release)
- [AGENTS.md](../../AGENTS.md) — agent-specific operational rules (MCP dev mode, Zod discipline, PR rules)

---

## Philosophy

Passing tests alone are not sufficient. The workflow is:

1. Write the smallest failing test at the nearest layer.
2. Make the smallest patch that turns it green.
3. Manually verify the real behavior (browser, MCP smoke, or daemon log).
4. Lock the verified flow into `canvas-viewer-browser`/`web-browser` or E2E coverage.

Skip step 3 only for pure helper changes with no observable runtime effect. Skip step 4 only when the verified scenario is already covered by an existing automation.

---

## Standard Workflow

```bash
# 1. Run the narrowest project first
pnpm test --project mcp-node
pnpm --filter @kamiazya/whiteboard-web test   # apps/web jsdom, when the change touches UI

# 2. After targeted test passes, run the broader gate for the touched area
#    (not the whole repo: CI runs every suite your change reaches;
#    `pnpm test:affected` runs that same selection locally)
pnpm check:local         # every gate CI's check job runs
pnpm test:browser        # for browser-mode changes (canvas-viewer-browser + web-browser + canvas-render-browser + web-browser-window-state)
pnpm smoke:e2e           # for MCP tool / route / protocol changes
pnpm test:e2e:distribution # for packaged daemon / tarball / binary behavior (spends API quota: it chains the claude and codex CLI smokes, which skip when the CLI is absent)
```

A pull request that touches test files also runs CI's `stress-changed-tests` job: every changed
test file five times in fresh processes, then once with `--repeats=3` in one process, once for the
browser projects and once for the rest. A test that passes alone but leaves state behind for its own
next repetition (a fixed id seeded into IndexedDB with no per-test reset, say) is first seen red
there. `node .claude/scripts/stress-changed.mjs` runs the same thing locally against the files
changed since `origin/main` (`--base=<ref>` to change the base, `--only=node` or `--only=browser`
for one leg, `--dry-run` to print the plan); a test in `tools/arch-lint` keeps it in step with the
job.

vitest writes transformed-module copies to `<tmpdir>/<21-char id>/ssr` (and `client/`). Each
project's directory is removed when the run closes, but a run through a single config with no
`projects` array leaves its directory behind even when it passes — 3 to 80 MB a run. So every
package's `test` script is a bare `vitest run` over an aggregate `vitest.config.ts`, and
`apps/web`'s wrapper runs each half through `vitest.suite.config.ts`;
`tools/arch-lint/src/package-test-script.test.ts` holds both. `vitest run --config
vitest.node.config.ts` by hand still leaks, and so does any run killed before it closes, the root
config's included. `node .claude/scripts/cleanup-worktrees.mjs` sweeps the ones nothing has written
to for a day (`--dry-run` lists them).

---

## Test Layer Selection

Choose the **narrowest** layer that can prove the behavior:

| Layer | Config | When to use |
|---|---|---|
| `mcp-node` | `vitest.node.config.ts` (`packages/mcp-server`) | Pure functions, stores, routes, server behavior, persistence logic, schemas, CLI helpers |
| `arch-lint-node` | `vitest.node.config.ts` (`tools/arch-lint`) | A guard over files that belong to no one package: workflows, the Dockerfile, root manifests, docs, the rule corpus, `apps/web`'s source, and the architecture boundaries. It reads text and runs no product code, so it runs at pre-push and in CI's `test-shared` on every change. A test under `packages/*/src` that reads a repo-root file belongs here unless `repo-root-reads.test.ts` lists it with a reason |
| `canvas-viewer-node` / `canvas-viewer-jsdom` | `vitest.node.config.ts` / `vitest.jsdom.config.ts` (`packages/canvas-viewer`) | `packages/canvas-viewer` parsing, hooks, and components when browser layout and pointer behavior are **not** the core risk |
| apps/web jsdom | `apps/web/vitest.config.ts` | React components and hooks when real layout, focus, pointer, or browser APIs are **not** the core risk |
| `web-browser` | `apps/web/vitest.browser.config.ts` | `apps/web` tests that need real browser APIs unavailable in jsdom: IndexedDB, OPFS, `window.showOpenFilePicker`, popovers/dialogs/focus/scroll/restore flows, and other platform APIs. File suffix: `.browser.test.tsx` |
| E2E | `tests/e2e/` | Real routes, server composition, sync-stream (SSE) timing, daemon process lifecycle, persistence order, packaging, or multi-step product journeys |

The UI lives solely in `apps/web` since the MCP-UI retirement (ADR 0001); `packages/mcp-server` is backend-only and has no jsdom/browser layer of its own.

**Promotion rules:**

- Do not jump to broad E2E first if a smaller failing test can isolate the bug.
- When an E2E catches a bug, add the nearest-layer test as well unless the root cause only exists at the composed-system boundary.
- Prefer `web-browser` over apps/web jsdom whenever the scenario involves focus, pointer, dialog, popover, scroll, or restore behavior.

**Server logs under `mcp-node`.** The suite drives refusals, corrupt rows and thrown handlers on
purpose, so `vitest.log-setup.ts` turns off the logger's default stderr destination for the
project: a passing run prints no pino records. Records still reach every other destination, so
assert on them with `captureLogsForTests(level)` (and `restore()` in `afterEach`). A test that
asserts on the line stderr itself receives opts back in with `setStderrLogDestination(true)` and
calls the restore it returns — the same call, in the failing test, shows its records while you
diagnose it. Only the test setup calls the switch; the daemon and the packaged entry always log to
stderr, and a process a test spawns keeps its own stderr.

---

## Property-Based Testing

Use PBT when the behavior is better described as an invariant over many inputs than as one fixed example.

**Prefer PBT for:**

- Process-boundary contracts: MCP tool schemas, HTTP response schemas, persisted JSON parsers
- Security boundaries: auth routing, Origin/CORS policy, path confinement, token redaction
- Migration and compatibility logic: old/new versions, malformed payloads, unknown fields
- State machines: browser document controller, daemon lifecycle, head/version state
- Concurrency and race risks: save/export/import ordering, late failures, retry/reload behavior

**File naming:**

- `*.property.test.ts` — invariant tests over generated inputs
- `*.model.test.ts` / `*.model.test.tsx` — model-based state-machine tests
- `*.race.test.ts` / `*.race.test.tsx` — scheduler or ordering tests

**Shared utilities:**

- Import `fc`, `fcTest` and `withDefaults` from the package's own `test-utils/fast-check.ts` (in `mcp-server`, `src/shared/test-utils/fast-check.ts`) instead of importing `fast-check` directly. Each of those files re-exports the one prelude in `@kamiazya/whiteboard-model/test-utils`, and `tools/arch-lint/src/fast-check-prelude-check.test.ts` fails a package that defines its own.
- Arbitraries that generate valid model values (nodes, edges, canvases, a schema's own `zod-arbitrary`) live in `packages/model/src/test-utils/` and are exported through that same `@kamiazya/whiteboard-model/test-utils` entry, so codec, canvas-render and the rest share them rather than copy them. An arbitrary that only one package needs stays in that package's `test-utils/`.

**Replayability:** Avoid `Math.random()`, wall-clock timing, real network, and unseeded global state inside generated runs.

---

## Mutation Testing

Use [StrykerJS](https://stryker-mutator.io/) for mutation testing on the configured target set.

```bash
pnpm mutation:contracts
```

This runs Stryker with `packages/mcp-server/stryker.config.mjs`, which uses a dedicated Vitest config (`vitest.stryker.config.ts`) to keep the dry run stable. **Do not use `vitest.stryker.config.ts` for normal test runs or CI** — use `vitest.node.config.ts` instead.

That config includes only the tests that can reach a mutated module — every test that imports one, directly or through the modules between — rather than the whole `mcp-node` suite. The set is computed from the source's import graph (`packages/mcp-server/scripts/mutation/covering-tests.mjs`) each time the config loads, so a test that starts importing a mutated module joins the lane without a list to edit. Stryker abandons the lane when its initial run outlasts `dryRunTimeoutMinutes` (set in the Stryker config, with the duration it was sized from) or when any test in that run fails, so a test that reads the machine it runs on cannot be in it.

### Purpose and scope

Mutation testing checks whether the current test suite notices plausible implementation changes. It is a complement to example tests and PBT, not a replacement.

Keep Stryker scope **narrow**:

- Intended for contract/helper surfaces: schemas, parsers, diagnostics redaction, path guards, small pure helpers.
- Do **not** expand runs to browser-mode, Playwright E2E, canvas-render/canvas-viewer SVG rendering, daemon lifecycle smokes, or broad React interaction flows unless a dedicated Stryker target is added for that surface.

### Survivor classification

When Stryker reports survived mutants, classify each one before acting:

| Class | Description | Action |
|---|---|---|
| **Real risk** | Mutant represents a behavior change a user or contract would notice | Add a deterministic regression or PBT property that kills it |
| **Equivalent** | Mutant produces identical observable behavior (e.g. `>= 0` vs `> -1` on integers) | Report as equivalent in PR body; no new test needed |
| **perTest-escaping** | Test suite does cover the line but Stryker's per-test coverage or related-test selection does not select the killing test | Document position; confirm with a focused manual check |
| **Intentionally permissive** | Contract deliberately allows a range of values that the mutant also satisfies | Note the intent in the PR body; no test needed |

Do not chase 100% mutation score as a product goal. Equivalent mutants and intentionally permissive contracts are normal.

### Target selection rules

Add a file to the mutation target set when:

- It implements a security boundary (auth, CORS, path confinement, token redaction).
- It parses or validates a cross-process contract (MCP schema, HTTP schema, persisted JSON).
- It implements a state-machine transition or diagnostic aggregation logic.
- Example and PBT coverage already exists and a mutation run would add clear signal.

Do **not** add browser-only components, Playwright helpers, daemon process orchestration, or files whose only tests are Stryker-incompatible (e.g. `vi.spyOn(process.stderr, 'write')` conflicts with Stryker's worker isolation).

### Production code policy

Treat surviving mutants as review input, not as automatic justification for changing production behavior. Before changing a parser or guard based on a mutation survivor:

1. Confirm the mutant represents a real product or contract risk (not an equivalent mutant).
2. Ensure the change is consistent with the stated contract and existing tests.
3. Add a concrete regression or PBT that would have caught the original gap.

If a surviving mutant reveals a gap but the production fix is out of scope for the current PR, file it as a whiteboard document of `type: issue` (see the `ticketing` skill, `.claude/skills/ticketing/SKILL.md`) and address it separately.

### Current mutation target set

The target list is not copied here, because a copy goes stale silently: the files that own it are `packages/mcp-server/stryker.config.mjs` (the `mutate` array run by `pnpm mutation:contracts`) and, for `canvas-render`'s separate lane, `packages/canvas-render/stryker-targets.mjs`. Both are guarded — `tools/arch-lint/src/stryker-targets.test.ts` fails on a `mutate` entry that names no file, and `canvas-render`'s `mutation-lane-coverage.test.ts` pins its list exactly.

## Browser Testing

The real-browser Vitest projects are below. `vitest.projects.json` holds the list the root `vitest.config.ts` registers; `docs-contract.test.ts` fails if this table stops naming one:

| Project | Package | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| `canvas-render-browser` | `packages/canvas-render` | Cross-platform SVG-serialization determinism: the same scene must render byte-identical SVG in a real browser as it does in `canvas-render-node` |
| `canvas-viewer-browser` | `packages/canvas-viewer` | Popovers, dialogs, scroll, focus, keyboard, pointer, and restore flows where browser layout and pointer behavior are the core risk |
| `web-browser` | `apps/web` | `apps/web` app browser regressions: popovers, dialogs, focus, keyboard, restore flows, and tests requiring real browser APIs unavailable in jsdom (IndexedDB, OPFS, `window.showOpenFilePicker`) |
| `web-browser-window-state` | `apps/web` | Tests that leave the browser WINDOW in a state the next file cannot tolerate (today: entering real fullscreen, after which Chromium refuses `page.viewport`). Named `*.window-state.browser.test.tsx` and run alone — the reason is in `apps/web/vitest.browser-window-state.config.ts` |

```bash
pnpm run test:browser         # canvas-viewer-browser + web-browser + canvas-render-browser + web-browser-window-state
pnpm run test:browser:replay  # same, plus a step-by-step DOM replay of EVERY test in .vitest/index.html
pnpm run test:browser:trace <one failing file>  # same projects, a Playwright trace for EVERY test and its DOM snapshots
```

The default run retains a Playwright trace only for a FAILING test, and that
trace has no DOM view — action log, stacks and screenshots, but no time-travel
through the page. Two ways to get one:

- `test:browser:replay` turns on vitest's `browser.traceView` and the HTML
  reporter: a DOM snapshot at every interaction and assertion, replayed in
  `.vitest/index.html` (open it in a browser) with the failed step in red.
  It records DOM snapshots rather than served resources, so it is cheap
  enough to cover every test: measured on `apps/web`'s 20 page files, the
  report data was 774KB gzipped with replays against 177KB without.
- `test:browser:trace` records Playwright's own DOM snapshots, which means
  every resource vite served — 302MB against 7.5MB on 16 page files and 22GB
  over a whole `web-browser` run. Use it for ONE failing file when the
  network log or the provider's screenshots are what you need. Before it
  starts, it asks `vitest list --filesOnly` what the same arguments select and
  refuses more than ten files (`tools/checks/src/browser-trace.mjs`) rather
  than start a run that can fill the disk — so `--testTimeout 60000` alone or
  a bare `apps/web` is refused, however the options are spelled.

**jsdom exclude policy**: apps/web's jsdom config must exclude `.browser.test.ts` and `.browser.test.tsx` files. Tests that depend on IndexedDB or other real browser APIs belong in `web-browser`, not jsdom. Mixing them causes silent no-op failures or missing-API errors.

Failure traces are stored under `<package>/tmp/vitest-traces` — `packages/canvas-render/tmp/vitest-traces` for `canvas-render-browser`, `packages/canvas-viewer/tmp/vitest-traces` for `canvas-viewer-browser`, `apps/web/tmp/vitest-traces` for `web-browser`. Check traces before adding temporary debug code. Remove temporary debug overlays and instrumentation before finishing.

In CI the runner is discarded with those files, so a browser job that fails uploads them as an artifact, kept for 7 days: `browser-traces-test-browser-<shard>-attempt-<n>` from `test-browser`, and `browser-traces-stress-changed-tests-attempt-<n>` from the browser leg of `stress-changed-tests`. A CI-only failure often prints nothing but the trace's path, with no source frame; the stack is in the trace. Fetch it with `gh run download <run-id> --pattern 'browser-traces-*'` and open the `.trace.zip` with `pnpm --filter @kamiazya/whiteboard-web exec playwright show-trace <file>`.

Prefer `web-browser` over apps/web jsdom whenever the scenario involves:
- Focus, pointer, keyboard, or scroll behavior
- Popover or dialog lifecycle (opening, closing, trap focus)
- Restore flows that depend on real DOM timing
- Any behavior where jsdom silently falls back to no-op
- IndexedDB, OPFS, or other real browser APIs not available in jsdom

---

## E2E Testing

Use E2E when the behavior depends on real app composition rather than an isolated unit, store, route helper, hook, or component seam.

**Prefer E2E for:**

- Real routes, server middleware, sync-stream (SSE) timing, daemon startup/shutdown, and persistence order
- Browser-to-daemon migration journeys
- Packaged CLI, tarball, binary, and install-layout behavior
- MCP protocol smoke flows that must validate the real server entrypoint
- User journeys where mocks would hide routing, runtime config injection, or process-boundary behavior

**Do not use E2E** for pure parsing, schema validation, isolated store logic, or component state testable in `mcp-node`, apps/web jsdom, or `web-browser`.

**E2E placement:**

- `tests/e2e/distribution/` — packaged daemon, server-mode, tarball, and install-layout smokes, plus the release-gate matrix that lists them (see its `README.md`). This is the only directory under `tests/e2e/` today.
- MCP protocol smokes are not under `tests/e2e/`: the shared implementations live in `packages/mcp-server/src/server/mcp/*.smoke-impl.ts` and the CLI wrappers in `packages/mcp-server/scripts/smoke/` (see Smoke & Distribution Tests below).
- Real-browser regressions are Vitest browser projects (see Browser Testing above); the one browser-driving smoke in the distribution chain is `pnpm smoke:read-plane`, listed in `tests/e2e/distribution/README.md`.

Keep E2E suites small and focused. If E2E finds a bug, add the nearest-layer regression unless the root cause only exists at the composed-system boundary.

---

## Smoke & Distribution Tests

MCP startup, protocol, and distribution-artifact smokes run as Vitest projects. The shared implementations under `src/server/mcp/*.smoke-impl.ts` and `*.distribution-impl.ts` are used by both the Vitest tests and the CLI wrappers listed under CLI wrapper scripts below. `pnpm smoke:e2e` is the exception: a standalone script with no Vitest counterpart (see its own section).

### `mcp-smoke` — included in `pnpm test`

Runs alongside `mcp-node` during normal `pnpm test`. No build prerequisite. The project runs with `maxWorkers: 1` (`packages/mcp-server/vitest.smoke.config.ts`), so each test's daemon process runs alone; the daemon listens on an owner-only socket rather than a TCP port (ADR-0050), so this is about process and data-dir contention, not port conflicts.

| Entry | What it covers |
|---|---|
| `pnpm smoke` | Startup-only: MCP server starts without fatal errors and stays alive for 3 s |
| `mcp-e2e-checkpoint.smoke.test.ts` | Checkpoint flow over stdio: `tools/list` equals `ALL_REGISTERED_TOOLS`, then `wb_workspace_edit` → `wb_facet_set` → `wb_version_save` / `wb_version_list` / `wb_version_restore` |

Run all mcp-smoke tests together:

```bash
pnpm --filter @kamiazya/whiteboard-mcp test:smoke    # vitest run --project mcp-smoke
```

### `pnpm smoke:e2e` — standalone script, NOT in `pnpm test`

`packages/mcp-server/scripts/smoke/mcp-e2e-smoke.mjs` is a node script, not a Vitest test: no project spawns it, so `pnpm test` and `test:smoke` never run it. CI runs it as its own step after `mcp-smoke`; run it yourself after an MCP tool or route change.
