# Connect the web app to a local daemon

The web app (`apps/web`) can run entirely in the browser with no daemon —
documents are stored in IndexedDB and never leave the device. This guide
covers connecting it to a local daemon (started with `whiteboard daemon run`),
and moving a workspace kept in your browser onto it.

## How the app reaches the daemon

The hosted app reaches a local daemon only through the **whiteboard browser
extension** ([ADR-0050](../contributing/adr/0050-local-daemon-trust.md)):

1. The page asks the extension.
2. The extension starts a small **native messaging host** — a program the
   `whiteboard` command registers with your browser.
3. The host relays the request to the daemon over the daemon's owner-only
   local socket, and adds the daemon's credential itself.

The daemon listens on **no network port**. On Linux and macOS it listens on
a Unix socket in your per-user runtime directory (`$XDG_RUNTIME_DIR/whiteboard/`,
or a `whiteboard-<uid>` directory under the system temp directory), readable
by you alone. On Windows it listens on a named pipe whose name is random per
start. Its record in the data directory (`daemon.json`, owner-only) says
where; the CLI, the stdio MCP entry and the native host all read it there.

The browser starts the native host only for the extension its manifest
names, so no web page and no other extension can take its place. A page
never talks to the daemon over HTTP, and the daemon serves no page of its
own.

**Without the extension**, the hosted app keeps its data in the browser, and
says that the extension is what connects it to a local daemon.

Running `whiteboard daemon run` interactively prints one line saying the
daemon is up (its pid and socket) and opens the hosted app in your
default browser once the daemon is listening. A script that needs to read
that line passes `--json`, which prints it as one JSON object instead. Pass `--no-open` (or set
`openBrowser: false` in a
[config file](../reference/configuration.md#config-file-local-daemon)) to
disable this. See
[Auto-opening the browser](../reference/configuration.md#auto-opening-the-browser-whiteboard-daemon-run)
for the conditions under which it is suppressed (CI, containers,
non-interactive shells).

A daemon that receives no request for 15 minutes stops on its own, unless a
page is still connected to it: an open tab keeps it running however long
nobody types. `whiteboard daemon run` then prints `whiteboard daemon stopped:
no request within its idle timeout.` to stderr and exits `0`; run it again to
continue.

After you upgrade `whiteboard`, a daemon that was already running keeps the old
build. `whiteboard daemon doctor --json` reports a `daemon.version` check as a
warning (the overall status is `warning` and the exit code stays `0`) when the
version in the daemon's record differs from the build you are running, and
points at `whiteboard daemon stop --json`. Stop it and start it again to pick
up the new one.

## When the daemon cannot be stopped or started

`whiteboard daemon status --json` says what the CLI makes of the daemon's
record (`daemon.json` in the data directory), in its `reason` field.
`whiteboard daemon doctor --json` reaches the same verdict and words it as a
finding with a remediation. `whiteboard daemon stop --json` and
`whiteboard daemon run` read the record the same way.

| `reason` | What it means | What to do |
|---|---|---|
| `null` (`ok: true`) | The daemon the record names is running. | Nothing. |
| `record-not-found` | There is no record: no daemon is running on this data directory. | `whiteboard daemon run` |
| `process-not-running` | The record names a process that has exited. | `whiteboard daemon run` starts over the record. `daemon stop` removes it. |
| `pid-reused` | The record's pid now belongs to a process that started after the record was written, and nothing accepts a connection on the record's socket. The daemon has gone. | `whiteboard daemon run` starts over the record. `daemon stop` removes it and signals nothing. |
| `identity-unconfirmed` | The record's pid looks like a later process, but something serves the record's socket and does not confirm that pid. It either answers as another process, or accepts the connection and gives no answer within 1.5 seconds. When the answer named its pid, `servingPid` gives it. | Stop the process serving the socket, then `whiteboard daemon run`. Use `servingPid` when it is present. Otherwise, find the socket's owner with `ss -xlp` or `lsof`. `daemon stop` refuses here: it signals nothing and keeps the record. |
| `record-token-missing` | The record has no token. When `pidAlive` is `true`, something still holds the record and this record cannot reach it. When `pidAlive` is `false`, the daemon has gone. | If `pidAlive` is `true`, stop that daemon with the build that started it. Otherwise, `whiteboard daemon run`. |
| `record-other-version` | This build cannot interpret the record, and the daemon it names is still there. Most likely, a daemon of another version wrote it. `record.version` gives that version when it can be read. | Stop that daemon with the version that started it, then `whiteboard daemon run`. Do **not** remove `daemon.json`: that daemon would keep serving with no record, so no build could stop it. `daemon run` would then fail on its socket. |
| `record-unreadable` | The record could not be read at all, so nothing is known of the daemon it may name. Most often the data directory is writable by other users or is a symlink, or `daemon.json` is a symlink, has another hard link, or belongs to another user. `recordFound` says whether a `daemon.json` is there. `daemon doctor` gives the exact cause in the finding's `detail`. | Fix what `detail` names, for example `chmod 700` on the data directory, then run `whiteboard daemon status` again. Do **not** remove `daemon.json`: the daemon it names may still be serving. |
| `record-malformed` | The record names no daemon, or this build cannot interpret it and the daemon it names has gone. | Remove `daemon.json`, then `whiteboard daemon run`. |

`pidAlive` means the same under every `reason` that carries it: `true` when
something may still hold the record, because the daemon it names is running or
something serves the record's socket. It is `false` when that process has
exited, and under `pid-reused`, where another process has the pid but nothing
serves the socket.

For `record-other-version`, and for `record-token-missing` while `pidAlive`
is `true`, `daemon stop` and `daemon run` print no JSON. They exit `1` with
one line on stderr that names the record file and says what is still running.
They do the same for `record-unreadable`, naming the cause. Over a
`record-malformed` record, `daemon stop` reports
`record-not-found`, and `daemon run` starts and writes a new record in its
place.

`daemon stop --json` reports its own outcome in `action` and `reason`:

- `stopped` (`reason: null`): the daemon exited and its record was removed.
- `not-running`, with `record-not-found`, `process-not-running` or
  `pid-reused`: there was nothing to stop. A record that outlived its daemon
  is removed.
- `refused`, with `identity-unconfirmed`: see the table above. The result
  carries `servingPid` when the process serving the socket named itself.
- `refused`, with `kill-failed`: the stop signal could not be sent to the
  recorded pid, for example because another user owns that process. Nothing
  else was changed.

## Collect a support bundle

`whiteboard daemon support-bundle` writes the daemon's `status` and `doctor`
results to a folder as redacted JSON, for attaching to a bug report. It reads
the record and runs the checks only; it does not start, stop or signal the
daemon.

```sh
whiteboard daemon support-bundle --json --output-dir=./whiteboard-bundle
# Another data directory than the default:
whiteboard daemon support-bundle --json --output-dir=./whiteboard-bundle --data-dir=<path>
```

| File | Content |
|------|---------|
| `status.json` | What `daemon status --json` reports: `ok`, `reason`, `recordFound`, `recordFresh`, `pidAlive`, and the record's `pid`, `version` and `startedAt` |
| `doctor.json` | Every `daemon doctor --json` check: `id`, `status`, `summary`, `detail` and `remediation` |
| `manifest.json` | `createdAt`, `packageVersion`, `platform` (OS and Node version), `mode` (`daemon`), and the sections above. Written last, so every file it lists is already there |

What the bundle never contains:

- The record's token, or any `Authorization`/`Bearer` value.
- Document content, uploaded files, or the input and output of MCP tool calls.
- Absolute paths in the check text: each one is replaced with
  `[REDACTED_PATH]`, so the data directory is not named.
- Log lines. The daemon writes its log records to stderr and keeps no log file.

The output folder may be missing, in which case it is created, or empty. The
command refuses any other folder and writes nothing:

- A folder that is not empty: `Could not write support bundle. The output
  directory must be empty.`
- A path that is a file or itself a symlink, or that passes through a symlink
  in a folder someone else could have placed it in: `Could not write support
  bundle. The output path must be a real directory, not reached through a
  symlink in a folder other users can write.` A symlink is followed when the
  folder holding it is owned by you or root and is not group- or
  other-writable, so macOS's `/tmp` (a link to `/private/tmp`) is fine. On
  Windows every symlink in the path is refused.

On success, stdout is one JSON line,
`{"schemaVersion":1,"ok":true,"outputDir":"<absolute path>","files":["status.json","doctor.json","manifest.json"]}`,
and the exit code is `0`. On any failure, stdout is empty, stderr carries one
line that names no path, and the exit code is `1`. Nothing already written is
removed.

## Get the `whiteboard` command

Every `whiteboard ...` command on this page is the CLI that
`@kamiazya/whiteboard-mcp` ships; the package's one executable is
`whiteboard`. Install it once so the command is on your `PATH`:

```bash
npm install -g @kamiazya/whiteboard-mcp
```

Without installing, `npx -y @kamiazya/whiteboard-mcp daemon run` runs any of
them (the arguments after the package name are the command's own). That is
fine for starting the daemon, but not for step 3 below: `native-host install`
records the path of the `whiteboard` it ran from, and the copy `npx` unpacks
is in a cache directory it replaces on the next release. Run that step from
the global install; the command warns on stderr when it finds itself in
`npx`'s cache.

## Set it up

While releases are `0.0.x`, the extension is not published to any store; you
load it by hand.

### 1. Build the extension

From a checkout of this repository:

```bash
pnpm install
pnpm --filter @kamiazya/whiteboard-extension build
```

This writes one build per engine under `apps/extension/dist/`:
`production` (Chrome, Edge and other Chromium browsers) and
`firefox-production` (Firefox). The `development` builds additionally admit
a `localhost` page, for working on the web app itself.

### 2. Load it into your browser

- **Chrome, Edge, Brave, Chromium:** open the extensions page
  (`chrome://extensions`, `edge://extensions`), turn on **Developer mode**,
  choose **Load unpacked**, and pick `apps/extension/dist/production`.
- **Firefox:** open `about:debugging#/runtime/this-firefox`, choose **Load
  Temporary Add-on…**, and pick `manifest.json` inside
  `apps/extension/dist/firefox-production`. A temporary add-on is removed
  when Firefox closes, so load it again after a restart.
- **Safari:** not yet. Safari's extension ships inside a macOS app, which is
  a later stage; in Safari the app keeps its data in the browser.

### 3. Register the native host

```bash
whiteboard native-host install --json
```

This needs no administrator rights: it writes the host's manifest at user
level, naming only the whiteboard extension as allowed to start it, plus a
small launcher that records which Node, which `whiteboard` install and which
data directory the host relays to. Pass `--data-dir=<path>` if your daemon
uses a data directory other than the default. Run before the first
`daemon run`, it names the same `~/.whiteboard` the daemon will create. The
launcher is written only into a data directory that is yours and that other
users cannot write — `install` makes it owner-only, and refuses one another
user owns, one that is world-writable, a symlink, or an existing launcher
that is a symlink or someone else's. Run it again after moving or
reinstalling `whiteboard`, including when a new release replaces the copy it
ran from.

Where the manifest goes depends on the platform:

- **Linux:** into each installed browser's user directory — Chrome
  (`~/.config/google-chrome/NativeMessagingHosts`), Chromium, Edge, Brave,
  Firefox (`~/.mozilla/native-messaging-hosts`) and the Snap Firefox
  (`~/snap/firefox/common/.mozilla/native-messaging-hosts`). A browser whose
  directory does not exist yet is skipped; start it once, then run `install`
  again.
- **macOS:** into each installed browser's directory under
  `~/Library/Application Support/` (Chrome, Chromium, Edge, Brave, and
  Firefox's `Mozilla/NativeMessagingHosts`).
- **Windows:** the manifests are kept under the data directory, and a
  per-user registry key names each one (`HKCU\Software\Google\Chrome\NativeMessagingHosts`,
  and the Chromium, Edge and Mozilla equivalents). Every one is registered,
  whether or not that browser is installed.

`--manifest-dir=<path>` and `--firefox-manifest-dir=<path>` write to one
directory of your choosing instead.

**Snap Firefox on Ubuntu asks you once.** Its native messaging goes through
a desktop portal, and the first time the extension starts the host Firefox
shows a permission prompt. Setup never grants it for you. If you refused
and want to be asked again, remove the stored answer with
`flatpak permission-remove webextensions io.github.kamiazya.whiteboard snap.firefox`
(the `flatpak` command manages the portal's permission store even without
any Flatpak apps), or reset every portal permission Firefox holds with
`flatpak permission-reset snap.firefox`.

### 4. Connect

Start the daemon with `whiteboard daemon run`,
then in the hosted app open the workspace popover and choose **Connect
through the extension**. The app reloads onto the daemon's workspaces.

## Move this workspace to the daemon

A browser can keep only so many documents in one workspace, because the
whole workspace lives in the tab's memory. On a desktop the limit is 2,000
documents, and on a phone or tablet (or a device reporting 4 GB of memory or
less) it is 500. From 1,400 documents (300 on a phone) the document list
suggests moving the workspace. At the limit, creating or duplicating
another document is refused with that same suggestion. Editing
the documents you already have keeps working
([ADR-0044](../contributing/adr/0044-workspace-capacity.md)).

Once a daemon is connected, you can move everything this browser keeps in
one step from **Settings → Connections → This workspace**:

1. Open **Settings → Connections** and find the **This workspace** section.
2. Click **Move to daemon…**, choose the daemon workspace to move into, and
   confirm.
3. When the move finishes, the result stays visible in that section. Use
   **Reload and continue from the daemon** to switch to working from the
   daemon, or keep working in the browser.

The move carries your documents and their edit history, the **Trash**
(so a trashed document can still be restored on the daemon), every **saved
version** with its label, and every image any of these use — including an
image only a trashed document or an older version shows. Documents keep
their identity, so links between them keep working on the daemon. If a
path already exists in the chosen daemon workspace, both versions are kept
and the pre-existing one is marked *shadowed* — nothing is renamed or
overwritten. Your saved versions keep their dates; the move adds one more,
marking the move itself.

Images travel through a live document on the daemon. If the workspace has no
live document at all, only trashed ones, its images cannot be sent: the result
names each as failed ("no live document to send that picture through"), and
the browser copy is kept. Restore a document on the daemon, then move again.

The move is one request of at most 24 MiB, and the Trash is what gives
way: once the workspace, its saved versions and the trashed documents taken
so far reach that limit, each further trashed document stays behind. The
limit is on the total, so many medium-sized trashed documents reach it as
surely as one large one, and moving again leaves the same ones behind —
empty the Trash of what you no longer need to let the rest go. Anything
this browser cannot read stays behind too. The result names each one when
the move finishes, and the browser copy is kept so nothing is lost.

One move also carries at most 2000 trashed documents and 120,000 saved
versions. Past either, the browser leaves the rest behind and names them (for
saved versions, the oldest automatic checkpoints go first), and keeps its
copy. A daemon sent more refuses the whole move with
`promote_too_many_carried` and keeps none of it.

The daemon checks each saved version against the document as it stood at
that version, and those checks may read at most 1,000,000,000 characters
and entries between them — about a minute of checking, enough for the whole
automatic history of a board at every limit. When a workspace's saved versions add up to more, the daemon refuses
with `promote_too_many_carried` and states that budget, and the browser
moves again at once carrying the newest saved versions that fit. The result
says how many older saved versions stayed behind, and the browser keeps its
copy, since it is the only place those versions are still held.

One move carries at most 2000 documents, the most a browser keeps on a
desktop. The daemon refuses a larger workspace whole, with the error
`promote_too_many_documents`, and keeps none of it. The same 2000 is the most
a daemon workspace holds, so a move into a workspace that already holds
documents is refused, with `too_many_documents`, when the two together would
hold more — and at 2000 the daemon refuses any new document, however it is
added, with the same error. Folders have a ceiling of their own, 4000, and a
move that would leave the workspace holding more is refused with
`too_many_folders`.

A saved version is held to the same limits as the documents themselves: a
move whose saved versions include one with a body, node text or board past
its limit is refused whole, under the error a sync write past that limit
gets (for example `markdown_too_large`), and keeps none of it.

Once the daemon confirms it holds every document, image, trashed document
and saved version that moved, the old browser copy is removed — its Trash
and saved versions with it: the daemon is the workspace's one keeper, and this browser
keeps a **cached replica** instead — it stays editable when the daemon
cannot be reached, and your edits reach the daemon when it returns. The replica holds
the images its documents show too, up to 64 MiB per workspace; an image past
that limit, or one the daemon could not serve when the replica last synced,
reads *Image unavailable offline* until a later sync can fetch it. What the
replica shows depends on what is actually on this device and what the daemon
last said: a copy that is readable in memory, a copy that only your passkey
can open (with an **Unlock with your passkey** action that needs no
network), or a copy that is present but locked until the daemon can be
reached again (with a Reconnect action). Another tab that was showing the
moved workspace switches to a workspace this browser still keeps, and says
the workspace moved to the daemon.

The passkey unlock is what lets a copy survive closing the tab, and you
switch it on per copy: see
[Read a copy offline](#read-a-copy-offline) below. Until you do, a copy
stays readable only until the tab closes. If anything could
not be confirmed (for example an image upload failed), the browser copy is
kept unchanged and the result says so, naming why. The daemon stores PNG,
JPEG, GIF, WebP and SVG images up to 16 MiB each, so an image of another type
or size stays behind until you replace it; a dropped connection is cured by
moving again, which is safe and simply re-merges.

## See and remove the copies this device keeps

**Settings > Connections > Copies on this device** lists every copy of a
workspace this browser holds: the ones it keeps itself, and the cached
replicas of daemon workspaces. A replica row says which daemon it came from
and when it last synced, and offers **Delete copy**.

Removing a cached copy is housekeeping rather than a change of access — the
daemon still keeps the workspace, and this device can cache it again. What
does not come back is anything in that copy which had not reached the daemon
yet, so the confirmation says so before you commit to it. The copy the
session is currently showing is not offered a delete, and neither is a
workspace this browser keeps itself: that one is the only copy of its data
anywhere, and the way to let go of it is to move it to a daemon first. A copy
open in another tab when you delete it locks there and says it was deleted,
so nothing typed in that tab can write it back.

## Read a copy offline

A cached replica, the images it holds included, is encrypted on this device,
and its key is held only while the tab is open. To open a copy after the tab
has closed and the daemon is unreachable, use **Make readable offline** on
its row in **Settings > Connections > Copies on this device**.

The action creates a passkey in this browser only. It is not registered with
the daemon, and the app never asks for one on its own. The copy's key is
locked with that passkey, and the row then reads *Readable offline with your
passkey.* The next time the daemon cannot be reached, the copy offers
**Unlock with your passkey**: one gesture, no network.

- The action works only while the daemon that keeps the workspace is
  connected, because its key is needed to lock the copy. Otherwise the row
  says so and the button is disabled.
- **If you lose that passkey, this device's copy cannot be read again.** The
  daemon still keeps the workspace, so a fresh copy can be pulled; anything
  this device had not yet sent is gone.
- A browser whose passkeys cannot do this says *This browser cannot make a
  copy readable offline.* and nothing is changed.
- If the daemon refuses this copy's key outright (the workspace is gone, its
  copies may no longer be kept offline, or your access was withdrawn), the
  locked key is removed too, and the copy no longer offers an unlock. A
  daemon that is merely unreachable changes nothing.
- **Turn off** on the row removes the locked key, so the copy is again
  readable only while a tab holds it. The passkey stays in your passkey
  manager; delete it there if you no longer want it.

## See what this device keeps of a daemon-kept workspace

Once a workspace is kept by a daemon, **Settings → Connections → This
workspace** shows a short line describing what this device keeps of it,
below the move description:

- *Needs a connection. No copy is kept on this device.* — nothing is stored
  here; the workspace is unreadable while the daemon is unreachable.
- *A copy is kept on this device while this tab stays open.* — an offline
  copy is kept, readable while the daemon is unreachable, for the current
  session.
- *A copy is kept on this device for a limited time.* — an offline copy is
  kept, readable until it expires.

This line is read-only status; nothing on this screen changes it — the
workspace's offline policy is set by the daemon operator (see
[security model → Replica key](../explanation/security-model.md#replica-key-offline-read-plane)
for what each policy means and how it is set today).

# Define your own stencils

A **stencil** says what a box IS — a datastore, a gateway, a queue — and sets its appearance
(the bundled ones spend silhouette alone), so a drawing carries its own vocabulary instead of
one invented per board.

Six ship with the bundled `visual` plugin:

| id | what it means | drawn as |
|---|---|---|
| `visual.actor` | whoever the drawing is for: a person, a client, a calling system | an ellipse |
| `visual.gateway` | where traffic enters or is routed: a gateway, a load balancer, a proxy | a hexagon |
| `visual.service` | something that runs and answers: an API, a worker, a function | an octagon |
| `visual.datastore` | anything that holds state and is read back: a database, a bucket, a cache | a cylinder |
| `visual.queue` | something in flight rather than at rest: a queue, a topic, a stream | a parallelogram |
| `visual.external` | something the drawing does not own: a third-party API, a vendor service | a diamond |

Every member has its own silhouette and none sets a colour, so the distinctions survive a
projector, a colour-blind reader and a greyscale print, and colour stays free to say something
else about the box — healthy or failing, say. That rule is
[ADR-0036](../contributing/adr/0036-semantic-axes.md) §5.

The editor draws the same six: pick one under **Facets…** on a selected box and the box takes
its silhouette, with the label wrapped to fit inside it and centred line by line. Each stencil
also carries a small badge at the top of the box, so two kinds that differ by silhouette alone
(the octagon and the hexagon) stay apart at a glance:

| stencil | badge |
|---|---|
| `visual.datastore` | a database |
| `visual.service` | a server |
| `visual.gateway` | a network |
| `visual.queue` | stacked layers |
| `visual.actor` | a person |
| `visual.external` | a link |

The badge is drawn for a box that wears a stencil. A symbol you set by hand on a plain box is
not drawn on the box; it shows where a box is too small to read, such as the minimap and a file
row. Boxes shorter than 48px leave the badge off so it does not sit on the label.

## Wearing one

`stencil` sits beside `op`, next to `node`, on `node.add` and `node.patch`:

```json
{
  "op": "node.add",
  "node": { "type": "text", "text": "orders", "width": 200, "height": 80 },
  "stencil": "visual.datastore"
}
```

`node.patch` dresses boxes that already exist and takes a selector, so one op can dress every
box in a group. An explicit `color` beside the stencil wins over the stencil's own.

Leaving `stencil` out says the op names none, and `"stencil": null` says the same thing — so a
batch that sets it on some boxes and null on others is not refused. On a `node.patch`, null
leaves the box wearing whatever it already wears; there is no way to take a stencil off, because
undressing would have to decide what becomes of the colour and the silhouette it wrote.

`wb_facet_list` reports the ids you may use, and a refusal here lists them too — so there is no
list to memorise and none baked into the tool schema.

## Growing the vocabulary

When a drawing needs a word the six do not have, the workspace can define its own. A
**stencil library is a document**: an ordinary markdown document at the path `stencils`,
carrying the facet `visual.stencils/v0`.

```json
{
  "workspaceId": "<your workspace>",
  "documentIds": ["<the stencils document>"],
  "facets": {
    "visual.stencils/v0": {
      "stencils": {
        "lakehouse": {
          "displayName": "Lakehouse",
          "color": "3",
          "facets": { "visual.shape/v0": { "kind": "hexagon" } }
        }
      }
    }
  }
}
```

That is a `wb_facet_set` call — a library needs no special tool. Its stencils are then
`workspace.<name>`, so the one above is worn as `"stencil": "workspace.lakehouse"`, beside the
bundled six.

### Finding what a workspace defines

Pass `workspaceId` to `wb_facet_list` and the answer adds that workspace's own stencils beside
the deployment's:

```json
{ "workspaceId": "<your workspace>", "assetKind": "stencils" }
```

```json
{ "id": "workspace.lakehouse", "kind": "stencils", "namespace": "workspace",
  "displayName": "Lakehouse" }
```

Without `workspaceId` the answer is the deployment's vocabulary alone, and nothing is read from
the workspace at all — so a caller that only wants to know what the server registered pays
nothing for libraries it never asked about. A `workspaceId` naming a workspace that does not
exist is refused rather than answered: the deployment's six coming back would read as "this
workspace defines none".

Because a library is a document:

- its body is yours, so the vocabulary can explain itself in the same file it is defined in;
- it syncs, versions and forks with the workspace, like anything else you write;
- a stencil in it is validated exactly as a bundled one is — a colour (a preset `"1"` to `"6"`
  or a hex colour), and facet payloads checked against the plugin that owns them — and a write
  of a library with a bad stencil is refused, naming the stencil and the facet; a bad one that
  arrives some other way (a synced edit) is left out while the others keep working.

### What a stencil may not carry

A stencil says what a box is, never where it goes or what it says. Position, size and text are
refused by name. That is what keeps a vocabulary reusable: the same `lakehouse` dresses a box
anywhere on any board.

A box with a silhouette centres its label, across and down, inside the shape; a plain rectangle
keeps the label at its top left. Stencils do not set this: the silhouette does, so every stencil
that sets one gets a centred label. To override it for one box, set its text placement in the
Facets panel.

### Choosing silhouettes and colours

Two stencils a reader cannot tell apart are worth less than one. The silhouettes a stencil can
set (`visual.shape/v0`) are `ellipse`, `diamond`, `hexagon`, `parallelogram`, `cylinder` and
`octagon`; a stencil that sets none draws the default rectangle, the same as an undressed box.

**Know the ceiling before you design against it.** There are six silhouettes besides that
rectangle, and the bundled six use all of them. Anything your library adds therefore repeats
the silhouette of a bundled stencil, or of another of your own. That is a real limit of what a
board draws, not an oversight, and nothing refuses it: a library may collide deliberately.

Two ways to live with it:

- **Replace rather than extend.** If your domain has its own six nouns, define all of them in
  the library and use only those on a board. A board that never mixes the two vocabularies
  never shows the collision.
- **Keep the collision far apart.** A `lakehouse` that looks like the bundled `gateway` costs
  nothing on a board that has no gateway on it.

A stencil may also set a `color`, as the example above does, and it is yours to spend. The
bundled set leaves colour to whatever second axis a drawing declares, so a library that sets
one gives that up on the boxes wearing it.

## Limits today

- **One library per workspace**, at the path `stencils`. The facet is what makes a document a
  library, but nothing can yet ask which documents carry a facet, so the path is the rule
  rather than a default.
- **At most 256 stencils per library.** A write of a larger one is refused, and the refusal
  says how many it holds. A library that grows past the limit some other way (a synced edit)
  is read as its first 256 valid stencils by name. The others are left out.
- **A stencil sets appearance only.** A default size is defined in
  [ADR-0034](../contributing/adr/0034-stencil-and-recipe.md) and not implemented.

# Draw on a canvas

Circle an idea, underline a box or scribble a note in the margin with the
**Draw** tool, then move, recolour or erase what you drew.

## Draw

Pick **Draw** (the pencil) in the toolbar, or press `D`, and drag across the
board. What you drew stays as a smooth stroke, with no arrowhead at either
end. A tap that does not travel leaves nothing behind.

On a phone the toolbar folds onto two rows so every tool stays in sight:
**Hand**, **Select**, **Connect**, **Draw** and **Eraser** along the bottom,
with undo, redo, **Add** and the zoom buttons above them.

Strokes you draw one straight after another, close together, become one
drawing: a handwritten word selects, moves and recolours as a whole.

## Choose a colour and a width

While **Draw** is armed, a strip of pen options sits just above the toolbar:

- **Color** — **Default** (the board's own ink, shown as a dot of that ink) or
  one of the six preset colours. The swatches are drawn in the board's theme,
  so they show the ink you will get.
- **Width** — **Thin**, **Medium** or **Thick**, each sample a line of
  visibly heavier weight.

Where the strip has no room for both groups in one row — on a phone — the
colours take one row and the widths the row below it. **Zoom to fit** leaves
room for the strip, so nothing it frames ends up underneath it.

The next stroke you draw takes the colour and width you picked, and the stroke
under your pen already shows them while you draw. The pen keeps your choice
for the rest of the browser tab, on every canvas you open in it. A stroke
drawn with the default pen — no colour, thin — looks exactly like one drawn
before pens had options.

With a keyboard, `Tab` reaches the strip; the arrow keys move between the
choices in each group. On a touch screen every choice is a finger-sized
target.

## Erase drawings

Pick **Eraser** in the toolbar, or press `E`, and drag over the drawings you
want gone. Every drawing your sweep touches is marked while you drag and
removed when you let go — with a mouse or a finger alike. A single press on a
drawing erases it too.

The eraser takes only drawings: boxes, connections and lines ruled between two
points stay where they are, and so does a locked drawing. A drawing made of
several strokes loses only the strokes you crossed. One sweep is one step, so
one undo brings back everything it erased. A screen reader hears "Erased 2
drawings" for the sweep and "Restored 2 drawings" for the undo.

Press `Esc`, or pick another tool, to put the eraser down. `Esc` takes you back
to the tool you had before it, so after a correction you are still drawing.

## Move a drawing

Switch back to **Select** (`V`), then press the stroke and drag it. The whole
drawing travels; nothing about its shape changes. With a mouse or a finger
alike, dragging the stroke anywhere along its length moves it.

A selected drawing shows a square handle at each end. Dragging one moves that
end, and dropping it on a box attaches the end to the box. On a touch screen
each end takes a finger-sized press around the handle.

A drawing does not show grab points along its length: its shape is the path
your hand took, and reshaping it is drawing it again. A line ruled between two
points — one dragged out of a box's connect handle — keeps its round bend
handles, so its bends can still be placed by hand.

## Recolour, resize, label or delete a drawing

Select the drawing, then:

- press the **⋯** button that appears above its top-right corner (on a touch
  screen it is a finger-sized target), or
- right-click it, or press and hold it on a touch screen.

Each opens the drawing's menu: **Color**, **Width**, the arrowheads at its ends,
**Edit label**, **Group** / **Ungroup** for strokes drawn as one, **Lock**
(when the page offers locks) and **Delete**. With a keyboard, `Delete` or
`Backspace` removes the selected drawing too.

While a drawing is selected the Display panel opens with a **This drawing**
section above the canvas settings; a drawing has no shape, stencil or tags,
so the section points you to the menu above.

A screen reader finds each stroke in the canvas's contents list as "Drawing",
and hears "Selected: Drawing" when one is selected; its end handles read
"Move the start of this drawing".

A drawing cannot carry a comment: comment on the box it circles instead.

# Export a canvas to PNG or SVG from the daemon

The web editor's Export menu renders in your browser. When you want the **daemon** to render a
canvas instead — from a script, a cron job, or a build step, with no browser open — call its
export routes. They write the file and answer where they put it.

There is no `whiteboard` command for this yet; the routes are the supported way in, and `curl`
is enough to drive them.

## Before you start

- A running daemon (`whiteboard daemon run`; see
  [connect-to-local-daemon](connect-to-local-daemon.md)).
- `curl` built with Unix-socket support (`curl --version` lists `UnixSockets`) and `jq`.
- The fonts your canvas needs installed on the daemon, or a PNG draws their characters as empty
  boxes — see [install-fonts-for-export](install-fonts-for-export.md).

The daemon listens on no network port. It serves an owner-only Unix socket, and authenticates
every route with a bearer token; both are in its record, `daemon.json` in the data directory
(`~/.whiteboard/`, or `$WHITEBOARD_DATA_DIR`):

```sh
RECORD="${WHITEBOARD_DATA_DIR:-$HOME/.whiteboard}/daemon.json"
SOCKET=$(jq -r .socketPath "$RECORD")
TOKEN=$(jq -r .token "$RECORD")
```

Treat the token as a password: anything holding it can read and change every workspace.

## Export a PNG

Address the canvas by its workspace and its document id. A fresh data directory has one
workspace, `default`; the workspace's listing names every document with its id and its path:

```sh
curl --unix-socket "$SOCKET" -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  http://daemon/api/workspaces/default/documents
# {"documents":[{"documentId":"01ARZ3NDEKTSV4RRFFQ69G5FAV","path":"plans/architecture",...}]}

curl --unix-socket "$SOCKET" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"scale": 2}' \
  http://daemon/api/workspaces/default/documents/01ARZ3NDEKTSV4RRFFQ69G5FAV/export
```

The host name after `http://` is ignored; the socket decides where the request goes. The id
survives a rename, so a script that saved one keeps working after the canvas moves.

The answer says where the file went and what it could not draw:

```json
{ "filePath": "<data dir>/exports/…/architecture.png", "undrawable": [] }
```

The body is optional. What it takes:

| Field | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `scale` | Zoom factor, above 0 and at most 8. |
| `padding` | Pixels of margin on every side, 0–1024. |
| `theme` | `light` or `dark`, whatever the canvas is set to. |
| `style` | `clean` (the default), `document` for the theme the canvas names, or a theme id. |
| `outputPath` | Where to write the file instead of the exports directory. |
| `overwrite` | `true` to replace a file already at `outputPath`. |

## Export an SVG

The same request at `…/export-svg`, without `scale`. An SVG keeps its text as text, so characters
the daemon has no font for still read correctly in any viewer that has one.

```sh
curl --unix-socket "$SOCKET" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"style": "document"}' \
  http://daemon/api/workspaces/default/documents/01ARZ3NDEKTSV4RRFFQ69G5FAV/export-svg
```

## When it refuses

A refusal is JSON with a code to match on and a sentence to show:

```json
{ "error": "not_found", "message": "Document not found: default/plans/architecture" }
```

`404` means the workspace or the document is not there; `400` names the field that was wrong;
`401` means the token did not match the running daemon — read `daemon.json` again: unless you
gave it one, a daemon mints a new token each time it starts.

← Back to [How-to guides](README.md)

# Export and import a document

Save one document as a file, and bring a file in as a document. Works the same
whether the browser or the daemon keeps the workspace, except where noted.

## Save a document

Open the document, then **More actions → Export…**:

- **Export as PNG** or **Export as SVG** — on a canvas: a picture of it. The picture leaves
  out the comments: no pins, cards, region outlines or highlighted passages.
- **Export as PNG (with comments)** or **Export as SVG (with comments)** — on a canvas: the
  same picture with the comments drawn in, as the editor shows them.
- **2× resolution (PNG)** and **With background** — on a canvas, two checkboxes at the
  bottom of the submenu, remembered in this browser, that apply to all four picture entries. By default
  a picture is 1×, filled with the white paper of the light theme the export is drawn in.
  Tick **2× resolution** for a PNG twice as many pixels wide and tall (an SVG has no pixels
  and is unaffected); untick **With background** for a transparent picture. The menu stays
  open when you tick one, so you can set both before choosing a format.
- **Selection only (N items, PNG/SVG)** — on a canvas with nodes selected, a third checkbox
  above those two. Ticked, the four picture entries draw just the selection: a selected
  group brings the nodes inside it, and an edge, a line or a comment comes along only when
  what it is attached to does. It is not remembered — it applies to this open of the menu —
  and **Save as JSON Canvas** always saves the whole document.
- **Save as Markdown (.md)** — on a note, the only entry its Export… submenu offers: the
  OKF Markdown source, with the document's name as the frontmatter `title`. A note has no
  picture export. The file is text only: an image in the note is saved as its
  `![alt](asset:…)` line, not as pixels ([add an image to a note](add-an-image-to-a-note.md)),
  and an embedded document as its `![[…]]` line. The entry says so under its name. After the
  save, a toast at the bottom of the screen reads "Saved as Markdown", and when the note
  has a picture or an embedded document it adds a second line: the pictures and embedded
  diagrams are not included, and Print / Save as PDF makes a handout with them. A screen
  reader hears the same words once. For a handout, print the note instead (below).
- **Save as JSON Canvas (.canvas)** — on a canvas: the JSON Canvas source, including the
  `x-whiteboard` extension. The comments are not in it: a conversation stays with the
  document in its workspace, and no file carries it.

The browser downloads the file, and a notice confirms it ("Saved as Markdown"). An image on
a canvas is saved as an `asset:` reference to the workspace's file, not as its pixels, so
the notice says the images are referenced. Use PNG or SVG when the pixels must travel.
See the [export formats reference](../reference/export-formats.md#web-app-exports).

## Print a note, or save it as a PDF

Open the note, then **More actions → Print / Save as PDF…**. The note switches to **Read**
for the print, and the browser's print dialog opens; choose a printer, or **Save as PDF** as
the destination for a file. When the dialog closes the note goes back to the view you had.

What prints is the read view and nothing else: the title, then the body with its pictures
and embedded canvases, over as many pages as it takes. It prints in the light theme, dark
ink on white paper, whatever theme the app is showing; the screen keeps its own. A body that
already opens with the title as its heading prints it once. A page breaks between paragraphs,
pictures and embeds, never through one, and never right after a heading: a heading prints
on the same page as the block it introduces, a picture or an embed included. A single
block taller than a page, such as a long code block, is the exception: it starts on a new
page and runs on over the pages it needs, with nothing cut off. The app around the note — the top bar, the toolbars, the scroll overview — does
not print. Comments on an embedded canvas are left out, as they are wherever a canvas is
shown inside something else. The browser's own **Print** (`Ctrl+P` / `Cmd+P`) prints the
same thing in **Read** and **Split**; from **Write**, use the menu entry.

## Bring a file in

On the document list, choose **New → Import file…** and pick a file, or drop files onto the
list. Accepted: `.md`, `.markdown` (a note), `.canvas`, `.json` (a canvas, JSON Canvas 1.0).

- The document is created in the folder you are viewing. Its file name becomes the path;
  when that path is taken, a number is added (`-2`, `-3`).
- A note's name is its frontmatter `title`, or the file name when there is none. A canvas is
  named after the file. Markdown with no frontmatter becomes a plain note.
- One imported file opens; several leave the last one selected, and any that failed are
  listed by name with the reason.
- A file that is not one of the accepted kinds, or that does not parse, is refused with a
  notice saying so; nothing is created and the page stays where it is.
- Images a canvas references by `asset:` are not carried by the file, so they appear only
  when the workspace already holds them.
- A `.canvas` file an older version saved with its comments inside (`x-whiteboard.comments`)
  is refused, and the reason names that key: remove it from the file to import the board.
  Comments are never read out of a file, so importing one without the refusal would have
  dropped them without a word.

# Find documents from chat

Ask your agent to find documents by what they contain — the
`wb_document_search` MCP tool searches full text, not just titles.

What it covers:

- markdown bodies
- canvas text: text nodes, group labels, and **edge labels** (a diagram's
  meaning lives in its relations, so they are searchable content)
- document names and paths
- the display names of the folders a document sits in: after renaming a
  folder to "Operations Team", "operations" finds the documents inside it.
  A document that only its folder's name matched ranks below every document
  whose own name, path or text matched.

Japanese (and other CJK) queries work without any dictionary or download,
down to a single character — 「た」 finds 「たささたはな」, so a query answers
while it is still being typed. Accents on Latin letters do not have to match:
"cafe" finds "Café" and "equipe" finds "Équipe", either way round, while
Japanese voiced kana stay distinct (が does not match か). Results come back ranked, with a context excerpt around each match (a
`[[link]]` in an excerpt reads as the name of the document it points at, and
an excerpt never cuts one in half), and can
be narrowed by `kind` (markdown / spatial) or by tags.

Example prompts:

> 「検索基盤について書いた文書を探して」
> "Find the canvas where something depends on redis"

The same search is available to tools over
`GET /api/v1/workspaces/:id/search?q=…`. The query string reads four keys:

| key | meaning |
|---|---|
| `q` | the words to match, at most 1,024 characters |
| `kind` | `markdown` or `spatial`, to narrow by kind |
| `tag` | a tag the document carries; repeat it (`tag=a&tag=b`) to require several, at most 1,024 |
| `limit` | at most this many results (1–50, default 10) |

A search needs `q`, a `tag` or a `kind` (a filter answers alone). Any other
key is refused with `400 invalid_request` naming it, rather than ignored —
`tags=x` would otherwise answer every document as though the filter had
applied.

The query is bounded because every word in it is looked up across every
document the workspace holds: `wb_document_search` and the route refuse a
longer `q` with "a search query is longer than the 1024-character limit", and
more than 1,024 tags with the tag-count limit. The web app's search box stops
taking characters at the same limit. A query is a few words; a longer text is a
document to compare against, not something to search for.

What one document contributes to the index is bounded too: at most 8,192
distinct terms (words, CJK characters and character pairs), counted from its
path and name and then through its text in order. Ordinary writing does not
come near it — the longest document in this project's own repository has under
3,000 — but a document that reaches it is found only by what it says up to that
point: a word that first appears after it does not find the document. The web
app's search box indexes the same way.

## Also search by meaning (optional)

By default search matches WORDS. It will not find a document that says the
same thing in different words, or in a different language — ask for
「通信が切れたときの復旧」 and a note titled *Reconnect runbook* stays
hidden, because the two share no text.

Turning on semantic search adds that. A local embedding model runs beside
the daemon, and the two rankings are FUSED: a document both halves like
rises above one that only one half likes. Word matching is not replaced,
but it is no longer the only voice — on a large workspace a weak keyword
match can be ranked below a strong match by meaning, and fall off the end
of the results you asked for.

It is off by default because it is not small: the embedding runtime is
~384MB installed, and the model itself is a further ~118MB download (~470MB
at full precision — see below). Neither arrives unless you ask for it. Three
deliberate steps turn it on:

```bash
# once — install the CLI and the embedding runtime side by side
npm install -g @kamiazya/whiteboard-mcp @huggingface/transformers

# once — download the model into your data directory (add --full for the
# higher-precision weights)
whiteboard search fetch-model --json
```

Then set `WHITEBOARD_SEMANTIC_SEARCH=1` in **every process that answers a
search**, because each one decides for itself whether to use the model:

- the daemon: `WHITEBOARD_SEMANTIC_SEARCH=1 whiteboard daemon run`;
- the MCP server your agent starts, which is what answers
  `wb_document_search` in a chat. Put the variable in that server's `env`
  block in your MCP client's configuration, and start it from the global
  install (`"command": "whiteboard", "args": ["mcp"]`) rather than through
  `npx`, which would not see the runtime.

**Install the runtime where `whiteboard` can find it.** The server loads
`@huggingface/transformers` by resolving it from its own package's directory,
so the runtime has to sit in the same `node_modules` tree as
`@kamiazya/whiteboard-mcp` — as the global install above puts them. A copy in
your project's directory, or `npx` unpacking the package somewhere else, is
invisible to it and `search fetch-model` answers `runtime-missing`.

**You choose how good a job it does.** The same model ships in two
precisions, and the download and the quality are the same dial:

| | download | measured quality |
|---|---|---|
| `WHITEBOARD_SEMANTIC_SEARCH=1` | ~118MB | the default |
| `WHITEBOARD_SEMANTIC_SEARCH=full` | ~470MB | 0.051 nDCG@10 higher |

That 0.051 is about 11% better ranking, measured on a public Japanese
retrieval benchmark rather than asserted. Add `--full` to the fetch command
if you want that side of it — fetch the precision you intend to run, since
the daemon never downloads on its own.

`whiteboard search fetch-model` verifies by USE rather than by looking for
files: it reports success only once an embedding actually comes back at the
width the search index is built for. If a step is missing it says which one
— `runtime-missing` means the first command, `weights-missing` means the
second.

With `--json` it prints one object with `"schemaVersion": 1` and a `kind` of
`ok` or `failed`; a failure carries `failure` (the names above, plus
`load-failed` and `unexpected-dimensions`), `remedy`, and, when there is
something more to say, a redacted `detail`.

Working from a clone of the repository instead? `pnpm --filter
@kamiazya/whiteboard-mcp search:fetch-model` runs the same command against
your checkout.

After that everything is local and offline: nothing is sent anywhere, and
the model is never re-fetched. The daemon never downloads on its own — if
the model is missing, search stays word-based rather than blocking on a
download, and says so in its log with the step that would fix it.

Measured on the project's judged corpus, with the model on: queries that
word-based search could not answer at all (a paraphrase, or a Japanese
question about an English document) are all answered, and every query that
already worked is unchanged. See
[ADR-0015](../contributing/adr/0015-search-quality-scoreboard.md) for the
numbers.

# Install fonts so exports are not empty boxes

Your canvas reads fine on screen but exports as rows of `□□□`? The daemon draws exports with the
fonts **it** has, and it ships with a Latin face only. Any script it has no glyph for — Japanese,
Chinese, Korean, Thai, Devanagari, Arabic, Hebrew — is painted as an empty box.

This is a property of the daemon, not of your canvas or your browser: the text is intact, and an
SVG export still carries it as text that any viewer with the font can read. Only the rasterised
formats (PNG) bake in what the daemon could draw.

It is specifically the **daemon's** exports — the PNG a script or tool of your own requests from
the daemon's HTTP export route (`POST …/export`; how to call it is
[export-a-canvas-from-the-daemon](export-a-canvas-from-the-daemon.md)). No MCP tool rasterises; `wb_scene_render`
returns SVG, which carries the text as text. The web editor's own Export menu renders in your
browser with your browser's fonts, so it can look fine while the daemon exporting the same canvas
gets boxes. The daemon's export routes say which characters they lost, in an `undrawable` field;
see
[export-formats](../reference/export-formats.md#characters-the-exporter-cannot-draw).

## Install one

1. Connect the web app to a local daemon (see
   [connect-to-local-daemon](connect-to-local-daemon.md)). Fonts live on the daemon, so this
   screen has nothing to offer without one.
2. Open **Settings → Fonts**.
3. Press **Install** next to the font covering the script you write in.

The daemon downloads it, checks it really is a font, and keeps it. Every later export uses it —
no restart, no configuration.

| Script | Font |
|---|---|
| Japanese | Noto Sans JP |
| Chinese (Simplified / Traditional) | Noto Sans SC / TC |
| Korean | Noto Sans KR |
| Thai, Devanagari, Arabic, Hebrew | Noto Sans Thai / Devanagari / Arabic / Hebrew |

A CJK font is 9–18 MB, because it carries thousands of glyphs. The others are under 1 MB.

All of them come from [Google Fonts](https://fonts.google.com/) and are licensed under the
[SIL Open Font License 1.1](https://openfontlicense.org/). Whiteboard does not redistribute
them; your daemon fetches them when you ask it to.

## Install one that is not listed

Any font already on your machine works. Copy the `.ttf`, `.otf`, or `.ttc` into the daemon's
`fonts` directory and it participates in the next export:

```
~/.whiteboard/fonts/
```

That is the location on every platform. If you set `WHITEBOARD_DATA_DIR`, it is
`$WHITEBOARD_DATA_DIR/fonts/` instead. (Where the home directory is not writable — some
sandboxes — the daemon falls back to `<temp>/.whiteboard-<uid>`.)

`.woff2` is deliberately **not** accepted: the export renderer cannot decode it, so a file
dropped in that format would sit there and never draw anything.

## A theme's font reaches the editor too

One family works differently: the handwriting family the sketch theme names (Yomogi). Once it
is installed on the daemon, the web app fetches the same bytes and draws with them on screen,
in thumbnails and in its own PNG export — see [choose-a-theme](choose-a-theme.md). The other
families in the list are export fonts: they fix a PNG's tofu and do not change what the editor
shows.

## Why the app does not just download the font it needs

Installing reaches the network, and the daemon is also driven by AI agents that act on
instructions found in the documents they read. Making this an agent-callable action would let a
malicious canvas talk an agent into making the daemon fetch things. So it is a button a person
presses, and the only thing it accepts is a name from the list above — never a URL, not even
yours. The reasoning is recorded in
[ADR-0012](../contributing/adr/0012-user-installed-fonts.md).
