body:
# Link documents and see what links back

Connect documents to each other, and read those connections from the other
side. Works the same whether the browser or the daemon keeps the workspace.

## Write a link

In a **markdown document**, type `[[` — a completion list of the
workspace's documents opens as you type, ranked by match; Enter inserts the
link. Each row shows the document's path beside its name, so two documents with
the same name stay distinguishable. The toolbar's Link action — or `Ctrl + K`
(`Cmd + K` on a Mac) while you are writing — offers the same list as a dialog
(and also handles external URLs). Select some text first and the link keeps it:
a document link written over a selection is `[[path|selected text]]`, the way an
external link always carried its text. A reference can name its target two ways:

- `[[path]]` — what the picker inserts when no text was selected. The link is
  shown with the
  target's **current display name**, so it always reads naturally, and
  moving the document rewrites references to the old path for you. The `[[`
  completion inserts `[[path|Name]]` instead, so the source reads as the
  name you picked; the address is still the path, and the name in the link
  is just the words it shows.
- `[[<document id>]]` — survives everything; what the picker inserts for
  the rare path that could be mistaken for an id.

Type a name that matches no document and the completion list offers
a `Create 'name'` row. Your words become the note's **name**, and its path is
derived from them the way a first rename derives one — `Lecture 6 notes` makes
`lecture-6-notes` (`-2` if that is taken), in the folder of the document you are
writing. The link is written to match, `[[lecture-6-notes|Lecture 6 notes]]`, so
it resolves and still reads as you typed it, and a short notice says
`Created 'Lecture 6 notes'`. Text that is already a path (`notes/plan`) keeps
it. Where the editor cannot make documents the row is not offered.

Write `[[path|your own words]]` when the link should read as something
other than the target's name. A `[[Display name]]` is **not** a link — it
stays literal bracket text; display names label links at render time
instead of addressing them. A link or embed of a document with no name is
labelled as the documents list shows it — **Untitled 2** for `untitled-2`,
the last part of the path otherwise — never by its address.

On a **canvas**, a document embedded through the palette's Document entry,
a file node pointing at a document path, and a `[[...]]` inside a text node
all count as references too.

## Embed a document

Write `![[path]]` on a line of its own to show the target *inside* this
document instead of linking out to it. The `[[` completion works here too,
so type `![[` and pick the document:

- A **markdown** target renders its body inline, as if the text were
  written here. Embeds nest, three levels deep; a document that embeds
  itself, directly or through another, shows a placeholder at the point
  the loop closes. One view draws at most 128 embedded documents in all,
  counting canvas miniatures and file-node previews, and the canvases they
  show hold at most 4000 nodes, edges and lines between them; past either,
  an embed shows its placeholder and a file node its card.
- A **canvas** target renders as a framed miniature of the whole canvas,
  scaled to the column, under its display name. The name is a link that
  opens the canvas. File nodes inside the miniature keep their card form;
  only the canvas you open expands them. A canvas with nothing on it shows
  a muted "Empty canvas" line under its name instead of a miniature.

While the target is still loading, the embed shows its name in a frame with
a muted "Loading…" line; the content replaces it when it arrives. A target
that cannot be found shows its name as a link instead.

An `![[...]]` mixed into a sentence behaves like a `[[...]]` link labelled
with the target's name. An embed counts as a link for the Linked from chip
below, so the embedded document lists this one as linking to it.

### Embed part of a document

Add `#` and a name to point inside the target:

- `![[notes/plan#Launch]]` embeds the **section** under the heading
  "Launch" — the heading and everything up to the next heading of the same
  or a higher level.
- `![[boards/roadmap#Launch]]` embeds the **group** labelled "Launch" on
  that canvas: the group's frame, the nodes inside it, and the edges
  between them. Give a group a label to make it addressable this way.

The match is by text, exact first and then ignoring case; when two headings
or groups share a name, the first one on the page wins. A part that does
not exist shows the address as a link and nothing else. The same `#` works
on a plain `[[path#Launch]]` link, which then reads as `Plan › Launch`.

## Follow a link

Click a `[[...]]` link — or the link an `![[...]]` embed shows — to open that
document in place. This works in the markdown editor's preview and on a
canvas, for a link drawn inside a text node.

In the workspace index, a link in the selected document's preview, or in
Peek, opens that document the same way. Links inside a file card's picture
and in a version preview do nothing when clicked.

The cached copy you read while the daemon is unreachable follows links the
same way: a link in a note or on a canvas, or a file node you double-click,
opens the linked document from that copy, in place. A link to a document the
copy does not hold does nothing.

In the markdown editor's source, hold Ctrl (Cmd on a Mac) and click a
`[[...]]` link to open its document. From the keyboard, put the caret inside
the link and choose **Open link under caret** in the editing actions menu.
On a link that names no document the same menu offers `Create 'text'` where
the editor can make documents; it makes the note as above and rewrites that
link to point at it.

A followed link opens the document at its top; a `#` part names what the link
points at but does not scroll to it.

A document link never makes the browser navigate away. Ordinary links (a web
address, or a relative path such as `guide.md`) keep the browser's usual
behaviour.

In the inline chat view (`canvas_view`), document links do nothing; see
[View a canvas inline in your AI chat](view-canvas-in-chat.md#links-in-the-view).

Read mode shows the document's name once: a body that opens with a `# Heading`
repeating the name does not print it a second time under the header.

## See what links back

Every document's header carries a Linked from chip (the waypoints icon)
showing how many documents link here. Click it to open the list — each
entry shows the linking document and a snippet of the text around the
reference (or the canvas relationship). Click an entry to jump to it.

The chip shows `0` on a document nothing links to yet; links written
anywhere in the workspace land here automatically.

Below the linked-from list, **Mentioned, not linked** surfaces documents
whose prose contains this document's display name without linking to it —
candidates for a link the author never wrote. Click a row to open it and
decide, or **Link it** to convert that document's mentions into real
`[[...]]` links in one server-side operation — written as
`[[path|Name]]`, so the prose keeps reading as the name. Mentions inside canvas
labels are listed but never rewritten (a link in a label would render as
literal brackets). The system still never links without a click — a link
is the author's claim.

## Rules worth knowing

- A link that does not resolve for the *reader* (an unknown target, a
  bracketed display name) never appears as a connection either — the two
  surfaces always agree.
- Deleting a document removes its outgoing references immediately.
- Moving a document rewrites inbound `[[path]]` links to the new path.
  Renaming (the display name) changes what links *show*, never what they
  mean. `[[<document id>]]` links survive everything.

# Organize documents into folders

A folder is the front of a document's path: `design/login` lives in `design`.
A folder exists while a document is in it, and moving a document is a change
of path; the document keeps its id, its links and its history through it.

A folder has two things a document has too: an **address** — its part of the
path, which is what links and the URL carry — and a **name**, which is what the
list, the tree, the folder path above the list and the move picker show. A
folder you make here gets its address from its name once, when it is made,
and from then on the two are separate: renaming the folder changes only its
name. A folder nobody has named shows its address.

An address is ASCII — letters `a`–`z`, digits and hyphens — so it reads the same
in every URL and `[[link]]`. It is made from the name: lower-cased, accents
taken off their letters (`Équipe Ops` becomes `equipe-ops`, `Straße` becomes
`strasse`, `Æsir` becomes `aesir`), and every run of spaces or punctuation
turned into one hyphen. A name with nothing the address can spell — `第六週`,
or only emoji — becomes `folder`, or `folder-2`, `folder-3` … when that is
taken; a new document named that way becomes `note` or `canvas` the same way.
An address another folder or document beside it already holds is numbered past
it in the same way.

## Move a document to a folder

Open the document's menu — right-click its card or row, tap the **…** button
on it (shown on a touch screen), long-press it, or press Shift+F10 on a focused
card — and choose **Move to folder…**. With the document open, the same entry is in its
**More actions** menu at the top right, and the page follows the document to its new address.
The picker lists the workspace root and every folder, plus **New folder…**:

- Arrow keys walk the list, **Enter** picks, **Escape** cancels.
- Each folder is listed by its names from the top down — `Class / Week 6` —
  so two folders called the same in different places can be told apart.
- **New folder…** asks for a name and moves the document into it. A `/`
  nests: `Class/Week 6` makes a folder called **Class** with a folder called
  **Week 6** inside it — or, when the top level already has a folder called
  Class, makes only **Week 6** inside that one. Each part that matches a folder
  already there — by its name or by its address, ignoring case — is that
  folder, the last part included: typing `Q3 Planning/Hiring` when that folder
  exists moves the document into it and makes nothing.
- If the destination already has a document with the same last segment, the
  move is refused with the path that collided and nothing moves.
- If a document already in the folder shows the same name — its name, or its
  last path segment when it has none, compared ignoring case and surrounding
  spaces — the move is refused with that name and nothing moves. Rename one of
  the two first. This holds for dragging, for a rename that changes the path,
  and for a folder moved under a folder with a same-named folder.

With a mouse or a pen you can also drag a card or row onto a folder (the
picker says so once, under its list, beside the keyboard way back to it:
`Shift + F10` on a card, then **Move to folder…**) — a folder
card, a folder in the tree beside the list, or **Workspace** for the root. The
folder highlights while the document is over it. On a touch screen the menu is
the way; dragging is not offered, so a long press cannot be mistaken for the
start of a drag.

A drop that cannot be made — the folder already holds a document showing the
same name, say — moves nothing, and the reason appears at the bottom of the
screen until you dismiss it.

A move is announced as "Moved _name_ to _folder_", with the folder's name —
including the name you just gave a folder the move made.

## Rename a folder

Right-click a folder (a card in the list or an entry in the tree) and choose
**Rename…**, or focus it and press **F2**. **Shift+F10** or the Menu key opens
the same menu from the keyboard. In the tree a **…** button shows beside a
folder while the pointer is over it or the row has focus. On a touch screen use
the **…** button beside the folder — the segments of the folder path above the
list carry one too — or long-press it. Type the new name and press **Enter**; **Escape** cancels. Only the name
changes: the folder's address, every document's path under it and every link
into it stay as they are.

The name cannot be blank, cannot contain `/` (which separates folders), and
cannot be the name another folder directly beside it already shows — compared
ignoring case and surrounding spaces, so `week 6` and `Week 6` are the same
name. A refused name is said beside the field before anything is saved, quoting
the other folder's name as it is written and, for a folder inside another, the
folder it is in: 'Another folder in "Q3 Planning" is already called "Hiring"'. Two
folders that came to share a name by syncing two copies of the workspace keep
both names; nothing is renamed for you.

A document is renamed the same way: **Rename…** in its menu, or **F2** on its
focused card. A saved rename is announced as "Renamed _old name_ to _new
name_".

Names nobody typed follow the same rule without asking you. A note that is
still unnamed takes its name from its first heading only when no other
document in its folder already shows that name; otherwise it stays
**Untitled** until you name it. **Duplicate** names the copy
"Name (copy)", or the first "Name (copy 2)", "Name (copy 3)" … that nothing
beside it shows; a copy of an unnamed document starts from what its row shows,
so a copy of a document listed as "Untitled 3" is "Untitled 3 (copy)". The copy is selected in the list, and a
"Duplicated _name_" notice offers **Open** for it.

**Duplicate** copies the whole document, its comments and open proposals
included. **Duplicate without comments**, next to it in a document's menu, in the
preview beside the list, and in an open document's **More actions**, copies only what the document says:
the copy starts with no comment threads and no proposals, and the original
keeps every one of its own. The copy is named and placed the same way, and
the notice reads "Duplicated _name_ without comments". Both
are offered on every document; on one that has no comments they make the
same copy.

A daemon from before **Duplicate without comments** existed copies the
comments anyway. The app notices and says so — "This daemon is too old to
duplicate without comments — update it" — rather than reporting a clean
copy; the copy that daemon made is left for you to keep or delete.

When a duplicate fails, the page reads the list again, in the browser and on
a daemon alike. A failure can come after the copy was already made — the
answer lost on its way back — so when the copy is in the list, the page treats
it as made: the copy is selected and the notice says "Duplicated …", with no
failure shown. Only when no copy arrived does the page say the duplicate
failed, above the list.

A document that has documents under it (`plan` beside `plan/outline`) is
listed as a folder too, but there is no folder of its own to name there, so
its menu has no **Rename…**; rename the document instead.

## Make a new folder

**New folder** above the list (in the two-column view) makes a folder inside
the folder you are in — at the workspace root, a top-level folder. The same entry is in a folder's own
menu, as **New subfolder…** (or **New folder…** on **Workspace** in the folder
path). It asks for a name; **Create folder** opens the new folder, showing the
name you gave it, with keyboard focus on its name in the folder path and a
screen reader told "In _name_, empty". After a move, focus goes to the folder
the document went to (or the document itself, after **Move documents here…**).
Closing any of these dialogs with **Escape** or **Cancel** puts focus back where
you opened it from — the **New folder** button, or the folder or document whose
menu you used.

A folder exists only while a document is in it, and the dialog says so before
you create it: the new folder is empty until you put a document there, and its
name is kept in this browser tab until then — a reload or coming back to the
folder in the same tab still shows it, and so does a folder you make inside it
— and saved with the folder once a document lands in it. A new tab or a new
browser session does not have it. The empty folder offers **New note here** and **New canvas here**,
which create the document inside it, and **Move documents here…**, which lists
every other document in the workspace with a checkbox and where it is now: tick
the ones to file there and choose **Move here**. Leaving it empty lets it go,
name and all. The same duplicate rule as a rename applies.

A `/` nests here exactly as it does in **Move to folder… > New folder…**, and
the dialog says so under its field: `Workshops/Template` makes a folder called
“Workshops” with a folder called “Template” inside it, and opens “Template”. A part that matches a folder already there is that folder, so
only the missing levels are made; typing a path whose every folder already
exists is refused with the last folder's name, since nothing would be made.

The page keeps a folder's name the same way when a move takes the last document
out of it: move a document back in during the same visit and the folder comes
back under its name rather than its address.

# Organize documents with tags

Tags written in a markdown document's properties become searchable and
filterable in the document browser. A board, a box and an edge take tags
too, from the editor's panels.

## Add tags

Open a markdown document, open its properties (the info button beside the
title), and add tags. Tags are OKF frontmatter — they travel with the
document on export.

On a board, tag a box or an edge from its Facets panel: right-click it and
choose **Facets…**, or select it and open **Display**, where the selection's
facets lead the panel; the **Tags** row sits under the visual style. The
board's own tags are in the Display settings, below the selection's, under the
theme.

Every tag row works the same way: type a tag and press Enter or a comma to
finish it, and press a chip's × to remove it. A tag is either a plain word
(`draft`) or a **scoped** `key:value` pair (`health:failing`), and the box
offers what the board and the rest of the workspace already use — the keys
before you type a colon, the values under that key after it. A tag with a colon that is not `key:value`
(`Health:OK`) is refused with the rule; correct it and finish again.

The same rule holds when an agent writes a document's whole markdown body:
`wb_workspace_edit`'s `document.set` and `document.create` ops (and
`POST /api/v1/workspaces/:workspaceId/documents`) refuse a frontmatter tag such
as `Health:OK` or `a:b:c` with the rule, and write nothing. Plain tags
(`Machine Learning`, `v1.2`) pass. A document that already carries such a tag
— imported from another tool, say — still opens and keeps it; it is replaced
only through a write that no longer carries it.

With several boxes selected, a tag added or removed on one is added or
removed on all of them; what each box already carried stays.

## Read the legend

When a board's colours follow a scoped key — every `health:ok` box green,
every `health:failing` box red — a **legend** appears in the board's
top-left corner listing that key's values with the swatch each is drawn
in, boxes and edges each in their own kind of swatch. It is part of the
board, so an SVG or PNG export carries it too; in the editor it collapses
to its title. A board whose colours follow no key has no legend: colour
you chose by hand is yours, and nothing is drawn to say a key does not
explain it. When the legend is there and some other colour is not
explained by a key, one muted line says so.

## Declare the vocabulary

A workspace can say up front which keys exist, which values a key admits,
what colour each value is drawn in, and whether a key is **one value at a
time**. That declaration is a **tag library**: an ordinary markdown
document at the path `tags` carrying the `visual.tags/v0` facet, the same
shape as the [stencil library](define-your-own-stencils.md#growing-the-vocabulary).
It is written through the MCP server — one `wb_facet_set` call on that
document:

```json
{
  "workspaceId": "…",
  "documentIds": ["<the document at tags>"],
  "facets": {
    "visual.tags/v0": {
      "keys": {
        "health": {
          "description": "Whether the component is serving",
          "exclusive": true,
          "values": {
            "ok": { "color": "4" },
            "degraded": { "color": "3" },
            "failing": { "color": "1" }
          }
        },
        "region": { "exclusive": true, "values": { "eu": {}, "us": {} } },
        "phase": {}
      }
    }
  }
}
```

A key with no `values` admits any value; a key with `values` admits only
those. A key that is not `exclusive` may carry several values on one object
(`region:eu` and `region:us` together), which is the default.

What the library changes:

- **A write outside it is refused before anything is written.** Tagging a
  box `health:unknown`, or adding `region:us` to a box already carrying
  `region:eu` under an exclusive key, is refused by `wb_facet_set` with the
  admitted values in the message, and a batch refused on one document has
  written nothing to the others. A document whose markdown body declares
  such a tag in its own properties is refused the same way — when it is
  created and when it is replaced — and a refused create leaves no document
  behind. Every tag row in the editor refuses the same tag by the same rule,
  and keeps what you typed so you can fix it.

  One write is not held to it: what the editor syncs as you type. A sync
  message carries the document's state rather than a request to change it,
  so there is nothing there to refuse; the row you type into is where that
  write is checked.
- **The rows complete from the declaration.** Under a declared key, a tag
  row offers the admitted values beside whatever the workspace already
  uses, on notes, boards, boxes and edges alike.
- **Colour by intent.** A box or an edge that carries a value with a
  declared colour, and has no colour of its own, is drawn in that colour —
  on the board, in the minimap, in a past version's preview, in the
  document browser's cards, its preview pane and Peek, in an SVG or
  PNG export, by `wb_scene_render`, and in the inline view `canvas_view`
  shows in chat — so the legend lists the key because the library said so
  rather than because someone coloured every box by hand. A board drawn
  INSIDE another document is coloured the same way: a file node's
  miniature, a `![[board]]` embed in a note or a text node — on the
  canvas, in the note's preview, and in the document browser's cards,
  preview pane and Peek — and the cached copy you read while the daemon is
  unreachable. A `![[board]]` embedded in a NOTE carries its legend too,
  under the board inside the embed's frame and at the legend's own size, so
  the note's preview, its print or PDF and its export say what the colours
  mean. A file node's miniature and an embed in a canvas text node carry the
  colours only; their legend stays with the board itself. A colour set on the
  box itself always wins, and a box carrying two declared colours under two keys gets
  neither. The board reads the library when it opens, and the document
  browser when it is shown; after editing the `tags` document, reopen the
  board, or return to the browser, to see the change.
- **The declaration is discoverable.** `wb_facet_list` with a
  `workspaceId` answers the library under `tagLibrary` beside the tags in
  use, so an agent can read the vocabulary it will be held to.

## Colour a tag

A tag can be coloured without writing the library by hand, in a workspace the
browser keeps and in one the daemon keeps. In the **Display** panel's **Tags** row (and the same row
in a note's header), open a `key:value` chip's menu and choose **Set
colour…**, then one of the six swatches the box colour row uses, or **No
colour** to take the colour back. The colour is written into the workspace's
tag library, so every box or edge carrying that tag and no colour of its own
is drawn in it, and the legend lists the key — a colour you set on a box with
a swatch stays yours and is never explained by a key, which is why it gets no
legend.

The first colour you set creates the library document at `tags` if the
workspace has none. The document list shows it labelled **Tag library** — on
its card and among search results — and its preview says it keeps the
workspace's tag colours rather than that nothing is written. Deleting it is
allowed, but the confirmation says first that every tag colour set in the
workspace goes with it.

A few things worth knowing:

- Only `key:value` tags have a menu; a plain tag has nowhere in the library
  to be coloured.
- The first colour on a key that declared no values gives that key a list of
  admitted values — the one you coloured and every value the workspace already
  carries under it. A key with values refuses others, so a new value under it
  is then refused until it is added to the library.
- The legend appears when the key tells boxes apart by colour: colouring
  `tier:service` while a box tagged `tier:database` stays uncoloured lists
  both; colouring the only value on the board lists nothing. The keys `frame`,
  `kind` and `stencil` are the board's own distinctions, so a tag under one of
  them is drawn in its colour but never listed.
- The colour is an edit to the `tags` document, not to the board you are on:
  it does not join the board's undo. **No colour** reverses it.
- In a workspace the daemon keeps, the colour is written to the daemon, so a
  daemon that is not reachable refuses it. Over HTTP the same write is
  `PUT /api/v1/workspaces/<id>/tag-library` with `{ "library": { … } }`, the
  whole library, and it needs `canvas:write` like `wb_facet_set`.

## Find by tag

In the document browser:

- The **tag strip** above the file panes lists every tag in use anywhere in
  the workspace — on notes, boards, boxes and edges — plain tags first, then
  each scoped key with its values under it (`health` · ok · failing), each
  with a count of what carries it (hover for the breakdown). Click one to
  filter to the documents carrying it; click it again to clear.
- The **search box** understands two forms: plain text matches tags along
  with names and paths, and `#tag` matches *only* documents carrying exactly
  that tag.
- Document cards and search results show each document's tags.

A board's own tags show in the document browser under either keeper. What
a board's boxes and edges carry is counted on the strip but is never a
document tag: filtering by such a tag finds the boards whose boxes carry
it, and the MCP search (`wb_document_search`) names the matching boxes.

# Report a gesture problem

When a touch or drag on the canvas misbehaves — a press that does not pan, a pinch that jumps —
the app has already recorded what happened. The editor keeps a rolling record of the last ~200
pointer events and what the canvas decided for each one, so you do not need to reproduce the
problem on demand or attach a debugger to your phone.

## Copy the trace

1. Right after the misbehaving gesture, open **Settings**.
2. Open **Developer**.
3. Tap **Copy trace** under *Gesture diagnostics*.

The trace is now on your clipboard as JSON. Paste it into a bug report, an issue, or a chat with
whoever is investigating.

Do this soon after the problem: the record is a rolling window, and roughly 40–60 later
taps will push the interesting events out of it.

## What the trace contains

Event kinds, screen coordinates, the internal names of controls that were pressed, mode names
(such as `panning`), your browser's user-agent string, the running bundle's file name, and the
viewport size. It never contains document content — no text, no node data, no titles.

Nothing is sent anywhere by itself. The trace leaves your device only when you copy and share it.

## What an investigator can do with it

Each pointer entry records the element it landed on and whether it reached the editor at all, so
a trace shows a press consumed by another element in front of it. The canvas's gesture decisions
are also made by a pure function over these events, so a developer can replay a pasted trace in a
test to reproduce the decisions away from your device. The app has no screen or command that
replays a trace for you.

For a developer, the test reads the trace with `parseGestureTrace` and folds it with
`replayNavigation`, both from `apps/web/src/components/spatial-editor/gesture-trace.ts`:

```ts
const trace = parseGestureTrace(pastedText)
const modes = replayNavigation(trace.entries)
```

Each trace carries a `format` number. `parseGestureTrace` throws if the format is missing or is
not the one the current build reads, and also if an entry carries an event type or field the
current build does not know. A trace recorded by an older bundle is refused instead of being
replayed against events whose fields have since changed. If it is refused, ask for a fresh trace
from a device running the current deploy.

# Review proposed changes and restore a version

Two safety nets sit beside every document: the **Proposals** panel, where changes a connected AI
agent wants to make wait for your decision, and **History**, where saved versions of the document
can be previewed and restored.

## Review a proposal

Proposals come only from a connected AI agent. There is no way to propose a change yourself: you
edit the document directly. When an agent works through `wb_body_edit` or `wb_canvas_edit`
without applying directly, its changes are stored as a proposal instead of changing the document,
and they wait in the Proposals panel (and on the document itself) until you adopt or dismiss them.

With no agent connected, or nothing pending, the panel reads "Nothing waiting". To connect an
agent, follow [Quick install](../../README.md#quick-install) in the repository README.

## Find a saved version

Open **History** to list the document's versions. Two kinds appear:

- **Bookmarks** you take with the bookmark button or `⌘/Ctrl+S`.
- **Automatic checkpoints**, saved about five minutes after you stop editing, while the document
  is open. Closing the tab inside that window saves the pending checkpoint as the page goes away;
  the browser treats that write as best-effort.

A document you have never edited for five minutes, or closed abruptly, may therefore show "No
versions yet". Bookmark a point whenever you want one for certain.

## Restore a version

1. Press a version in **History**. The document shows that version read-only, in place of the
   editor, while the live document stays as it was.
2. Press **Restore** (the circular-arrow button at the right of the bar; on a phone it shows the
   icon alone). **Stop viewing** at the left puts the live document back instead.

Restoring is safe to undo: the state you had just before restoring is kept as a version of its
own, and the History panel says so ("Restored. The state before restoring is kept as a version.").
Your pan and zoom on a canvas stay where they were.
