The dev scripts and CI set `differential`; a release leaves it unset, so the Rust core routes. To roll back to the TypeScript, set `WHITEBOARD_CORE=ts` (read when the daemon starts). Check the daemon's log for a `core-load-failed` warning if routing seems to be in TypeScript anyway. | `rust` |
| `WHITEBOARD_CORE_MISMATCH` | What a difference found under `differential` does: `log` reports it, `throw` fails the layout that found it (and a missing artifact fails too), which is what a test run wants. | `log` |
| `WHITEBOARD_CORE_LAYOUT` | Who lays a whole canvas out when the daemon renders it (`wb_scene_render`, the canvas snapshot, and the PNG and SVG file export, `/export` and `/export-svg`): `ts` (the TypeScript), `differential` (both run; the TypeScript's scene is drawn and any difference in the scene, the anchors or the reported degradations is handled as `WHITEBOARD_CORE_MISMATCH` says), or `rust` (the Rust core). The core answers only a layout whose options it can be handed as data (a measurer it can repeat, the bundled light or dark theme as the base appearance, the clean style, the document's own theme or a bundled theme by id); every other layout, and any it declines, is drawn by the TypeScript whatever this says. The core measures with the faces the daemon itself measures with: the vendored Roboto faces and one face for each installed font family. A layout whose installed face the core cannot read (a WOFF file under a `.ttf` name, or a face whose character map lists a character twice) or one over 32 MiB is drawn by the TypeScript, and so is every layout when the faces add up to more than 64 MiB. The dev scripts and CI set `differential`; a release leaves it unset, so the Rust core lays out what it can answer. To roll back to the TypeScript, set `WHITEBOARD_CORE_LAYOUT=ts` (read when the daemon starts); with `WHITEBOARD_CORE=ts` as well, the daemon loads the core only at boot, for OKF Markdown and JSON Canvas. | `rust` |
| `WHITEBOARD_CORE_DIR` | The directory holding the wasm artifact (`whiteboard_wasm.js` and `whiteboard_wasm_bg.wasm`), which the daemon loads at boot to read and write OKF Markdown and JSON Canvas. Unset, the daemon reads the copy its package carries, else `packages/core-wasm/artifacts` beside it in this repository. | unset |
| `VITE_WHITEBOARD_CORE` | The web app's counterpart of `WHITEBOARD_CORE`, read when the app is built or served: `ts`, `differential` or `rust`, for the page and its layout worker alike. Unset, the dev server (`pnpm --filter @kamiazya/whiteboard-web dev`) runs `differential`, a production build routes in `rust`, and a test run routes in `ts`. It is read at build time, so rolling a deployed web app's routing back to the TypeScript is a rebuild with `VITE_WHITEBOARD_CORE=ts`. Every build bundles the wasm, whatever this is set to, because the page reads and writes OKF Markdown and JSON Canvas only through the Rust core: a production build fails unless the artifact is staged first (`pnpm --filter @kamiazya/whiteboard-core-wasm build:wasm`), and `WHITEBOARD_SHIP_CORE_WASM=0` is refused. An unknown value fails the build or the first layout rather than falling back. | `differential` in the dev server, `ts` in a test run, otherwise `rust` |
| `VITE_WHITEBOARD_CORE_LAYOUT` | The web app's counterpart of `WHITEBOARD_CORE_LAYOUT`: who lays a whole canvas out in the page and its layout worker, `ts`, `differential` or `rust`, read when the app is built or served. The core measures with the page's own measurer, which it asks as it lays the canvas out; a layout it cannot be handed or one it declines is drawn by the TypeScript whatever this says: today a board embedded in a note's preview, and the version history's picture of a past board. It needs the core loaded, so with `VITE_WHITEBOARD_CORE=ts` nothing is compared. Rolling a deployed web app's layout back to the TypeScript is a rebuild with `VITE_WHITEBOARD_CORE_LAYOUT=ts`. An unknown value fails the build or the first layout rather than falling back. | whatever `VITE_WHITEBOARD_CORE` is: `differential` in the dev server, `ts` in a test run, otherwise `rust` |
| `VITE_WHITEBOARD_CORE_MISMATCH` | What the web app does with a difference found under `differential`: `log` reports it in the developer console and draws the TypeScript's routes, `throw` fails the layout that found it (and an artifact that cannot be fetched fails too), which is what a browser test run wants. | `log` |
| `MCP_HTTP_DEBUG` | When set to `1`, the HTTP MCP server emits `mcp-http:init` / `mcp-http` log records (JSON lines on stderr, `scope` `mcp-http`) to help diagnose request flow. | unset |
| `WHITEBOARD_OTEL` | Turns on OpenTelemetry tracing for the local daemon (`whiteboard daemon run`), server mode (`whiteboard server run`) and the stdio MCP entry. On for `1`, `true` or `yes`; anything else is off. Without `OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT`, each span is written to **stderr** as one JSON line (`scope` `otel`), which is safe beside stdio JSON-RPC. Off, the tracing SDK is never loaded, so there is no cost. A failure to start the SDK is logged (`initTracing failed; tracing disabled`) and the process carries on untraced rather than refusing to start. See [Observability](../contributing/observability.md) for what is traced. | unset (off) |
| `OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT` | An OTLP/HTTP collector to send spans to, for example `http://localhost:4318`. Setting it turns tracing on by itself; `WHITEBOARD_OTEL` is not also needed. The exporter also honours the standard OTLP variables it reads itself, such as `OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_HEADERS` (credentials for a hosted backend) and `OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_TIMEOUT`. | unset (stderr JSON lines when `WHITEBOARD_OTEL` is on) |
| `WHITEBOARD_OTEL_ROLE` | The `whiteboard.role` span resource attribute for a process whose entry does not name its own. The daemon reports `daemon`, server mode `server`, and the stdio entry `stdio-mcp`, so you normally never set this. | `unknown` |
| `WHITEBOARD_FILE_GC_INTERVAL_MS` | How often the background file-GC sweeper runs `purgeDanglingFiles` across every workspace (DB-registered plus upload-only workspaces found on disk). Must be a bare non-negative base-10 integer string (`/^\d+$/`); a present value that is anything else (`1.5`, `1x`, negative, scientific notation, or beyond `Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER`) **aborts startup** rather than silently becoming the default; blank counts as unset. Surrounding whitespace is trimmed, since it is a transport artifact of compose files and shell quoting rather than an intent. Accepted values above `2147483647` (the `setTimeout` maximum, ~24.8 days) are clamped down to that maximum. `0` disables the periodic sweep entirely — dangling files then accumulate until purged manually via the purge route. Runs in both the local daemon and server mode; in server mode every instance sweeps, with no lease between them (see [ADR-0020](../contributing/adr/0020-coordination-boundary.md)). | `86400000` (24h) |
| `WHITEBOARD_FILE_GC_GRACE_MS` | Minimum age (by file mtime) an unreferenced upload must reach before a purge pass — manual or via the periodic sweeper — deletes it. Protects the window between an upload finishing and the document edit that references it landing. Must be a bare non-negative base-10 integer string (`/^\d+$/`), the same strictness as `WHITEBOARD_FILE_GC_INTERVAL_MS` above; a present value that is anything else **aborts startup**. Lenient parsing would read `1h` as **1 millisecond** and `30m` as 30, collapsing the very window this setting exists to hold open, so a freshly-written upload would be deleted before the save referencing it landed. | `3600000` (1h) |
| `WHITEBOARD_WORKSPACE_TAIL_MS` | How often this instance — a local daemon or a server-mode keeper — follows the stored record for each workspace that has a connected client (a live-sync event stream), so a browser attached to THIS instance receives what ANOTHER process wrote. **The local daemon (`whiteboard daemon run`, and the dev daemon) follows every 500 ms unless you set it**, because the agent's `stdio` process is a second writer over the same data directory: an edit the agent makes reaches an open page within about half a second (96-403 ms measured end to end), and nothing is polled while no page is subscribed. A pass over a workspace nothing wrote to is one read of its frontier — 0.5ms for one subscribed workspace, 2-3ms for ten, 12-20ms for fifty, about 0.1%, 0.5% and 2.4-4% of a core at 500 ms. **Server mode follows only when set** — a single instance already learns about its own writes and would be polling for nothing — so set it when more than one instance serves one record ([Running several instances](../how-to/self-host-with-docker.md#running-several-instances)). Must be a bare positive base-10 integer string. `0` and a blank value mean off — `0` is how you stop the local daemon following without removing the variable — while anything else (`2s`, `1.5`, `-1`, `1e3`) **aborts startup**, so a mistyped value neither becomes an unintended interval nor silently disables following you asked for. Propagation is eventual by design ([ADR-0020](../contributing/adr/0020-coordination-boundary.md)): a client that misses a round converges on the next one, so this is a latency dial rather than a correctness one. Independently of the tail, every process reads through to the stored record on each workspace access (one frontier read, about 0.1ms), so a request is never answered from a copy another process has already outdated. A pass that finds a write is not free: catching one workspace up is CPU-bound and holds the daemon for the duration — measured at 7.7ms for a small record, and 283ms for one with 300 commits of history that gained 50 — and a pass pays that once per subscribed workspace. A short interval over many workspaces that are all being written spends most of the daemon on following. | `500` (local daemon); unset, off (server mode) |
| `WHITEBOARD_REPLICA_TIER` | The read plane's default offline-replica tier (see [the security model](../explanation/security-model.md#replica-key-offline-read-plane)): `no-offline` (the daemon refuses to hand out a workspace's content key at all), `offline` (handed out with no expiry), or `bounded` (handed out with a `leaseExpiresAt`, which the browser — not this daemon — honours). Precedence: a per-workspace override set via `PUT /api/workspaces/:workspaceId/replica-tier` (`runtime:admin` bar) wins when present; otherwise this env var; otherwise `offline`. `PUT { tier: null }` clears the override back to that same fallback chain. Blank counts as unset; any other value **aborts startup**. | `offline` |
| `WHITEBOARD_REPLICA_LEASE_TTL_MS` | How long a `bounded`-tier lease lasts before the browser must discard the key it was handed. Must be a bare non-negative base-10 integer string, the same strictness as `WHITEBOARD_FILE_GC_INTERVAL_MS`; a present value that is anything else **aborts startup**. Has no effect unless the effective tier is `bounded`. | `604800000` (7 days) |
| `WHITEBOARD_DATABASE_URL` | Where this instance's rows live. Unset means the file in the data directory, which is what a single daemon has always used. More than one instance cannot share that file — SQLite's locking does not survive a network filesystem, and two machines cannot share a local one at all — so point every instance at one libSQL server instead (`libsql://…`, `https://…`, or `http://…` for a loopback sqld in development). A value that is not a URL, or uses another scheme, or uses `http:` for a non-loopback host, **aborts startup**: falling back to the local file would give each instance its own database, diverging with no error anywhere. The files that are not rows still live in the data directory, so a shared volume serves them: `tenants/<tenantId>/blobs/…` (the content of deleted documents, kept for the trash) and `tenants/<tenantId>/workspaces/<id>/files/` (uploaded images). Setting this makes `whiteboard server backup` report the database as out of scope rather than captured — it still copies the blobs, which nothing else is backing up, and names what is yours to arrange. `whiteboard server restore` then accepts such a backup only into a deployment that also keeps its rows elsewhere. `backup` still refuses a directory that is *supposed* to hold the rows and does not, since these commands run host-side where a container's env-file is not loaded — and it reads `<dataDir>/storage.json`, which the server writes each time it opens its database, so a stale `whiteboard.db` left behind when you moved the rows out is left out of the copy rather than travelling into the backup as if it were current — along with its `-wal`/`-shm` sidecars, since the newest commits live in the `-wal` and a fragment of them is no better than the whole fossil. | unset (the data directory's `whiteboard.db`, opened in WAL mode) |
| `WHITEBOARD_BACKUP_DIR` | Where scheduled backups are written, and the setting that turns them ON. Unset means no scheduled backups — there is no destination worth guessing, since writing copies beside the data they protect is not a backup and anywhere else is a path only you know. Must be an ABSOLUTE path: a relative one resolves against the daemon's working directory, which is whatever your init system happened to pick, so `./backups` would mean something specific to you and land somewhere else. Each pass writes one timestamped directory (`2026-03-04T05-06-07.000Z`) holding that night's rows, plus `blobs.json` listing the blobs it needs. The blobs themselves live ONCE in a shared `blobs/` and `files/` beside those directories, not inside each one ([ADR-0021](../contributing/adr/0021-durability-boundary.md) decision 5) — measured on a 51MB store growing 5% a day, seven retained backups took **403MB** as whole copies and **66MB** as a mirror, and the pass stopped getting slower as the store grew (486ms to 147ms at day six). Retention deletes a blob only when no retained backup still references it, so a blob your documents have finished with survives as long as a backup that needs it does. A backup is assembled under `<name>.incomplete`, and only when every store has finished is every file in it flushed to disk and the directory renamed into place, so a directory with a timestamped name is always a complete one, across a crash or power loss too; if a pass is killed outright you may see an `.incomplete` left behind, which nothing counts as a backup and the next pass clears. Consequence worth knowing: a single timestamped directory from here is NOT restorable on its own — carry the whole backup directory. A one-off `whiteboard server backup --json --output-dir=X` still keeps its mirror inside X and remains carryable. Backups are taken WITHOUT stopping the server ([ADR-0021](../contributing/adr/0021-durability-boundary.md) decision 3), and in a separate process, so a snapshot does not stall the one that is serving you — measured at 1107ms of total unresponsiveness in-process against 100ms out of it, for a 100MB database, and the in-process figure grows with the database. If you run several instances over one data directory, **one of them takes each night's backup** — they agree through a lease row in the database they already share ([ADR-0020](../contributing/adr/0020-coordination-boundary.md)), so you set this the same way on every instance and get one backup rather than N. Retention is inside that lease with the backup, since N instances pruning would each be deleting from a set the others are changing. An instance that cannot reach the shared database skips the pass rather than assuming it is alone. | unset (no scheduled backups) |
| `WHITEBOARD_BACKUP_CRON` | **When** scheduled backups run, as a 5- or 6-field cron expression. Cron rather than an interval because an interval cannot say *when*: "every 24h" starts 24 hours after the daemon last restarted — whenever the container happened to come up — so it lands mid-working-day as readily as at night. A backup is a database snapshot plus a copy of every blob, which is real load, and only you know your quiet window. An expression that cannot be parsed **aborts startup**; so does one that can never fire (`0 0 30 2 *` is valid cron for the 30th of February, and a scheduler armed with it is configured, plausible-looking and permanently idle). Has no effect without `WHITEBOARD_BACKUP_DIR`, and setting it alone aborts startup. | `0 3 * * *` (daily at 03:00) |
| `WHITEBOARD_BACKUP_TZ` | The IANA zone `WHITEBOARD_BACKUP_CRON` is read in — `Asia/Tokyo`, `Europe/Berlin`. **Usually you do not need this.** Unset, the schedule follows the zone the process is already keeping time in, so setting `TZ` for the deployment (which also dates your logs) is enough; the zone is read via `Intl`, not `TZ` directly, because Windows has no such variable and takes its zone from the OS. What an unset value costs you is nothing but the override — a container with no zone configured at all runs on **UTC**, which is why a carefully chosen 3am can turn out to be someone's afternoon. Set this only when backups should run on a different clock from the rest of the deployment. Either way the daemon logs the zone it resolved and the instant the next pass falls on when it starts, so which 3am you got is checkable rather than inferred. An unknown zone **aborts startup** — but only when you set it: a system zone the scheduler cannot read (a blank `TZ`, or a POSIX offset like `JST-9` that names no IANA zone) costs the name in that log line and nothing else, since the schedule still runs on the process's own clock. Has no effect without `WHITEBOARD_BACKUP_DIR`. | unset (the zone the process runs in) |
| `WHITEBOARD_BACKUP_KEEP` | How many scheduled backups to keep; older ones are deleted after each successful pass. Retention counts only the directories this scheduler wrote, so your own files alongside them are neither deleted nor counted against the window. A failed pass deletes nothing — otherwise a bad night leaves you with fewer backups than before you configured this. `0` **aborts startup**: it would mean taking a backup and immediately deleting every backup including that one. Has no effect without `WHITEBOARD_BACKUP_DIR`, and setting it alone aborts startup. | `7` |
| `WHITEBOARD_DATABASE_AUTH_TOKEN` | Bearer token for `WHITEBOARD_DATABASE_URL` when the server requires one (Turso, an authenticated sqld). Ignored for a `file:` database. Empty or whitespace is treated as unset rather than sent as an empty credential. | unset |

## Auto-opening the browser (`whiteboard daemon run`)

`whiteboard daemon run` opens the official hosted app
(`https://kamiazya-whiteboard.pages.dev/`) in your default browser once the
daemon is listening. The daemon itself serves no page: the app reaches it
through the whiteboard browser extension (see
[Connect to a local daemon](../how-to/connect-to-local-daemon.md)).

This only happens when ALL of the following hold; any one failing suppresses
it silently (logged at `debug`, never printed to stdout/stderr):

- you did not pass `--no-open` or set `openBrowser: false` in a
  [config file](#config-file-local-daemon),
- stdout is an interactive TTY (so scripts, CI runners, and piped output never
  trigger it),
- `CI` is not set in the environment,
- the process is not running inside a container (Docker, Podman, …).

Honored on the `whiteboard daemon run` CLI path only — `server/index.ts` (the
dev-watch entrypoint behind `pnpm mcp:http:dev`) and `whiteboard server run`
(server-mode) never call this, so repeated `tsx watch` restarts during local
development do not spawn a new tab per restart, and a server-mode deployment
never pops a browser on its host.

### Wildcard subdomain patterns

`WHITEBOARD_SERVER_ALLOWED_ORIGINS` (server mode) accepts a
`https://*.example.com`-shaped entry alongside exact origins. This is
meant for deployment-preview shapes such as Cloudflare Pages branch previews
(`https://*.your-project.pages.dev`), where every branch gets its own
subdomain and listing each one explicitly is impractical.

Rules:

- The wildcard `*` must be the **entire leftmost label** and nothing else —
  `https://*.example.com` is valid; `https://foo*.example.com`,
  `https://*.*.example.com`, and bare `*` are all rejected.
- Only **one label** is matched: `https://preview.example.com` matches
  `https://*.example.com`, but `https://a.b.example.com` does not.
- The pattern must be `https://` — wildcards are never accepted for
  loopback `http://` origins.
- The static suffix after the wildcard must retain at least two labels
  (`example.com`, not `.dev` or `.com` alone). This is a structural check,
  not a public-suffix-list lookup — **`https://*.pages.dev` passes it but
  admits every Cloudflare Pages project**, not just yours. Always scope the
  pattern to your own project label, e.g.
  `https://*.your-project.pages.dev`.

## Config file (local daemon)

As an alternative to exporting env vars by hand, every command that locates the
local daemon — `whiteboard daemon *`, `whiteboard mcp`, `whiteboard native-host`
and `whiteboard search fetch-model` — and the `server/index.ts` HTTP entrypoint
auto-load a config file. Only the current working directory is searched — ancestor directories
are deliberately NOT walked up, so a config file planted in a parent
directory (e.g. the root of an untrusted cloned repo) can never inject a
token. The first match wins, searched in this
order in the current directory:

1. `.whiteboardrc`
2. `.whiteboardrc.json`
3. `.whiteboardrc.yaml`
4. `.whiteboardrc.yml`
5. `.whiteboard/config.yaml`
6. `.whiteboard/config.yml`
7. `whiteboard.config.json`
8. `package.json` (`"whiteboard"` field)

`~/.whiteboard/config.yaml` is read as well, as the per-machine defaults —
so a `dataDir` in it redirects every command, wherever it is run. A file found
in the current directory is layered on top: each key it sets wins over the
home file's, and every key it does not set keeps the home file's value.

**A config file in the current directory may not set `dataDir` or `token`.**
The current directory is wherever you, or an MCP client, started the command —
for `whiteboard mcp` that is usually whatever repository is open, which may be
one you cloned and never read. A file there choosing where your data lives or
which token guards the daemon would let that repository's author take it over.
So a current-directory file that sets either key stops the command with exit
code 1 and a message naming the file and the key; it may still set `logLevel`
and `openBrowser`. Put `dataDir` and `token` in `~/.whiteboard/config.yaml`,
the only file that may set them (there is no flag that names a config file).
For the same reason a current-directory file may not use `$import` (the
config loader's key for pulling in another file): it would make the command
read and parse any file you can read, before any key is checked. Such a file
stops the command the same way, before the file it names is opened.
`~/.whiteboard/config.yaml` may still use `$import`.
Likewise, every file in the list above that exists in the current directory
must be a regular file of at most 1 MiB, and `.whiteboard` there must be a
real directory: a symbolic link, a FIFO or a device in any of those places
stops the command before anything is read. A link would let the
repository choose which of your files gets parsed — and a parse error quotes
what it read — and a FIFO would hang startup. Every listed place is checked,
not only the one that would win. `~/.whiteboard/config.yaml` may still be a
link (or live in a linked `~/.whiteboard`), as a dotfile manager leaves it.
When the current directory IS your home directory, that file is found there
and keeps its trust, and the files there are not held to this check. A current-directory file that sets only `logLevel`
therefore changes the log level and nothing else: your home `dataDir` and
`token` still apply. Only declarative JSON/YAML/rc formats
are supported — `whiteboard.config.js` and similar JS loaders are deliberately
NOT searched, so a config file can never execute code at daemon startup.

Example `.whiteboard/config.yaml`:

```yaml
logLevel: info
openBrowser: false
```

Supported keys: `token`, `logLevel` (`debug` / `info` / `notice` / `warning` / `error` /
`critical` / `alert` / `emergency`), `dataDir`, and `openBrowser` (boolean;
see [Auto-opening the browser](#auto-opening-the-browser-whiteboard-daemon-run)).
Unknown keys are logged as a warning and dropped rather than silently
ignored — `port` and `allowedWebOrigins`, which configured the loopback
listener the daemon no longer has, now land there too; an invalid value
(wrong type, unknown level, etc.) aborts
startup with an error naming the file path and the offending key.

**Precedence: command-line flag > environment variable > config file > built-in
default.** Any `WHITEBOARD_*` env var that is already set always wins over the
same value in a config file, and `--data-dir` wins over both. The file is read
once per command, so `whiteboard daemon run` and the commands that look for the
daemon it started (`status`, `stop`, `doctor`, `support-bundle`, …) agree on
the data directory. A malformed file stops each of these commands with exit
code 1 and the file path, rather than letting one of them look in a different
directory from the rest. The daemon logs which config file it loaded (path
only, never the token value) at startup.

Two scoped exceptions worth knowing:

- **`dataDir`** is not honored by `whiteboard server *` (server mode takes
  `--data-dir` or `WHITEBOARD_DATA_DIR`; a container has no daemon config file)
  or by the `server/index.ts` HTTP entrypoint, which resolves its data directory
  at module import time, before a config file can be loaded — a `dataDir` key
  there produces a startup warning instead of silently doing nothing; use
  `WHITEBOARD_DATA_DIR` on that entrypoint instead.
- **`openBrowser`** is honored on the `whiteboard daemon run` CLI path only —
  see [Auto-opening the browser](#auto-opening-the-browser-whiteboard-daemon-run).
  An explicit `--no-open` flag always wins over this key.

**Security note:** a `token` value in a config file is a dev-only
convenience — treat it like a `.env` file with a secret in it (do not commit
it, restrict its file permissions). Prefer `WHITEBOARD_DAEMON_TOKEN` (or
`--token-stdin`) for anything beyond local development.

## Live-sync stream limits

A page receives live edits over one event stream (`GET /api/sync/stream`;
any other method, `HEAD` included, is answered `405` with `Allow: GET` and
opens nothing).
The web app opens **one stream per browser profile**, shared by all of its tabs
through a SharedWorker; where SharedWorker is unavailable (Chrome on Android)
each tab opens its own. These limits are fixed, not configurable:

| Limit | Value | Applies to | When it is reached |
|---|---|---|---|
| Open streams per user | 16 | server mode | The next open is refused with `429 too_many_streams` and `Retry-After: 5`. The page keeps retrying with backoff and connects once one of that user's streams closes. |
| Open streams in total, per instance | 1024 | server mode | Same refusal, for everyone, until a stream closes. |
| Data written to a stream and not yet read by the page | about 43.7 MiB (two of the largest possible updates) | server mode and the local daemon | The keeper ends that stream. The page reconnects, subscribes again and reads what it missed from the keeper, so a slow reader loses nothing. |
| Data written to all of one user's streams and not yet read | about 87.3 MiB (two streams' worth) | server mode | The keeper ends that user's oldest stream that has data waiting, and keeps doing so until the total fits. Each page reconnects as above, so nothing is lost. |
| Data written to every stream on the instance and not yet read | about 349.3 MiB (eight streams' worth) | server mode and the local daemon | The keeper ends the oldest stream on the instance that has data waiting, whoever holds it, until the total fits. |

In server mode a stream belongs to the user who opened it: only that user may
subscribe it to a workspace, and a credential that names no user of the
tenant cannot open one (`403 requires_person_session`). Before each update is
sent down a stream, the instance holding it re-checks that its user is still a
member of the workspace and not deactivated, and ends the stream if not — so a
removal or deactivation made on another instance, or with
`whiteboard server deactivate-user`, takes effect on streams that are already
open. On the instance that handles the change it is immediate: removing someone
from a workspace ends their streams that follow that workspace, and
deactivating them ends every stream they hold.

## Large request limits

The requests that carry stored content — a document's or a workspace's sync
`update`, a workspace `promote`, a file upload, and an `/api/v1` document
created from its content — have bodies of up to 16 MiB (24 MiB for a
promote), and each is read whole before it is applied. A `POST /mcp`
JSON-RPC request, up to 4 MiB, is read whole too and counts the same way. Server mode therefore
limits how many of them it reads at once. These limits are fixed, not
configurable:

| Limit | Value | Applies to | When it is reached |
|---|---|---|---|
| Such requests in flight per user | 4 | server mode | The next one is refused with `429 too_many_requests` and `Retry-After: 1`, before any of its body is read. The web app's sync retries it after that delay, so an edit is delayed, not lost. |
| Such requests in flight in total, per instance | 16 | server mode | Same refusal, for everyone, until one finishes. |

On `/mcp` the refusal is the same `429` and `Retry-After: 1`, with a JSON-RPC
error body (`{"jsonrpc":"2.0","error":{"code":-32000,…},"id":null}`) rather
than `too_many_requests`. A call answered as an event stream (one that sends
progress or log messages before its result) counts until that stream ends,
not merely until it opens; a `subscriptions/listen` stream does not count.
A JSON-RPC batch (a body that is an array, which the 2025-03-26 protocol
revision allows) counts once for each request in it, since its requests run
at the same time: one holding more requests than the caller has room for is
refused whole with the same `429`, after its body is read and before any of
it runs.
A caller whose grant names no user on this instance
(a token for no person, or a person with no user here) is counted with every
other such caller as one user, so together they hold at most the per-user
limit.

A request counts from the moment its route starts reading the body until it
is answered, so ordinary edits, which are small and quick, rarely meet either
limit. The local daemon serves one person and applies neither.

## MCP stream limits

Two kinds of `/mcp` stream carry no tool call. Server mode bounds both; the
local daemon serves one person and leaves both as they are:

| Stream | Server mode | When it is reached |
|---|---|---|
| The legacy standalone stream (`GET /mcp`) | Not offered | Answered `405 Method Not Allowed` with `Allow: POST, DELETE`, as the MCP specification provides for a server that offers no such stream. Nothing is ever sent down it, so a client loses nothing: the MCP SDK's client treats a `405` here as "no stream". |
| `subscriptions/listen` streams open per user | 16 | The next one is refused with `429` and a JSON-RPC error body (`{"jsonrpc":"2.0","error":{"code":-32000,…},"id":null}`). A place frees when one of that user's streams ends, errors or is closed by its client. |
| `subscriptions/listen` streams open in total, per instance | 1024 | Same refusal, for everyone, until a stream closes. |

As with the large request limits, every caller whose grant names no user on
this instance counts as one user.

## Workspace limits

Every member of a server-mode tenant shares one workspace registry, so server
mode bounds how many workspaces one person's namespace holds. The limit is
fixed, not configurable:

| Limit | Value | Applies to | When it is reached |
|---|---|---|---|
| Workspaces per person's namespace | 1000 | server mode | The next create is refused and nothing is written: `POST /api/workspaces` answers `413 {"error":"too_many_workspaces"}`, and a tool call through `/mcp` with `createWorkspace: true` is refused with an error naming `too_many_workspaces`. Workspaces the person has joined in other namespaces do not count. |

A workspace moving into a namespace counts as a create there. Demoting or
removing the owner who holds a workspace, when it would move to a co-owner
whose namespace is full, is refused: `PATCH` or `DELETE
/api/workspaces/<workspace>/people/<user>` answers
`413 {"error":"too_many_workspaces"}` and nothing changes. Deleting a person
skips an owner whose namespace is full for the next-oldest one with room;
with none, the workspace is reachable by its identifier alone until an
operator's `whiteboard server grant-member` gives it an owner with room.

The limit is held per instance: creates landing at the same moment through
several instances of one deployment can each take the last place, leaving the
namespace a few past it. The local daemon serves one person and applies no
limit.

## Version history limits

The daemon keeps a bounded history per document, on the local daemon and in
server mode alike. These limits are fixed, not configurable:

| Limit | Value | When it is reached |
|---|---|---|
| Automatic checkpoints per document | 50 | The oldest are removed as new ones are taken. A restore's merge point, and the version it restored, are kept. |
| Manual versions per document | 200 | The next manual save — `POST …/documents/<path>/versions` or `wb_version_save` — is refused with `413 {"error":"too_many_versions"}` and nothing is saved. A promote into a document already at the limit still lands its content and skips the version it would have recorded there. Automatic checkpoints keep being taken. |
| Restore points per document | 200 | A restore records a merge point on each document it changed — one per document for a subtree restore — and these points are never removed. Past the limit a restore still lands its content and records no further point there. A restore that changes nothing (the document already holds that content) records no point at all. |
| Versions per page of `GET …/documents/<path>/versions` | 100 | The answer carries `nextCursor`; pass it back as `?cursor=` for the next, older page. `?limit=` asks for a shorter page. The web app reads every page. |

## Codex sandbox constraints

Inside the Codex sandbox, two issues are common:

- **Writing to `~/.whiteboard` may fail.** Without `WHITEBOARD_DATA_DIR`, the app falls back to `$TMPDIR/.whiteboard-<uid>` (owner-only; a directory another user owns or can write, or a symlink, is refused) and logs a warning naming that path. A temp directory is not durable, and a daemon or browser running outside the sandbox looks in `~/.whiteboard`, so work an agent saves there is not seen by them. Set `WHITEBOARD_DATA_DIR` to a directory both sides can reach.
- **Creating the daemon's socket may be blocked.** The daemon listens on a Unix socket under `$XDG_RUNTIME_DIR/whiteboard/` (or a `whiteboard-<uid>` directory in the temp directory); a sandbox that forbids creating or listening on it fails daemon startup. Run in an environment that allows it or adjust the sandbox configuration.

## Storage layout

A data directory holds, at its top level, what belongs to the keeper rather than to any one tenant:

- `whiteboard.db` — the SQLite database: workspaces, document snapshots and deltas, versions, and the sign-in and membership rows
- `daemon.json` — the running daemon's record (socket and token); owner-only
- `daemon-identity.json` and `macaroon-root-key.json` — the daemon's signing identity and the key its credentials are minted from; owner-only
- `fonts/` — fonts installed through the app
- `models/` — the semantic-search model weights, once `whiteboard search fetch-model` has downloaded them; left out of every backup, so run it again after a restore

A workspace's uploaded images sit under the tenant that owns them — on a local daemon there is one. The documents themselves, their versions and the index are rows in `whiteboard.db`, not files:

- `tenants/<tenantId>/workspaces/<workspaceId>/files/<fileId>` — a workspace's uploaded images
- `tenants/<tenantId>/blobs/<first 2 hex of the digest>/<rest>` — the content of each document deleted from a workspace, kept so the trash can restore it, and destroyed once that document is restored or deleted permanently from the trash

A data directory that still holds an earlier release's layout — `blobs/` or a `<workspaceId>/files/` at its top, or `trusted-web-origins.json` — is refused at startup rather than rearranged; the error says how to export its documents and import them into a fresh one.

Files a person asked to have written out (an exported PNG or SVG) land in `<workspaceId>/exports/` at the top of the data directory, not under the tenant. No MCP tool writes files into the tree: `wb_scene_render` and `wb_document_get` answer in the tool result.

See [architecture](../explanation/architecture.md) for how each layer reads and writes this tree.

# Export formats

The MCP server exposes two export-shaped tools, each rendered headlessly from
the document's persisted content — neither requires a connected browser client.

| Tool | Output | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `wb_document_get` | The document's own format | A markdown document comes back as OKF Markdown (YAML frontmatter + Markdown body), lossless round-trip with `wb_workspace_edit`'s `document.set` op. A spatial document comes back as JSON Canvas 1.0 with the `x-whiteboard` extension, round-tripping with other JSON Canvas-compatible tools. Either kind also carries the document's comment `threads` beside `content` when it has any; the conversations are not part of either format's content. |
| `wb_scene_render` | Vector image (`.svg`) | Rendered from the document's spatial layout (canvas-render's scene graph + SVG backend) — shapes, laid-out Markdown text, and routed edges. A canvas's comments (pins, cards, region outlines, highlighted passages) are left out unless the call passes `comments: true`. |

**The format is not a parameter.** `wb_document_get` answers in whatever
format the document is in, and says which in its `kind` field; there is no
"read this diagram as Markdown". SVG is the one cross-format output, and it is
an explicitly lossy projection rather than a way to read the stored content
(see [ADR-0009](../contributing/adr/0009-mcp-tool-naming.md)).

**An edge between two boxes that touch is drawn as a mark, not a route.**
When the boxes share a stretch of border, or overlap without one holding the
other, there is no distance to route through, so the edge is drawn as one
arrowhead whose tip sits on the target's facing side, centred on the stretch
the two facing sides share. Every routing style draws it the same way, on
the canvas, in the exports and in `wb_scene_render`. An edge that names a
side the contact does not use, or stores its own bends, is routed as before.
Boxes any distance apart, however small, are routed as usual.

**The daemon does not typeset math or draw diagrams.** `wb_scene_render`, the
daemon's `POST …/export` and the `canvas_view` widget draw a `$$` math block as
its TeX source as text, and a `` ```mermaid `` fence as a plain code
block. Inline `$…$` math is drawn as its source text everywhere, the web app
included. Fenced code blocks are syntax-coloured for the languages the layout
knows (the note preview, the daemon's renders and the exports alike), in the
light or dark palette of the surface they are drawn on. Footnotes are not
supported: `[^1]` stays in the text as written and its `[^1]: …` definition
is drawn as an ordinary paragraph where it was written. In the web app, the note preview, the canvas editor, a past version
opened from version history, and a canvas's SVG/PNG exports (see
[Web app exports](#web-app-exports)) typeset math blocks and draw Mermaid
diagrams — in the document's own text, in a note or board it embeds with
`![[…]]`, and in the note a canvas file node shows. A past version resolves no
embed, so there only the version's own text is typeset. On screen a block
shows its source until its engine has rendered it; an export waits for every
one. The thumbnails and previews in the web app's document list draw them as
source. A Mermaid diagram's labels are drawn as SVG text, so a `$$…$$` label
shows its source and HTML in a label shows as written; a diagram whose
`%%{init}%%` asks for HTML text stays a plain code block (see the
[security model](../explanation/security-model.md#math-and-diagrams-drawn-from-document-text-web-app)).

A document created before formats were recorded has no answer here and is
refused rather than guessed at; writing its content through a `document.set` op
gives it one.

A `file` node renders as a labeled box when exported to SVG; its referenced image
is not embedded in the output.

An inline Markdown image (`![alt](url)`) in a body draws its picture when the
surface resolves the URL to a workspace attachment, or when the URL is
`http:`, `https:` or `data:`. Any other URL — a bare or relative file path,
`file:` — draws as its alt text. A picture that is the whole of its paragraph
draws at its natural size, scaled down to the body's width, where the surface
knows that size: the web app's preview, read view, print and list thumbnail
decode it. Elsewhere, and for a picture inside a sentence, it is drawn one line
tall. The daemon's PNG export goes one step
further and draws only `data:` images: it never reads a file the URL names on
the daemon's host, and never fetches a remote one. Of those it draws only PNG,
JPEG, GIF, WebP and SVG, written as `data:<type>,…` or `data:<type>;base64,…`
with no other parameter, and only when it can read the image's size from its
header. An SVG image that asks for filter effects (a `<filter>`, a filter
primitive, or a `filter` attribute or style), uses a mask (a `<mask>`, or a
`mask` attribute, or a `mask` or `mask-*` style), declares an XML entity, or
holds an image of its own also draws nothing in a PNG: the time or memory its
drawing takes is not bounded by its size. Any other image draws nothing.

## How large a markdown document may be

One markdown write — the `markdown` field of a `wb_workspace_edit`
`document.create` or `document.set` op, or of `POST /api/v1/workspaces/{id}/documents`
— carries at most **262,144 characters** (256 Ki UTF-16 code units, frontmatter
and body together). A longer one is refused with "markdown is longer than the
262144-character limit for one document" before anything is stored. The count is
characters, not bytes, because the cost of storing a document follows the
character count: the limit is where one write still finishes in about a second.
`wb_body_edit` is held to the same ceiling: an edit that would leave the body
longer than that is refused, though an edit that shrinks an already-longer
body is accepted. Split longer content across documents.

The editor's own writes are bounded too, by the same number and the same
rule — growing a body past it is refused, shrinking one already past it is
not:

- **The markdown editor** refuses a paste or keystroke that would take the
  document past 262,144 characters, leaves the document as it was, and says
  so in a notice at the top of the editor.
- **A browser-kept workspace** does not save a body past the limit: the page
  goes back to what is stored, undoing that change and anything typed after it,
  and a notice at the top says the change was not saved and why. A refusal from
  the daemon's sync routes below is answered the same way, and never retried.
- **The daemon's sync routes** — a document's `update`, the workspace
  document's `update` and `promote` — answer `413` with
  `{"error":"markdown_too_large"}` and store nothing. They also refuse, in
  milliseconds, an update that inserts more than 262,144 characters in one
  piece, before applying it, and the same for an update of several separate
  inserts that together cost more to apply than one of that size: the cost of
  an insert grows with the square of its length, so two inserts of 200,000
  characters are refused while any number of the short inserts an editor
  sends are not. A promoted workspace is judged by its whole
  history: if a note once took one paste past the limit, even one cut back
  since, a workspace that already holds documents refuses it, naming the
  document, while a workspace with no documents yet takes it whole, since
  nothing is replayed there. The same `update` and `promote` refuse, with
  `400 {"error":"invalid_path"}`, an update or record that would put a document
  or a folder at a path outside the path grammar or longer than 1,024
  characters — which is also what keeps a tree of folders from nesting
  deeper than a path can name; a document already at such a path can still be
  moved to a valid one. The
  workspace document's `update` also refuses, with
  `400 {"error":"unreadable_document_meta"}`, an update that would leave a
  readable document or folder with meta this server cannot read — a document's
  kind, segment, id or timestamps, or any key on a folder besides its segment —
  which would hide it and everything below it. A document's `update` refuses,
  with `400 {"error":"invalid_document_root"}`, an update that adds a root
  container named after one of a document node's own keys (`documentId`,
  `segment`, `kind`, `name`, `nameChosen`, `createdAt`, `updatedAt`), or a
  content container under its own name but of another kind (a text named
  `nodes`). The workspace document's `update` and `promote` refuse it too, for
  an update or record that leaves a document's content container key
  (`nodes`, `body`, `threads` and the others) holding a plain value, a
  container of another kind, or nothing. A document's `update` and the
  workspace document's `update` and `promote` refuse, with
  `400 {"error":"document_kind_changed"}`, an update or record that leaves a
  document's envelope `kind` saying anything other than the kind its
  workspace node records; setting it on an unkinded document to that same
  kind is how a keeper claims one, and lands. A document's `update` and the
  workspace document's `update` and `promote` refuse, with
  `400 {"error":"reserved_map_key"}`, an update or record that writes a key
  named `__proto__` — a map entry, a root container, or a key inside a stored
  value; deleting one a record already holds lands. The workspace document's
  `update` and `promote` refuse, with `400 {"error":"retired_stored_shape"}`, an
  update or record that newly writes a shape an older version stored and this
  one no longer reads — a node, edge or canvas setting under `x-whiteboard`, a
  node in the node-kind union before `file`, `link` and `group` were reworked,
  a markdown body stored as an `okf-body` text node, or entries in the
  Excalidraw `elements` list — and, with `400 {"error":"retired_comment_plane"}`,
  a row in the flat `comments` plane. Deleting one a record already holds
  lands, so does an edit to a document that already holds one and adds none,
  and a promote into a workspace with no documents yet is refused naming the
  document, since there every shape the record holds is new. The workspace
  document's `update` also refuses, with
  `400 {"error":"document_name_too_long"}`, an update that gives a document a
  name longer than 200 characters. A name stored longer before that bound can
  still be kept or shortened. It refuses, with
  `400 {"error":"folder_name_refused"}`, an update that gives a folder a name
  that is blank, holds a `/` or is longer than 200 characters; a folder name
  stored before can still be kept or repaired. The workspace document's `update` and `promote`
  refuse, with `413 {"error":"too_many_documents"}`, an update or record that
  would leave the workspace holding more than 2000 documents; a workspace that
  already holds more still takes edits that add no document, and deleting is
  how it shrinks. Every other way a document is added holds the same ceiling
  and answers it the same way: a document's `update` to a path no document
  holds yet, `POST /api/v1/workspaces/{id}/documents`, a duplicate, a restore
  from the trash, and a version restored to a new path. `wb_workspace_edit`'s
  `document.create` refuses at that op, with the same message. Folders — the
  nodes a path's parts hang from, which hold no document themselves — have a
  ceiling of their own, 4000, answered with
  `413 {"error":"too_many_folders"}` by the workspace document's `update` and
  `promote`, and by a create, a move or a trash restore whose new folders
  would pass it, in the browser and on the daemon alike — and on the daemon
  by a document's `update` to a path no document holds yet and by a version
  restored to a new path, whose missing parent folders count the same way.
  A workspace already
  holding more still lists, and still takes a write that adds no folder.
  A sync `update` also refuses, with
  `409 {"error":"causal_gap"}` and nothing stored, an update that builds on a
  change the daemon does not hold; the web app sends it again, and it lands
  once the daemon holds what it builds on. The same answer refuses an update
  or a promoted record holding writes into a container created by a change
  those writes do not build on.
- **Rewriting references** is held to the same ceilings, the 262,144
  characters of a body and the 8,192 of a text node. Each link is longer than
  the name it replaces, and a moved document's new path can be longer than
  its old one, so either rewrite can grow a text. Link mentions (the
  Linked from panel's Link, `POST /api/v1/workspaces/{id}/documents/{documentId}/linkify-mentions`)
  that would carry the body or a node past its ceiling write nothing: the
  route answers `413` with `{"error":"markdown_too_large"}` or
  `{"error":"node_text_too_large"}`, and the mention stays listed. When a move
  follows references, a document the new path would carry past a ceiling is
  left as written, with its references still naming the old path, in the
  browser and on the daemon alike. The daemon reports it among the documents
  the move could not rewrite: in `wb_workspace_edit`'s
  `follow.failedDocumentIds`, or its log for the rename route. The move
  itself stands.

### How deeply markdown may nest

Markdown nests one level per marker: each `>` opens a blockquote, each `- `
on a line opens a list, each `*` an emphasis. Rendering (`wb_scene_render`,
the web preview, a text node drawn on a canvas) reads at most **64 levels**
of that nesting, counting the paragraph that holds the words. Anything deeper
is drawn as the plain text it contains, with its markers gone: `*` repeated
300 times on each side of `x` draws 62 nested bold spans around `x`. The
parser itself opens at most **32** nested quotes and lists: a `>` or a list
marker past the thirty-second is ordinary text, so `>` repeated 50 times
before `x` draws 32 nested quotes around a paragraph holding eighteen `>`
characters and `x`. A body that still nests deeper than the parser can follow
is drawn as one paragraph of its own source text. The stored body is never
changed; only what is drawn from it is.

### Markdown that would take too long to read

A few markdown shapes cost the parser time that grows with the square of
their length, so a body far inside the size limit could hold rendering for
minutes. Each is bounded, and only a body built to hit the bound reads
differently:

- **Emphasis, strikethrough and link ends.** One paragraph, heading or table
  cell hands at most **1,024** `*`, `_`, `~` and `]` characters to emphasis,
  strikethrough and link resolution; the rest of it shows them as the
  characters they are. That is 256 bold phrases in one paragraph. An `_`
  inside a word, as in `snake_case`, never counts.
- **Literal links.** A bare `www.` or `http://` address links at most
  **2,048** characters of path; past that the link ends and the rest is text.
  Of more than 256 punctuation marks closing an address, all but the last 256
  are part of the link.

A blank line between paragraphs gives each its own allowance, so splitting
the text is enough to have all of it read.

## How large a text node, a label, a comment, a tag and a document name may be

A text node's text — the `text` of a `wb_canvas_edit` `node.add` or
`node.patch`, and what a `node.splice` leaves — carries at most **8,192
characters**; a longer one is refused with "node text is longer than the
8192-character limit for one node". Laying text out is what that costs, and at
the limit one node still finishes in about a second. A splice that shrinks text
already over the limit is accepted.

The daemon's sync routes — a document's `update`, the workspace document's
`update` and `promote` — hold the same bound: an update that adds a node with
more than 8,192 characters of text, or grows a node's text past that, answers
`413` with `{"error":"node_text_too_large"}` and stores nothing; `promote`
names the canvas that holds the node. A node stored longer before the limit
can still be moved, restyled or shortened. A browser-kept workspace holds the
same bound: it does not save a change that adds or grows a node's text past
it — the page goes back to what is stored, undoing that change and anything
typed after it, and a notice at the top says the change was not saved and why.

A label — of an edge, a line or a group — carries at most **1,024
characters**, and one comment message at most **4,096**. Each is laid out
again on every render of its board, at a cost that grows with its length.
`wb_canvas_edit` refuses a longer `label` on `node.add`, `node.patch`,
`edge.add`, `edge.patch`, `line.add` and `line.patch`; `wb_thread_edit` refuses a longer `body` on `thread.add` and
`message.add`. The editor's label and comment boxes refuse a longer edit and
say why. The daemon's sync routes refuse an update that adds or grows one past
its bound with `413` and `{"error":"label_too_large"}` or
`{"error":"comment_too_large"}`, storing nothing; `promote` names the canvas
that holds it. A browser-kept workspace refuses the same change the way it
refuses an over-long node: nothing is saved, the page goes back to what is
stored, and the notice says why. A label or message stored longer before the
limit still reads, and can still be shortened.

A link node's URL, a file node's path, a file node's subpath and a group's
`background` image each carry at most **8,192 characters**. The first three
are drawn as the node's label on every render, at the same per-character cost
as a label, and a background is a location of the same kind; 8,192 leaves room
for long signed or query-heavy URLs. `wb_canvas_edit` refuses a longer `url`,
`file`, `subpath` or `background` on `node.add` and `node.patch`, and the web
app's link dialog stops taking characters at the limit. The daemon's sync routes refuse an update that adds or
grows one past it with `413` and `{"error":"node_location_too_large"}`, storing
nothing; `promote` names the canvas that holds it. A browser-kept workspace
refuses the same change the way it refuses an over-long node. A URL or path
stored longer before the limit still reads, and can still be shortened.

One tag carries at most **1,024 characters**, and one document, board, node
or edge at most **1,024 tags**. Every layout of a board reads each tag its
boxes and edges carry to draw its legend. `wb_facet_set` refuses a longer tag
in `tags.add` or `tags.rename`, more than 1,024 tags in one `tags.add`,
`tags.remove` or `tags.rename`, and a change that would leave something
carrying more than 1,024 — writing nothing for any document named. `wb_workspace_edit`'s `document.set` and
`document.create` refuse a frontmatter `tags` list past either bound the same
way. The daemon's sync routes refuse an update that adds a tag past the length
or grows a node's, edge's or board's tags past the count with `413` and
`{"error":"tags_too_large"}`, storing nothing; `promote` names the canvas that
holds them. A browser-kept workspace refuses the same change the way it
refuses an over-long node. Tags stored past either bound before it existed
still read, and still take a change that does not add to them.

A text anchor's `prefix` and `suffix` — the context either side of a quoted
passage — each carry at most **32 characters**. They tell one occurrence of a
repeated passage from another, and finding the passage compares them against
each occurrence, so their length is paid once per occurrence. Only the
**1,024 occurrences** nearest where the passage last was are compared: a
passage quoted that often is placed among those, and one further away is
not considered. `wb_thread_edit`
refuses a longer one on `thread.add`, and `wb_body_edit` on `body.replace`,
with "a text anchor's context is longer than the 32-character limit"; keep the
characters nearest the passage. The editor writes 16. An anchor stored with a
longer context still reads, and only its 32 characters nearest the passage
count toward placing it.

The quoted passage itself — a text anchor's `exact` — carries at most **1,024
characters**, a long paragraph. Every place that draws a passage finds it
again after each edit, resolved threads and decided changes included, and the
cost grows with the quote. `wb_thread_edit` refuses a longer one on
`thread.add`, and `wb_body_edit` on `body.replace`, with "a text anchor's
quote is longer than the 1024-character limit for the passage one anchor
quotes"; anchor a comment to a shorter passage, and split a longer
replacement across changes. The daemon's sync routes refuse an update that
would store one with `413` and `{"error":"anchor_quote_too_long"}`, storing
nothing, and a browser-kept workspace refuses it the same way. Commenting in
the editor on a selection or a block longer than that anchors the
conversation to its first 1,024 characters. An anchor stored with a longer
quote before this limit existed still reads, and a verdict on such a change
is still taken.

A document's display name carries at most **200 characters**, as a workspace
name does, however it is written: the `name` of `wb_workspace_edit`
`document.create` and `document.move` and of
`POST /api/v1/workspaces/{id}/documents`,
`PUT /api/workspaces/{id}/documents/{documentId}/name`, the web app's Name field
in the new-document and rename dialogs and its title box above an open
document — both stop taking characters at the limit, and the title box says
beside itself why a rename was refused — and a markdown document's
frontmatter `title`, which becomes its name. An
over-long `title` is refused before anything is written — `document.create`
creates nothing, and through `/api/v1` the answer is
`400 {"error":"okf_parse_failed"}` naming the `frontmatter-title` stage. A
blank name still clears it, and a name stored before the limit still lists.

A folder can carry a display name of its own, kept apart from its path the
way a document's is: naming a folder moves nothing, and the folder keeps the
path it was made with. A folder name holds the same 200-character bound, and
may not be blank or contain `/`, which is what separates folders in a path.
It is written by `wb_workspace_edit`'s `folder.rename` op and by
`PUT /api/workspaces/{id}/folders/name` with `{"path": …, "name": …}` (no
`name` clears it), and `GET /api/workspaces/{id}/documents` lists it as
`folderNames: [{"path", "name"}]` beside `documents` when any folder is
named. The name travels with the folder when it moves, and goes with it
when the folder empties and is removed. Only a folder can be named: the
path of a document that has documents below it is a document, not a folder,
and naming it answers `404`.

Two documents in the same folder may not show the same name, and neither
may two folders in the same folder. A create, a rename, or a markdown
document's frontmatter `title`, or a move (the daemon's path route and
`document.move`, for documents and folders alike) that would give a document the name another
document beside it already shows — its name, or its last path segment when
it has none — is refused, and so is a folder name another folder beside it
shows; names are compared ignoring case, surrounding spaces and Unicode
composition, so `Week 6`, ` week 6 ` and `WEEK 6` are one name. The refusal
answers `409 {"error":"display_name_taken"}` from `/api/v1` and the daemon's
name routes, and stops a `wb_workspace_edit` batch at that op; its message
quotes the name as the sibling shows it (`already called "Week 6"`), not as it
was given. A folder and a
document may share a name, and so may two documents in different folders.
Two names that only meet when two copies of a workspace merge — each named
while the other could not see it — are both kept: nothing renames either,
and either can keep its own name in a later write.

A document created with no name shows its last path segment; when that
would read the same as a name a sibling shows, the create is not refused and
instead takes the next free address (`plan` becomes `plan-2`), and the
returned `path` says where it landed.

A board declares at most **64** semantic axes in `visual.axes/v0` (the facet
keys it treats as meaning, which the legend scores on every layout).
`wb_facet_set` refuses a longer `axes` list with "more axes than the 64-axis
limit for one board", writing nothing. A declaration stored longer before the
limit still reads, and a declared key no box carries costs a render nothing.
The bound is checked where a tool writes the facet; an editor's sync update is
not judged against it, and a longer list arriving that way reads the same way.

## How long an id may be

An id a caller chooses for something it creates carries at most **256
characters**: a node's, an edge's or a line's `id` on `wb_canvas_edit`'s
`node.add`, `edge.add` and `line.add`, a
`threadId` on `wb_thread_edit`'s `thread.add`, a change's `id` on
`wb_body_edit`'s `body.replace`, and the `proposalId` either tool takes. A
longer one is refused with "an id is longer than the 256-character limit for
one id" before anything is written. Ids the server mints are 26 characters or
fewer. An id stored longer before the limit still reads, and an op that NAMES
an existing element — a patch, a removal, an edge end, a reply — still takes
it. `wb_body_edit` likewise refuses an `assumed` passage longer than the
262,144-character limit for one document, since no passage of a body is
longer than the body.

The daemon's sync routes — a document's `update`, the workspace document's
`update` and `promote` — refuse with `413` and
`{"error":"container_name_too_long"}`, storing nothing, an update that brings
a container into the record under a name longer than **1,024 characters**. A
comment thread and a proposal are each a container named by its id, so this
is how an over-long thread or proposal id arriving by sync is answered; kept,
a name far enough past it would leave a record that no keeper can load, every
document in the workspace with it. A container of any kind nested under a key
longer than 1,024 characters is refused the same way, because copying the
document — a save, a duplicate, a trip through the trash — would give the
copy a name that long. A container stored under a longer name or key before
the bound still takes a write, and a copy of its document stays readable. A
browser-kept workspace refuses the same change the way it refuses an
over-long node.

## How many nodes, edges and lines one canvas may hold

One canvas holds at most **2,000 nodes** and at most **2,000 edges and lines
together** — a line (ink) counts against the same bound as an edge, because
the layout routes both the same way and one costs what the other does. Every
render, export, layout read and tidy lays the whole board out again, and the
cost grows with how many edges and lines are routed among how many boxes:
about seven seconds for a board of 2,000 nodes and 2,000 edges, and minutes
for boards several times that size. `wb_canvas_edit` refuses the op that would
take a board past either bound, naming it — "the canvas would hold 2001 nodes,
past the 2000-node limit for one canvas", or "the canvas would hold 2001 edges
and lines, past the limit of 2000 edges and lines together for one canvas" —
and writes nothing; the same bound applies to a batch stored as a proposal. A
`tidy` op's `scope` and a `region.set` op's `nodes` list at most 2,000 ids,
and its `edges` at most 2,000.

Within those bounds, one render also caps the work two parts of edge routing
may do, because each can grow far faster than the board: the search that
finds a way around boxes when no simple route is clear, and the search that
picks which side of a box each edge leaves from and arrives at. A board built
to defeat either — hundreds of edges through 64 bends each over one square, or
a box walled in behind a curtain of thin boxes — took from minutes to a
quarter of an hour to render without the cap, and with it renders in about
the time an ordinary board of its size does. The largest ordinary boards the
project tests spend under a quarter of either allowance and render exactly
as they would without it. A board that does exhaust one still draws every
edge: past it, an edge no simple route reaches keeps its simple route even
where that runs through a box, and the side choice stops improving on the
sides it has reached.

The daemon's sync routes — a document's `update`, the workspace document's
`update` and `promote` — refuse an update that grows a board past either bound
with `413` and `{"error":"too_many_nodes_or_edges"}` (the code covers lines
too), storing nothing; `promote` names the canvas. A browser-kept workspace
refuses the same change the way it refuses an over-long node: nothing is
saved, the page goes back to what is stored, and the notice says why. A board
stored past a bound before it existed still reads, and still takes any change
that leaves it no larger — moving, restyling, or replacing one node with
another — so removing nodes, edges or lines is how it shrinks.

Line jumps (`lineJumps: "arc"`) draw at most **64 hops on one segment** and
**4,096 on one board**; a crossing past either cap is drawn as a plain
crossing, without its arc. Finding crossings has its own bound too: past
**4,000,000 candidate pairs** examined on one board, the search stops and no
further hops are drawn, while the hops already found are kept — so a board of
long, nearly parallel edges that never cross cannot make a render search
indefinitely. Edges and lines are searched in the order they are drawn. The
later edge hops over the earlier one; where it has no straight run to carry the
arc (the crossing falls on one of its bends) the earlier edge hops instead.

## How much referenced content one render loads

When `wb_scene_render` draws with `embedReferences`, and whenever `canvas_view`
answers, the server loads what the document points at — file nodes, `[[…]]`
links and `![[…]]` embeds, and what those documents name in turn — up to
**256 references**. A document named more than one way, by its id and by its
path, is read once and answers both.

The content those references load is bounded too: at most **1,048,576
characters** (four documents at the 262,144-character limit), counting a note's
body and the text of a board's nodes, and at most **4,000 nodes, edges and
lines** across the referenced boards — one maximal board's worth, which is as
much as a render draws nested anyway. References are loaded in the order the
document names them, and the first document that would go past either bound,
and every document not already loaded after it, is drawn by its name alone: a
file node shows its card, an embed its placeholder, and `canvas_view` sends
that reference with its id and name but no body or canvas. A later reference
to a document loaded before the bound was reached still answers with its
content, since it costs nothing more to read.

## How many open comment threads and proposed changes one document may hold

One document holds at most **500 open comment threads** and at most **1,000
open proposed changes**, across all of its proposals. Every render and export
of a canvas lays its comment bubbles and proposal bubbles out again, each
placed against every box and every bubble before it, so the cost grows faster
than the count: at 2,000 nodes, 500 open threads add about two seconds and
2,000 add about fourteen. Only OPEN ones count — a resolved thread, and an
adopted or dismissed change, stay in the document and are never deleted, so
resolving or deciding is how a document at a limit takes another.

`wb_thread_edit` (a `thread.add`, or a `thread.resolve` that reopens) refuses
the op that would pass the thread
limit — "the document would hold 501 open comment threads, past the limit of
500 open comment threads for one document" — and write nothing. A proposal
from `wb_canvas_edit` or `wb_body_edit` is refused when it would leave the
document past the change limit, counting the changes every earlier proposal
still holds open, so a series of small proposals is held to the same limit as
one large one.

The daemon's sync routes refuse an update that would pass either with `413`
and `{"error":"too_many_open_threads"}` or `{"error":"too_many_open_changes"}`,
storing nothing; a browser-kept workspace refuses it the same way it refuses a
board past its size, with a notice. A document stored past a limit before it
existed still reads, and still takes any change that opens nothing.

One comment thread holds at most **1,000** messages, resolved thread or not:
every reader of a thread — `wb_thread_edit`'s answer, `wb_document_get`, the
comments rail — reads all of them. `wb_thread_edit`'s `message.add` refuses
the reply that would pass it — "thread "t1" would hold 1001 messages, past
the limit of 1000 messages in one comment thread; open a new thread to
continue" — and writes nothing; a sync update is refused with `413` and
`{"error":"too_many_thread_messages"}`, storing nothing, by either keeper. A
thread already holding more than that still reads, and a message it holds can
still be edited, but it takes no further reply.

A comment anchored to several nodes at once names at most **2,000** of them —
a whole canvas's worth. Every render looks each named node up, resolved
threads included, so this is held whether the thread is open or not.
`wb_thread_edit` refuses a `thread.add` naming more ("a node set names more
nodes than the 2000-node limit for one comment anchor, a whole canvas's
worth"), and the daemon's sync routes refuse an update that would leave an
anchor naming more with `413` and `{"error":"comment_anchor_too_large"}`,
storing nothing. A thread stored with a larger set before this limit existed
is left out when the document is read; the document and its other threads
read as before.

## How many ops one call may carry

One call of an op-batch tool — `wb_canvas_edit`, `wb_body_edit`,
`wb_thread_edit` and `wb_workspace_edit` — carries at most **200** ops. A
larger batch is refused before any op is applied, with "more ops than the 200-op limit for one call"
(`wb_body_edit` says "passages"); split it across calls, and pass the same
`proposalId` to `wb_body_edit` to keep the passages in one proposal. A text
op whose offsets do not select its quote is found by searching the whole body,
so the bound is what keeps one call's cost near a second on the largest body a
document may hold. `wb_body_edit` stores a proposed passage at the offsets its
quote was found at, as `wb_thread_edit` does for a thread, so reading the
proposal back does not search again.

A `wb_canvas_edit` batch tidies at most once: a second `tidy` op is refused
with "a batch tidies at most once", and nothing is written. One tidy lays out
the whole board, so name every node to tidy in that op's `scope`, or tidy
again in another call.

A batch also places at most **2,000** nodes inside groups between all of its
ops — every member a `region.set` moves in, and every `node.add` with `within`
and no position. Each is packed around what its group already holds, so a
batch moving the same members back and forth between two groups would pay
for that packing once per op. The op that would pass the bound is refused
with "a batch places at most 2000 nodes inside groups", and nothing is
written; move the rest in another call.

Its `node.patch` ops patch at most **2,000** nodes between them, counting
every node an `all` or `within` selector reaches. A patch that changes text
or size measures each node it reaches, so a batch of selector-wide patches
would measure the whole board once per op. The op that would pass the bound
is refused with "a batch patches at most 2000 nodes between its node.patch
ops", and nothing is written; put the fields in one `node.patch`, or patch
the rest in another call.

## OKF frontmatter this server does not model

OKF ([Open Knowledge Format](https://github.com/GoogleCloudPlatform/knowledge-catalog/blob/main/okf/SPEC.md))
requires exactly one frontmatter field, `type`, and leaves producers free to add
any others. This server gives meaning to OKF's required `type`, its recommended
`title`, `description`, `resource` and `tags`, v0.2's trust pair `generated`
and `verified`, and its own `view` and `facets` extension keys.

**Every other root key is preserved verbatim.** Write a document through
a `document.set` op and read it back with `wb_document_get`, and keys this server
has no model for come back at the root they were written at, unchanged. That
covers OKF v0.2's provenance and lifecycle families — `sources`,
`usage_window`, `status`, `stale_after` — and the Attested Computation keys
`runtime`, `parameters`, `computation`, `executor` and `attester`, none of
which this server interprets.

**YAML anchors and aliases are refused.** A frontmatter that marks a value
with `&name` or repeats one with `*name` (a `<<:` merge key included) is not
stored: a `document.set` or `document.create` op and `POST
/api/v1/workspaces/{id}/documents` answer "YAML anchors and aliases are not
allowed in OKF frontmatter". OKF gives them no meaning, and an
alias makes a few bytes stand for a value of any size. Write the value out
each time it is needed; this server writes a repeated value out in full too.

**Frontmatter nests at most 32 levels.** The root mapping is one level, and
every mapping or list inside it one more. A deeper frontmatter is not stored:
the same write paths answer "OKF frontmatter may nest at most 32 levels of
mappings and lists". Each level is written two spaces further in, so a value
nested hundreds deep exports as hundreds of times its size. A document stored
with deeper frontmatter before this limit still reads and exports in full; it
is re-importing that export which is refused.

**Frontmatter is a restricted subset of YAML 1.2.** What this server writes is
always inside it, and a frontmatter outside it is refused with a message naming
the construct (`document.set`, `document.create` and `POST
/api/v1/workspaces/{id}/documents` answer `400 {"error":"okf_parse_failed"}`). Block and
flow mappings and lists, plain, single- and double-quoted scalars, `|` and `>`
block scalars, comments and a long key written as `? key` are read. Refused:

- tags (`!x`, `!!str`, `!!set`, `!!binary`), `%` directives, and `---` or `...`
  document markers inside the frontmatter;
- a byte-order mark anywhere, a carriage return that is not part of a CRLF line
  ending, raw control characters below U+0020 other than tab and line feed, and
  the control characters U+007F to U+009F outside double quotes (inside double
  quotes they are read);
- a tab used as indentation, in any construct, including continuation lines;
- a list or mapping used as a key (`[a, b]: 1`, `? {a: 1}`), a pair inside a
  flow list (`[a: 1]`), `?` inside a flow mapping, an empty key (`: x`), and an
  explicit `? key` for a key short enough to write inline (the explicit form is
  read only for a key written in more than 1,024 characters);
- a lone UTF-16 surrogate in a key or value, whether written raw or as an
  escape such as `"\uD800"`. The write side refuses it too, and a byte-order
  mark in a value, with `okf_not_yaml_safe`: a document stored with either before
  these limits still reads, but its export is reported as a per-document failure.

Tags in particular were read before and are refused now, so `x: !!set {a, b}`
is no longer a value this server stores.

## Who wrote a document

`wb_workspace_edit` takes an optional `actor` for the whole batch, and records
it as OKF `generated.by` alongside the server's clock as `generated.at`. Use
[OKF's actor convention](https://github.com/GoogleCloudPlatform/knowledge-catalog/blob/main/okf/SPEC.md):
`<producer>/<version>` for an agent or tool, `human:<id>` for a person,
`process:<id>` for an automated process.

- Identify yourself. A write with no `actor` is recorded as
  `process:whiteboard-server`, which is true but tells a later reader nothing
  about what produced the content.
- **A document that already declares `generated` keeps it.** Importing a
  document does not make this server its author, so an incoming stamp is
  honoured rather than replaced.
- `verified` is carried through as written, including the single bare mapping
  the spec allows, which is normalised to a one-element list. Nothing in this
  server adds a verification on your behalf: `generated` says who wrote the
  content, `verified` says who confirmed it, and they are different claims.
- The actor is a **self-report**, exactly as it is in OKF. Trust tiers derived
  from it are advisory signals, not access control.
- An actor carries at most **256 characters** — a name, which is stamped on
  every document a batch writes. `wb_workspace_edit`, `POST
  /api/v1/workspaces/{id}/documents`, and the `author` of `wb_thread_edit`,
  `wb_canvas_edit` and `wb_body_edit` refuse a longer one with "an actor is
  longer than the 256-character limit", writing nothing. A `generated.by`
  stored longer, or written in a document's own frontmatter, still reads.

Documents edited in the browser app do not yet carry `generated`; only writes
through the daemon's tools do.

Two consequences worth knowing:

- Preserved keys are emitted in lexicographic order, not authoring order. The
  same normalisation already applies to `facets`.
- A preserved value must survive being stored and written back out. These are
  refused with a typed error rather than stored as something else — a write
  over `/api/v1` answers `400 okf_not_yaml_safe`, naming the key:
  - `NaN`, `Infinity` and `undefined`, which YAML cannot carry;
  - a lone UTF-16 surrogate or a byte-order mark in a key or value;
  - an integer a double cannot hold exactly, in practice one past 2^53
    (9007199254740992), which would be rounded to the nearest double and read
    back as a different number; write it as a quoted string.
- A spelling that means the same number is normalised, not refused: `0x10`
  reads back as `16`, `0o17` as `15`, `1e3` as `1000`, `1.0` as `1`. A value
  written as `012` reads back as `12`, as YAML 1.2 defines it. A number
  used as a key becomes a string.

Values are not validated against the OKF spec: a malformed `verified` block is
carried through as faithfully as a well-formed one, because a consumer that
rejects a document for an unrecognized field is exactly what OKF's conformance
section forbids.

## The `x-whiteboard` extension contract

Extended JSON Canvas output is standard JSON Canvas 1.0 plus **exactly one**
extension key, `x-whiteboard`, allowed at three sites:

- **Document root** — canvas-target facets (`facets`, keyed
  `{namespace}.{name}/v{n}`: `visual.edges/v0` for edge routing and line
