  jumps, `visual.theme/v0` for the theme), the board's own tags (`tags`, a
  list of strings — plain tags and `key:value` scoped ones), the ink layer
  (`lines`) and the comment annotation layer (`comments`). Rendering
  preferences for things JSON Canvas already models, so a consumer that
  drops it still renders every edge, just with its own routing.
- **A node** — the canvas-embed extension (`kind: "embed"` plus a canvas
  reference). It records a reference only: the document keeps it and the
  reference graph counts it as a backlink, but nothing draws the embedded
  document and agents cannot author one through MCP. The node also carries node-target
  facets in the same `facets` bucket, and its `tags`.
- **An edge** — edge-target facets (`facets`), the edge's `tags` (a tag on an
  edge classifies the relation: the link between two services is healthy or
  failing as much as the services are) and the bends the line is drawn
  through (`bends`: canvas coordinates, in order, whole pixels here even
  though the document stores them as real numbers). Never an embed: what an
  edge holds that the format cannot state is geometry, not content.
  `visual.edges/v0` here overrides the board's routing for that one edge,
  field by field. A consumer that drops the extension draws the same edge
  with its own computed routing — bends are the clearest case of something
  JSON Canvas simply has no vocabulary for.

No other non-standard field is ever emitted, at any level. Foreign keys on an
imported document (another tool's vendor fields) are stripped on parse and
never re-emitted. Strict-mode output (`wb_document_get` with
`options.strict: true`) drops the `x-whiteboard` key entirely and is plain
JSON Canvas 1.0.

What may appear inside `x-whiteboard` is machine-readable:
[`x-whiteboard.schema.json`](x-whiteboard.schema.json) (JSON Schema,
draft 2020-12) is generated from the same Zod schemas the code validates
with, so it cannot drift from the implementation.

**What each mode costs, field by field**, is
[what a JSON Canvas export costs](json-canvas-loss.md) — every position the
document model can hold, and whether the format states it, rounds it, carries
it on the extension key, or cannot take it. Generated from the projection
itself for the same reason the JSON Schema is.

## Characters the exporter cannot draw

The daemon rasterises with the fonts **it** has — a vendored Latin face plus
whatever has been installed into its data directory, and deliberately nothing
from the operating system. A character no such face carries is painted as an
empty box.

It is worth reporting because of how it fails. Measurement is correct, so the
text wraps in the right places and every box is the right size; the only thing
wrong is that a reader cannot read it. The daemon's HTTP export routes
therefore answer with the characters they could not draw:

```json
{ "filePath": "…/canvas-a-8f3.png", "undrawable": ["日", "本"] }
```

`filePath` is absolute on the local daemon. A self-hosted server answers it
relative to the workspace's exports directory instead, so a member is not told
where the server keeps its data.

Empty is the normal answer. What the report means differs by format:

| Format | What was lost |
| --- | --- |
| PNG | The characters are gone from the image. |
| SVG | Nothing yet — the file still carries them as `<text>`, and any viewer whose own system has the face renders them correctly. The report is what a PNG of this file would lose. |

Fix it by installing a font for the script:
[install-fonts-for-export](../how-to/install-fonts-for-export.md).

**The web editor's own exports are a separate question.** They are rendered in
the browser, not by the daemon, so they use the browser's fonts and the report
above does not describe them. A daemon with no Japanese face and a browser with
one disagree about the same canvas — which is why installing a font is worth
doing even when the on-screen canvas looks fine.

## Tags, the legend and the workspace's tag library

A board whose boxes or edges carry scoped tags exports with its **legend** under the
drawing, at its left edge, whenever the board's colours follow a key, exactly as the editor
shows it (see
[organize with tags](../how-to/organize-with-tags.md#read-the-legend)). When the workspace
declares a [tag library](../how-to/organize-with-tags.md#declare-the-vocabulary) — the document
at `tags` — a box or an edge carrying a value the library colours, and having no colour of its
own, is drawn in the declared colour by `wb_scene_render` and by the daemon's `POST …/export`
and `POST …/export-svg` alike, so the legend lists the key by declaration rather than by
observation. A colour set on the element itself always wins. An untagged board never reads the
library, and a workspace without one exports as stored.

## Themes and `style`

A canvas may name a theme in its `visual.theme/v0` facet (bundled: `visual.sketch`,
`visual.neon`; see [choose-a-theme](../how-to/choose-a-theme.md)). Whether a render honours it
is the caller's choice, through one `style` field with one meaning everywhere it appears:

| `style` | draws |
| --- | --- |
| `clean` (default) | the bundled look, whatever the document says |
| `document` | the theme the canvas names, if any |
| a theme id, e.g. `visual.sketch` | that theme, without storing it — a preview |

It appears on `wb_scene_render`, and on the daemon's `POST …/export` (PNG) and
`POST …/export-svg` request bodies. The default is `clean` so an agent reading SVG never pays
for a theme's jittered geometry or glow unasked, and a `wb_canvas_snapshot` layout analysis
never moves because a theme did. A theme id nothing registered is refused — `wb_scene_render` answers
an error and the two export routes a `400 invalid_request` — naming the registered ids, the way a
theme write does.

A themed render also comes back on that theme's **paper**: the background is the theme
palette's surface for the mode asked for (`theme: "dark"` on a neon canvas gives `#030711`),
so an export is the board a person drawing on it sees rather than the theme's strokes on the
bundled sheet. A `clean` render keeps the bundled white or near-black surface. There is no request field for the background
colour.

Both request bodies refuse a field they do not define, naming it in a `400 invalid_request` —
`POST …/export` takes `padding`, `scale`, `theme`, `style`, `outputPath` and `overwrite`, and
`POST …/export-svg` the same without `scale`, since vector output has no resolution to set.

A PNG is at most **16384 pixels a side** and **67,108,864 pixels** (64 Mi) in all, measured
after `scale` and `padding`. A document whose export would be larger is refused with a
`400 invalid_request` naming the size it would have been, before anything is drawn; lower
`scale`, or export SVG, which has no limit.

The inline `data:` images a PNG export draws share the same **67,108,864 pixel** budget,
counted from the width and height each image's header declares and summed across the
document — a decoder allocates what the header declares, however few bytes encode it. A
document past it is refused with a `400 invalid_request` before anything is drawn; shrink or
remove an image, or export SVG.

Glow halos and comment drop shadows have a budget of their own, because a renderer blurs
the whole area each one covers: about **8 megapixels** of halo, counted at the export's
`scale` and only inside the picture, with a shadow's area counting twice. A board past it
is not refused; it is drawn with the LARGEST halos and shadows left off until the rest fit, and
every node, edge, label and comment is still drawn. An ordinary board stays well inside it —
a 150-node `visual.neon` board uses about 6 — but the boards that pass it are the ones whose
halos are largest: edges that cross the whole board, nodes the size of the board, and stacks of
long comments. A higher `scale` spends the budget faster, since a 2x PNG has four times the pixels
under each halo. SVG export, `wb_scene_render` and the web app's export apply the same
budget at 1x.

A theme's font family is declared in the SVG only where the daemon can measure it — the
vendored face or an installed one — and otherwise the bundled family is declared, so the face
named and the coordinates measured always agree. `unresolvedFamilies` reports nothing in that
case, because nothing is missing from the page. The daemon reads its fonts directory when it
warms the renderer, so a face installed while it is running is measured and declared from its
next start.

## Web app exports

The web editor's document row (More actions → Export) saves an open canvas
as SVG or PNG (a markdown note's Export… offers only **Save as Markdown (.md)**,
below), rendered with the light palette regardless of the UI mode so an
export's bytes never depend on a display preference — and with the document's
theme, if it names one, since that is part of the document rather than of the
display.

A picture is filled with the light palette's surface (white) by default, as a
`<rect>` covering the whole viewBox drawn before anything else, so a PNG is
opaque and an SVG dropped onto a dark slide still reads. The **With background**
checkbox in the Export… submenu turns the fill off, and the file is then
transparent, byte for byte what an export without the option draws. The **2×
resolution (PNG)** checkbox rasterises a PNG at twice the pixels in each
direction with the same drawing (the viewBox is unchanged); an SVG ignores it.
Both are remembered per browser and apply to all four picture entries. With nodes selected, a **Selection only** checkbox draws those four from the selection alone — each selected node read as the fragment `^id` names, so a group brings its members — keeping an edge or line only when both attached ends are inside, and a comment only when what it is about is; it is not remembered. The
daemon's `wb_scene_render` and `POST …/export` do not read these checkboxes; the
PNG route keeps its own `scale` parameter.

The export draws what the editor shows, including what the canvas points at:
its pictures, the note or board a file node points at, and what a text node
embeds with `![[…]]`. The comment layer — pins, cards, region outlines and the
highlights of threads about a passage — is left out of Export as PNG / SVG and
drawn by Export as PNG (with comments) / SVG (with comments). A file node
pointing at another board draws its miniature whatever its size on screen, as
`wb_scene_render` does with `embedReferences`. Math blocks and Mermaid diagrams
are drawn as the editor draws them, in a text node and in the note a file node
or an embed shows; `wb_scene_render` draws the same canvas with them as source.

Stored pictures are written into the file as PNG `data:` URIs, so a saved SVG
shows them anywhere it is opened. They are re-encoded from the pixels the
editor shows, so a photo takes more space than its original file and an
animated picture keeps its first frame. A picture whose PNG would be larger
than the 16 MiB upload limit, or one that cannot be read, is left out rather
than linked.

The PNG a browser export produces carries the editor's own font inside the
image data it rasterises from, so it draws the text the editor showed rather
than whatever font the operating system offers. A saved `.svg` names the family
instead of carrying it, as `Roboto, system-ui, sans-serif` — a viewer with Roboto
renders it identically, and one without it falls back to its system sans-serif face
(rather than a serif one) and gets a smaller file.

**Save as Markdown (.md)** (More actions → Export…, on a markdown note) downloads
the note as OKF Markdown: its frontmatter — `type`, tags, facets — and its body.
The document's name is written as the frontmatter `title`, a projection of the
workspace's display name, so a document with no name writes none. **Save as JSON Canvas
(.canvas)** (on a canvas) downloads the extended-mode JSON Canvas document. Both are the
document's own source rather than a picture. An image on a canvas is saved as an
`asset:` reference to the workspace's file, not as its pixels, so the notice says
"images are referenced, not embedded" when the canvas has one; the picture exports above
are the ones that carry the pixels.

Every export is offered under the document's name, in whatever script it is
written — a note called 概要 saves as `概要.md`. Only characters a filesystem
refuses (`/ \ : * ? " < > |`, control characters and bidirectional marks) are
replaced with `-`, the ends are trimmed, and trailing dots are dropped. A
document with no name, or one whose name leaves nothing else, is offered under
the last part of its path (`gaiyo.md` for `notes/gaiyo`).

**Import** reads the same two sources back: `.md`/`.markdown` through the OKF parser
(frontmatter optional) and `.canvas`/`.json` through the JSON Canvas parser, creating one
document per file; see [Export and import a document](../how-to/export-and-import-a-document.md#bring-a-file-in).

**Copy as JSON Canvas** (same menu) puts the extended-mode JSON Canvas
document on the clipboard as plain text — the quickest way to hand the exact
canvas to another tool or a debugging session from any device.

**PNG exports of a canvas carry their document**: the file embeds the canvas's JSON Canvas
document (extended mode, `x-whiteboard` included) in a PNG `iTXt` chunk under
the `whiteboard` keyword — the same pattern
draw.io uses. A shared PNG therefore carries its exact node coordinates and edges, not just
pixels; any PNG chunk reader can recover the document, and image viewers ignore
the chunk. Unlike draw.io, the app does not open such a PNG back as an
editable canvas: a PNG dropped into the editor is inserted as an image.

There is currently no raster (PNG) export tool and no tool that returns image
bytes as MCP `ImageContent` — `wb_scene_render` is the closest equivalent for
handing a rendered canvas back to an LLM.

# What a JSON Canvas export keeps, and what it costs

A whiteboard document is not a JSON Canvas file. JSON Canvas 1.0 is a **projection** of it
([ADR-0037](../contributing/adr/0037-model-and-format.md)), and first-party support means a
tested projection rather than an identity: a round-trip property over the expressible subset,
and this table for everything else.

The model can hold **50** field positions. **22** of them are something the format
can state; **28** reach a reader only through the single extension key, or not at all.

Two export modes, and the difference between them is exactly the `x-whiteboard` rows below:

- **`extended`** — JSON Canvas 1.0 plus the one extension key. Lossless over everything the key
  can hold. This is what `wb_document_get` emits by default.
- **`strict`** — plain JSON Canvas 1.0, the extension key removed entirely
  (`wb_document_get` with `options.strict: true`).

## Stated by JSON Canvas 1.0 — 17

Every reader of the format gets these, in both export modes. Nothing is lost and nothing needs the extension key.

| field | what a reader gets |
| --- | --- |
| `edges[].color` | survives both modes |
| `edges[].from.end` | survives both modes |
| `edges[].from.node` | survives both modes |
| `edges[].from.side` | survives both modes |
| `edges[].id` | survives both modes |
| `edges[].label` | survives both modes |
| `edges[].to.end` | survives both modes |
| `edges[].to.node` | survives both modes |
| `edges[].to.side` | survives both modes |
| `nodes[].background` | survives both modes |
| `nodes[].backgroundStyle` | survives both modes |
| `nodes[].color` | survives both modes |
| `nodes[].id` | survives both modes |
| `nodes[].label` | survives both modes |
| `nodes[].resource.content` | survives both modes |
| `nodes[].resource.location` | survives both modes |
| `nodes[].resource.subpath` | survives both modes |

## Stated, but not exactly — 5

The format has the field and cannot hold the value. What a reader gets instead is named per row; the document still draws in the right place.

| field | what a reader gets |
| --- | --- |
| `nodes[].height` | crosses as the nearest integer pixel |
| `nodes[].resource.mimeType` | crosses as the format's node kind |
| `nodes[].width` | crosses as the nearest integer pixel |
| `nodes[].x` | crosses as the nearest integer pixel |
| `nodes[].y` | crosses as the nearest integer pixel |

## Carried on `x-whiteboard` — 28

Survives the `extended` export and disappears from the `strict` one, which emits plain JSON Canvas 1.0. A reader that drops the key keeps the whole of what the format can state.

| field | what a reader gets |
| --- | --- |
| `edges[].bends[].x` | dropped by `strict` |
| `edges[].bends[].y` | dropped by `strict` |
| `edges[].facets/*` | dropped by `strict` |
| `edges[].tags[]` | dropped by `strict` |
| `facets/*` | dropped by `strict` |
| `lines[].bends[].x` | dropped by `strict` |
| `lines[].bends[].y` | dropped by `strict` |
| `lines[].color` | dropped by `strict` |
| `lines[].facets/*` | dropped by `strict` |
| `lines[].from.end` | dropped by `strict` |
| `lines[].from.kind` | dropped by `strict` |
| `lines[].from.node` | dropped by `strict` |
| `lines[].from.point.x` | dropped by `strict` |
| `lines[].from.point.y` | dropped by `strict` |
| `lines[].from.side` | dropped by `strict` |
| `lines[].id` | dropped by `strict` |
| `lines[].label` | dropped by `strict` |
| `lines[].to.end` | dropped by `strict` |
| `lines[].to.kind` | dropped by `strict` |
| `lines[].to.node` | dropped by `strict` |
| `lines[].to.point.x` | dropped by `strict` |
| `lines[].to.point.y` | dropped by `strict` |
| `lines[].to.side` | dropped by `strict` |
| `nodes[].embed.documentId` | dropped by `strict` |
| `nodes[].embed.versionRef` | dropped by `strict` |
| `nodes[].facets/*` | dropped by `strict` |

## Cannot cross at all — 0

Named here so the absence is a decision rather than a surprise.

_None today._

## What this table does not cover

- **What is inside a facet bucket.** A `…/*` row is one entry because the format can say a bucket
  is present and nothing about its contents, and those contents belong to whichever plugins a
  deployment carries. Every one of them is lost in `strict`, whatever it is.
- **OKF Markdown.** This is the spatial side only. A markdown document round-trips through OKF
  preserving root keys this codebase does not model, which is a different promise made a
  different way.
- **`wb_scene_render`.** SVG is an explicitly lossy rendering, not a document format, and has
  never claimed otherwise.
- **The comments.** A conversation is the document’s annotation layer, kept beside its content
  rather than in it ([ADR-0026](../contributing/adr/0026-annotation-layer.md) decision 1b), so
  no export carries it, `extended` included, and it is not a field position here. A file an
  older version exported with `x-whiteboard.comments` is refused on import, naming the key,
  rather than read with its comments silently gone.

# Keyboard shortcuts

Every shortcut below works on the spatial canvas editor. `Cmd` is the macOS
modifier; use `Ctrl` everywhere else — both satisfy the same binding.

Two rules hold for the whole table:

- **Every shortcut has a pointer path too.** Anything you can do with the
  keyboard is also reachable from an object's right-click menu, the
  empty-space menu, or the bottom dock — a shortcut is an accelerator,
  never the only way in.
- **Shortcuts never fire while you are typing.** Inside a node's text
  editor or a dialog field, the keys belong to the text — except
  `Cmd/Ctrl + Enter`, whose whole job is to save what you typed.

## Tools

| Shortcut | Action |
|---|---|
| `H` | Hand (pan) — drag anywhere to pan. A canvas opens in Select; one you come back to within the same browser session returns to whichever of Select and Hand you were last using on it |
| `V` | Select — click to select, drag to marquee |
| `C` | Connect — click one node, then another, to draw an edge |
| `D` | Draw — drag across the board to leave a freehand stroke, in the colour and width chosen in the strip above the dock |
| `E` | Eraser — drag over drawings to remove them; `Esc` puts it down |
| `N` | Add a note at the centre of the view, or inside the selected frame |
| `Space` + drag | Pan from any tool, without leaving it |

The five tools live in the bottom dock, and their letters show in its tooltips. The letters work from any tool and never while you are typing; with `Cmd/Ctrl` held, `C` and `D` stay copy and duplicate. On touch, two-finger drag pans and
pinch zooms in every tool.

## Selection and editing

| Shortcut | Action |
|---|---|
| `Cmd/Ctrl + A` | Select every node |
| `Shift` + click | Add or remove a node from the selection |
| `Tab` | Select the next node in reading order, visiting the connections and lines that leave a node right after it; with nothing selected, the first node |
| `Shift + Tab` | Step back through the same walk |
| `C` | With a node selected: start a connection from it (arrows choose the target, `Enter` connects, `Esc` cancels) |
| `Cmd/Ctrl + Arrows` | Select the nearest node in that direction |
| `Enter` / `F2` | Edit the selected node's text, a frame's label, or the selected connection's or line's label (a frame's, connection's or line's label is one line: `Enter` saves it) |
| `F6` / `Shift + F6` | Leave the canvas for the next control after it or the one before it (the header), keeping the selection; the canvas's own dock is skipped. With nothing after the canvas, `F6` wraps round to the first control in the page (the header), so it always moves focus. They work the same from a control in the canvas's dock, such as Undo |
| `Menu` / `Shift + F10` | Open the selection's menu — the one a right-click on it opens — at the selection; with nothing selected, the canvas menu |
| Arrow keys | Nudge the whole selection (`Shift` for a larger step) |
| `Cmd/Ctrl + Alt + M` | Comment on the selected node, nodes or connection: opens the comment composer, the same one **Comment on this** opens |
| `Delete` / `Backspace` | Delete the selected nodes, or the selected connection or line |
| Double-click | Edit a node's text or an edge's label; on empty space add a note there; on a group's name (above its top edge) edit the name; inside a group add a note in it. The same in Hand mode. Both clicks must land within a few pixels of each other: two quick clicks across the canvas are two clicks |
| `Cmd/Ctrl + Shift + L` | Lock or unlock the selection |
| `Cmd/Ctrl + Enter` | Save the text you are editing and close the editor |
| `Esc` | Cancel the current gesture, or clear the selection; on a connection reached with `Tab`, go back to the node it leaves; in a text edit, discard what you typed; with the eraser armed, put it down and go back to the tool you had before it; with the Connect tool armed and no connection half drawn, go back to Select |

**Reaching a node without a pointer.** The canvas is a Tab stop, announced as
"Canvas, 5 notes. Tab selects the first note" (frames, connections, drawings and lines are counted apart, a canvas holding only a drawing says "Canvas, 1 drawing. Tab selects the first drawing", one whose first node in reading order is a frame says "Tab selects the first frame", and once something is selected it says Tab selects the next node). With it focused, `Tab` walks the
nodes top to bottom, then left to right (two nodes at exactly the same spot always come in the same order),
and does not wrap: `Tab` on the last node, or `Shift + Tab` on the first, leaves
the canvas for the next control (the bottom dock, or the header before the
canvas), so the walk is never a trap. `Esc`
clears the selection and `Tab` starts the walk again; a second `Esc` with nothing
selected makes the next `Tab` the browser's, which is the way on to the bottom dock, and
the canvas then says so ("Tab leaves the canvas").
To leave without losing the selection, press `F6` (on past the canvas and its dock,
round to the header when nothing follows it) or
`Shift + F6` (back to the header, where the Display panel shows the selected
node) — the selection stays exactly as it was. A canvas with no nodes lets `Tab` go straight to the
dock. Locked nodes and locked connections are skipped, since they cannot be selected.

**Reaching a connection without a pointer.** The `Tab` walk visits each
connection right after the node it leaves, and each line right after the node
it starts (or ends) at; a line attached to no node comes after the last node.
A selected connection is announced with its place among the connections and
lines, as "Selected: Connection from Web App to API Gateway (2 of 5)". From
there `Enter` or `F2` edits its label, `Shift + F10` opens its menu (arrow
ends, sides, colour, comment, lock, delete), `Delete` deletes it, and `Esc`
goes back to the node you reached it from.
`Cmd/Ctrl + Arrows` jumps to the closest node in a direction, preferring the
one straight ahead over a nearer one off to the side; the plain arrow keys
still nudge.

**Connecting two nodes without a pointer.** Select a node and press `C`: the
connect starts from it and the canvas announces "Connecting from ...". The arrow
keys then choose the target in reading order (`Right`/`Down` forward,
`Left`/`Up` back), each outlined and announced as "Connect to ...", with its
text, or its kind and a short id when it has none. `Enter` makes the connection
and announces it, `Esc` cancels. `Tab` from the canvas still reaches the same
targets one by one. With nothing selected, `C` switches to the Connect tool as
before.

**The menu from the keyboard.** `Shift + F10` (or the `Menu` key) opens the menu
for what is selected, a node, a set of nodes, a connection, a line or a group, and puts focus on
its first row. `Arrow Up` / `Arrow Down` step through the rows, `Home` and
`End` jump to the first and last, `Enter` runs the one under focus, and `Esc`
closes the menu and returns focus to the canvas. While a menu is open no other
canvas key acts: the arrows do not nudge the node behind it, and the tool and
note letters stay silent.

**Align and distribute** have no shortcut — they live in the right-click
menu of a multi-node selection, as **Align** (six edges and centre lines)
and **Distribute** (horizontal, vertical). Align appears once two nodes are
selected; distribute once there are three, because it repositions the
middle ones and leaves the outermost two anchoring the span. Both align to
the selection's own bounding box, so the result does not depend on which
node you clicked first, and each is a single undo step. Choosing one closes the
menu so the result is in view, and a screen reader hears what was done (for
example "Aligned 3 nodes left").

**Tidy** (the right-click menu of a selection, or **Tidy canvas** on empty
space) lines boxes up and clears overlaps without taking anything out of its
frame: a frame's contents are tidied inside it, a frame drawn mostly inside
another, such as one made with **Frame selection**, counts as inside it, and
a frame grows down or right to make room rather than moving away from the
frames beside it. Frames are never left overlapping one another. A screen reader hears
what it did ("Tidied 6 notes in 2 frames"), or "Already tidy" when there was
nothing to move.

A locked node shows a small padlock in its top-right corner so you can tell it
from one that is simply unresponsive; the padlock appears in the editor only
and never in an export. A locked node or edge cannot be selected, moved, restyled, or deleted, and
MCP tools refuse to patch, tag, or set facets on it too. Right-click it and choose **Unlock** to
release it. Nodes and edges lock independently: locking a node does not
lock the edges attached to it, and an edge between two locked nodes stays
editable until you lock the edge itself. The lock is editor state — it is
stored alongside the canvas but never appears in an export.

A locked node takes the press: dragging it moves nothing, not even the frame
around it, and a brief "Locked — unlock from the menu" notice says why. A
frame holding an edge gives way to the edge, so you can select, label or
restyle that edge by pressing it; the frame is selected from its border.

A frame carries every unlocked node that sits wholly inside it, whether you
drag it or nudge it with the arrow keys, and the move is one undo step.
With a frame selected, or a node that sits inside one, `N` puts the new note
in that frame's next free spot (the innermost frame, when frames nest), 32px
clear of what it already holds, and grows the frame if it is full — down,
or right or left when growing down would run into a neighbour, so a grown
frame never reaches over another frame or its notes. So typing
a note, pressing `Escape` and pressing `N` again keeps filling the same frame. A new
note or frame never lands over a frame's name. **Add > Frame** puts each new
frame to the right of the last row of frames, on the same top line and 32px
apart, and starts a new row below once the row would leave the screen, so
frames made one after another read left to right in the order you made them. A frame is carried by its border band and its name strip. A drag that starts on
the frame's empty interior sweeps a selection band instead, so you can pick up
the notes inside without moving the frame; a tap there still selects the frame.
A press that moves less than a few pixels is a tap: the node stays exactly where
it was.

## Clipboard

| Shortcut | Action |
|---|---|
| `Cmd/Ctrl + C` | Copy the selection |
| `Cmd/Ctrl + X` | Cut the selection |
| `Cmd/Ctrl + V` | Paste |
| `Cmd/Ctrl + D` | Duplicate the selection in place |

Copy puts the selection on your system clipboard as JSON, so a paste works
in another canvas, another tab, or after a reload. Pasting content from
elsewhere follows what it finds: an image becomes an image node, our own
copied JSON becomes the nodes it describes, and any other text becomes a
note. Edges come along whenever both of their endpoints are selected.

A cut does not remove anything until you paste: the cut nodes stay in place
under a veil, a chip says how many are held, and a screen reader hears it ("1
node held — paste to place, Escape to cancel"). `Esc` lifts the hold.

Right-click empty space and choose **Paste here** to place the pasted
content at that exact point instead of the default offset.

## Arranging

| Shortcut | Action |
|---|---|
| `]` | Bring forward |
| `[` | Send backward |
| `Shift + ]` | Bring to front |
| `Shift + [` | Send to back |

Forward and backward step over the nearest node the selection actually
overlaps — stepping past something you do not overlap would change nothing
on screen. The same four moves sit in a node's right-click menu under
**Order**.

## Viewport

| Shortcut | Action |
|---|---|
| `Shift + 1` | Zoom to fit all content |
| `Shift + 2` | Zoom to the selection |
| `+` / `-` | Zoom in or out one step, about the middle of the view |
| `Cmd/Ctrl` + scroll | Zoom under the pointer |
| Scroll / two-finger drag | Pan |
| Double-tap in Hand mode (touch) | Zoom in on the point you pressed; with a mouse or pen a double-click edits or adds a note instead, and never moves the view |

Each canvas remembers where you were looking, for the rest of the browser
session: leave it or reload the page and it reopens at the same pan and zoom,
separately for each document. A new session, or a canvas that has no memory
yet, opens at the origin, and when none of its content is in view there (or
in the remembered position) it opens framed on the content, as **Zoom to fit**
would. Later edits never move the view.

When a panel covers part of the canvas, as the inspector does in a narrow
window, **Zoom to fit**, **Zoom to the selection** and the jump to a comment
frame their target in the part you can still see, and opening a panel over the
selected node moves it clear. **Zoom to fit** and **Zoom to the selection**
also keep what they frame clear of the dock along the bottom and of the
overview map in the corner, and leave room along the top for the action
buttons a selected node shows above itself.


The dock carries one view control — **zoom to fit** — and it is there in
every tool. On a touch screen it is joined by **zoom in** and **zoom out**,
which take the same step as `+` and `-`, so pinching is not the only way to
get closer. There is no zoom percentage anywhere: what you can ask for is
to see everything, or to get closer to something, and the magnification
between those two is not a number you have to manage.

A corner **overview** of the whole canvas shows whenever the editor is wide
enough to hold it beside the dock. It draws every box and every pen drawing,
each in its own colour, so a board that holds only a sketch still has one. In a narrower editor, such as a phone held
upright, it sits behind a map button just above the dock, hidden until you tap
it and hidden again on a second tap; the choice lasts for the browser session.
While you type into a note, label or comment the overview steps aside, so it
never sits under the formatting bar or the on-screen keyboard.

Zooming to the selection sits in a node's right-click menu as **Zoom to
selection**; it frames every selected node, not only the one you pressed.

## History

| Shortcut | Action |
|---|---|
| `Cmd/Ctrl + Z` | Undo |
| `Cmd/Ctrl + Shift + Z` / `Cmd/Ctrl + Y` | Redo |
| `Cmd/Ctrl + S` | Save a version |

One action is one undo step: pasting twenty nodes, duplicating a
selection, or nudging several nodes each undo in a single press.

## Help

| Shortcut | Action |
|---|---|
| `?` | Open the keyboard shortcut sheet |

The sheet lists every shortcut above for your platform (`⌘` on macOS,
`Ctrl` elsewhere), grouped as Tools, Navigate, Edit, Arrange, View, Text and Help, with Undo and
Redo under Edit and a closing line that Align, Distribute, Tidy and Frame selection
have no key and live in the Select tool's right-click menus (`Shift + F10` opens the same menus from the keyboard) — Align and Distribute on
a selection of two or more nodes — since the Hand tool's right-click offers
comments only. It also
opens from the **Keyboard shortcuts** button in the bottom dock, which is the
way in without a keyboard. Press `Esc` to close it; focus returns to where it
was. The dock's buttons show their shortcut in the tooltip where they have
one, as **Zoom to fit** does.

## Inside a menu

The right-click and **More actions** menus take focus on their first labelled
action (not a colour swatch; reach the swatches with `Up` or `Left`) and are one
Tab stop. `Up` and `Down` move between items and wrap; `Home` and
`End` jump to the first and last; typing a letter jumps to the next item that
starts with it. In a row of choices such as the colour swatches, `Left` and
`Right` move within the row. `Enter` or `Space` activates the item, and
`Esc` closes the menu and returns focus to the control that opened it.

## Writing in a markdown document

These keys work in a markdown document's source and in a canvas node's text
editor. `Cmd` is the macOS modifier; use `Ctrl` everywhere else.

| Shortcut | Action |
|---|---|
| `Cmd/Ctrl + B` | Bold the selection, or the word at the caret |
| `Cmd/Ctrl + I` | Italicise the selection, or the word at the caret |
| `Cmd/Ctrl + E` | Mark the selection, or the word at the caret, as code |
| `Cmd/Ctrl + K` | Link: open the link picker over the selection or the word at the caret; where there is nothing to pick from it wraps in `[[ ]]` |
| `Cmd/Ctrl + Enter` | Cycle a task checkbox on the line: none, unchecked, checked, none again. A screen reader hears "Task unchecked", "Task checked" or "Task removed". In a canvas node's editor it saves instead |
| `Tab` / `Shift + Tab` | Indent or outdent the line, or nest a list item under the one above it; a hand-numbered list is renumbered to match |
| `Enter` on an empty list item or quote line | Remove the marker and leave the list or quote. A blank line is left after the list, so the next line you type is a paragraph of its own rather than part of the last item |
| `Backspace` on an empty list item or quote line | Remove the marker, leaving an empty line |
| `Esc`, then `Tab` or `Shift + Tab` | Leave the editor forwards or backwards; `Tab` alone indents |

The formatting bar above a markdown document names each button's shortcut in its tooltip ("Task (⌘/Ctrl+Enter)"). It is one `Tab` stop. `Left` and `Right` move between its buttons, `Home` and `End` jump to the first and last, and `Tab` leaves it; coming back with `Shift + Tab` lands on the button you were last on.

## On the canvas with a screen reader

The text fields that open over a canvas say what they edit: "Text of Review"
for a note, "Name of frame cluster" for a frame's name, "Label of edge from A
to B" for a relation's label. A note's text is described as "Escape discards,
Ctrl+Enter keeps" (`Command` on a Mac); a frame's name and a connection's or
line's label, being one line, as "Escape discards, Enter keeps". On a touch
screen, where the editor shows its ✓ Done and ✕ Cancel buttons instead, it is
described as "✓ Done keeps, ✕ Cancel discards". Pressing
`Esc` announces "Discarded" so a thrown-away draft is not silent. The one exception is a note you have just
added: `Esc` on it keeps what you typed and says so ("Note kept: Review"),
because a typed note lost to the key that closes the editor would have no
undo. Press `Esc` on a new note before typing and it is removed; leaving the canvas
while a new note is still empty removes it too, and so does closing or reloading the page: the next time this tab opens the canvas, a note you added and never typed into is gone.

On an empty canvas the cue to add a note is part of the canvas's description, so
it is read with the canvas. Choosing a tool, by key or from the dock, announces
it ("Hand tool", "Select tool", "Connect tool", "Draw tool", "Eraser"). On a canvas with
notes, the Connect tool also shows what to press at the top of the canvas —
"Click the first note, then the second" ("Tap…" on a touch screen), then "Now
click the note to connect to" once the first is chosen — and the first line is
announced with the tool's name.

Every node, connection and line is listed by name for a screen reader, in the
order `Tab` walks them: nodes by where they sit, top to bottom and then left to
right, not by the order they were added, so a note placed above another is read
first, each followed by the connections and lines that leave it. The
canvas points at the selected one: a note by its first
line, a frame as "Frame cluster", a connection as "Connection from Review to
Ship: then". A stroke made with Draw is listed as "Drawing", and a line dragged
out to empty space as "Line from Review to empty space"; neither is called a
connection, because a line asserts no relation.
Selecting says where you are ("Selected: Review (2 of 5)", "Selected 3 nodes"),
including the frame a node sits in ("Selected: Web App, in Frontend (3 of 8)"),
and what you do is said back: "Note added", "Connected Review to Ship",
"Framed 3 nodes", "Deleted 2 nodes"; a second or later frame says its number
("Frame 3 added"), so frames added one after another are told apart. Moving a node across a frame's edge, by
nudging or dragging, is said too ("Web App moved into Backend", "Web App left
Frontend", "Web App moved from Frontend into Backend"); a move that stays inside
its frame says nothing at the time it happens. Once the arrow keys have rested
for a moment, a run of nudges is summed up once: "Web App moved 64 right, 32
down, in Backend" (or "not in a frame"). Choosing how edges are drawn in the
Display panel is said back the same way ("Edge routing: Orthogonal", "Line
jumps: On").

The controls around a selected node name it ("Resize Review, south-east",
"More actions for Review") and add three `Tab` stops, not thirteen: the
south-east resize handle (the arrow keys resize from it), the right-hand
connect handle and the actions button.

Whatever you finish on the canvas leaves the keyboard on it: keeping a label
with `Enter` (or `Ctrl + Enter`) or discarding it with `Esc`, completing a connection, choosing
Group from the dock, and closing a dialog or the context menu with `Esc`.
`Delete`, the arrow keys and undo work straight away, with no click first.

## Moving between pages

Opening a document, returning to the list or opening Settings has a screen
reader say where you are ("Roadmap, markdown note", "Plan, canvas",
"Documents"), and the browser tab is titled the same way ("Roadmap ·
Whiteboard"). Where keyboard focus lands depends on the page:

- **A note** puts it on the note's heading, directly above its text. A new,
  empty note is the exception: its editor takes focus, so you can type at once.
- **A canvas** puts it on the canvas itself, empty or not, so a shortcut such
  as `N` or an arrow key works the moment the canvas appears — straight after
  **Create a canvas**, with no click first.
- **The document list** puts it on its heading, and coming back from a
  document you opened from the list (**Back**, or the browser's back) puts it
  back on the row you opened it from instead — its card, its row in the folder
  tree or in the search results, or its Recent tile — so you carry on where you
  were. After following a link in the preview, it goes to the card of the
  document that held the link.
- **Settings** does not move focus, so the next Tab starts from the top of the page.

The first Tab stop on every page is **Skip to content**, hidden until it is
focused: it moves focus past the app's header and the page's own header to
the canvas, the note's editor, or the start of the page's content. When the
app first opens on a page that puts focus on its heading, the first `Tab`
still goes to **Skip to content**; after that, `Tab` from a page's heading
goes on into the page.

## Searching the document list

In the document list's search box, the results are one key away, and a screen
reader hears how many there are once the search settles ("3 results for
“map”", or "No results for “map”"). A search that takes longer than a moment
shows "Searching…". The box is a combobox over its results: focus stays in it
while the arrow keys highlight a result, so you can keep typing, and a screen
reader names the highlighted one.

| Shortcut | Action |
|---|---|
| `ArrowDown` / `ArrowUp` in the search box | Highlight the next or previous result; `ArrowUp` on the first highlights none |
| `Enter` in the search box | Open the highlighted result, or the first when none is highlighted |
| `Escape` in the search box | Drop the highlight; with none, clear the search |
| `ArrowDown` / `ArrowUp` on a result reached with `Tab` | Move to the next or previous result; `ArrowUp` on the first returns to the box |
| `Enter` on a result | Open the document |

# What the OCIF projection keeps, and what it costs

[OCIF v0.7.0](https://spec.canvasprotocol.org/) is a **third projection** of a whiteboard
document ([ADR-0038](../contributing/adr/0038-ocif-projection.md)), beside JSON Canvas 1.0 and
OKF Markdown. The claim first-party support makes is the same one ADR-0037 made for JSON
Canvas: a round-trip property over the expressible subset, and this table for everything else.

This is the codec library’s projection (`toOcif` / `parseOcif`); no MCP tool, route or menu
produces an OCIF document yet, so read it as what the projection costs, not as an export you
can run today.

The model can hold **50** field positions. **27** of them are something OCIF can
state in its own vocabulary; the remaining **23** ride an extension of ours.

**Nothing is dropped**, and that is the difference worth knowing before choosing a format.
OCIF’s conformance rules require a reader to preserve an extension it does not understand, so a
document that goes out to a foreign tool and comes back still holds every position it left
with. A strict JSON Canvas export, by contrast, deletes its extension key outright.

Read this beside [the JSON Canvas table](json-canvas-loss.md): the rows are the same positions,
and where the two disagree is where the choice of format costs a reader something real.

## Stated by OCIF v0.7.0 — 23

A conforming reader gets these and UNDERSTANDS them. A facet bucket is in here because OCIF’s `data[]` is the same mechanism — one ordinary extension per facet, keyed by the facet key — not because it is tolerated on a vendor key.

| field | what a reader gets |
| --- | --- |
| `edges[].facets/*` | stated by the format |
| `edges[].from.node` | stated by the format |
| `edges[].id` | stated by the format |
| `edges[].to.node` | stated by the format |
| `facets/*` | stated by the format |
| `lines[].facets/*` | stated by the format |
| `lines[].from.end` | stated by the format |
| `lines[].from.point.x` | stated by the format |
| `lines[].from.point.y` | stated by the format |
| `lines[].id` | stated by the format |
| `lines[].to.end` | stated by the format |
| `lines[].to.point.x` | stated by the format |
| `lines[].to.point.y` | stated by the format |
| `nodes[].embed.documentId` | stated by the format |
| `nodes[].facets/*` | stated by the format |
| `nodes[].height` | stated by the format |
| `nodes[].id` | stated by the format |
| `nodes[].resource.content` | stated by the format |
| `nodes[].resource.location` | stated by the format |
| `nodes[].resource.mimeType` | stated by the format |
| `nodes[].width` | stated by the format |
| `nodes[].x` | stated by the format |
| `nodes[].y` | stated by the format |

## Stated, but not in the same shape — 4

The format has somewhere to put the value and not the same shape for it. What a reader gets instead is named per row, and this projection reads it back the same way, so the row is what a round trip through a foreign tool really costs.

| field | what a reader gets |
| --- | --- |
| `edges[].from.end` | crosses as @ocif/edge's single `directed` boolean — the format has no per-end marker on a relation |
| `edges[].to.end` | crosses as @ocif/edge's single `directed` boolean — the format has no per-end marker on a relation |
| `lines[].from.kind` | crosses as an @ocif/arrow's coordinates — the shape carries where the line runs and not what it was attached to, so a node end arrives as that node's centre |
| `lines[].to.kind` | crosses as an @ocif/arrow's coordinates — the shape carries where the line runs and not what it was attached to, so a node end arrives as that node's centre |

## Carried on a `@whiteboard/*` extension — 23

A conforming reader must PRESERVE an extension it does not understand, so a round trip through a foreign tool deletes none of these. What is lost is comprehension, not data: the tool carries the bytes and cannot act on them. There is no second mode here that drops the key — that is JSON Canvas’s `strict`, and OCIF has no equivalent.

| field | what a reader gets |
| --- | --- |
| `edges[].bends[].x` | preserved, not understood |
| `edges[].bends[].y` | preserved, not understood |
| `edges[].color` | preserved, not understood |
| `edges[].from.side` | preserved, not understood |
| `edges[].label` | preserved, not understood |
| `edges[].tags[]` | preserved, not understood |
| `edges[].to.side` | preserved, not understood |
| `lines[].bends[].x` | preserved, not understood |
| `lines[].bends[].y` | preserved, not understood |
| `lines[].color` | preserved, not understood |
| `lines[].from.node` | preserved, not understood |
| `lines[].from.side` | preserved, not understood |
| `lines[].label` | preserved, not understood |
| `lines[].to.node` | preserved, not understood |
| `lines[].to.side` | preserved, not understood |
| `nodes[].background` | preserved, not understood |
| `nodes[].backgroundStyle` | preserved, not understood |
| `nodes[].color` | preserved, not understood |
| `nodes[].embed.versionRef` | preserved, not understood |
| `nodes[].label` | preserved, not understood |
| `nodes[].resource.subpath` | preserved, not understood |
| `nodes[].tags[]` | preserved, not understood |
| `tags[]` | preserved, not understood |

## Cannot cross at all — 0

Named here so an absence would be a decision rather than a surprise.

_None today._

## What this table does not cover

- **What is inside a facet bucket.** A `…/*` row is one entry. Unlike the JSON Canvas table,
  here that is a statement about scope rather than about loss: each facet crosses as its own
  OCIF extension, so its contents survive whatever they are — this table simply cannot
  enumerate what a deployment’s plugins put there.
- **What OCIF can state that this model cannot hold.** Rotation, 3D positions, ports,
  inheritance and pages are all in the specification and have no position here to lose. A
  document arriving with them keeps them as unread extension data.
- **OKF Markdown.** This is the spatial side only.
- **The comments.** A conversation is the document’s annotation layer, kept beside its content
  rather than in it ([ADR-0026](../contributing/adr/0026-annotation-layer.md) decision 1b), so
  the projection does not carry it. A file an older version wrote with a `@whiteboard/comments`
  entry is refused on import, naming the entry.

# Tutorials

Learning-oriented, guided lessons. A tutorial takes a newcomer from nothing to a working
result by following concrete steps — it teaches by doing and does not stop to explain every
option (that is what [Reference](../reference/) and [Explanation](../explanation/) are for).

- **[Getting started](getting-started.md)** — run the browser app from a checkout, draw, and see it persist.

Planned tutorials (added in a later migration slice):

- **Connect an AI agent** — wire an MCP client and have an agent draw with you.
- **Try the local daemon** — run the daemon and persist to your filesystem.

# Getting started

whiteboard's canvas runs right in your browser. When the **browser** is the
keeper, your
drawings live in your own browser (IndexedDB) — no account, and nothing leaves
your machine while you work.

Today you run the browser app locally from a checkout. **Prerequisites:** Node.js
and pnpm (run `corepack enable` if you don't already have pnpm).

```bash
git clone https://github.com/kamiazya/whiteboard.git
cd whiteboard      # pnpm workspace root — required for catalog: dependency resolution
pnpm install
pnpm --filter @kamiazya/whiteboard-web dev   # open http://localhost:5173
```

On a fresh browser the page asks what you'll make first — pick **Canvas**
(notes you place and connect in space) or **Markdown note** (start writing;
you can put it on a canvas later) and it opens ready to work in.

![Onboarding chooser](../assets/onboarding-chooser.png)

Once you have documents, the page lands on your document browser. On a
touch screen, tap a card to open the document, and tap its **…** button (or press
and hold the card) for its actions (open, pin, rename, delete). With a mouse, a click previews a
document in the pane beside the list, and a double-click — or Enter on a
focused one — opens it. That holds for the cards, the **Recent** strip and
search results alike. Each card shows a small picture of its document — a
note's picture is cropped to the text it holds — and a document with nothing
in it yet shows its kind with **Empty** under it. Each search result says
where its document is by the names of its folders, as the folder tree shows
them (hover the line for the document's address). Search keeps your query in the box when you open a
result and come back. A **Recent** strip above the cards lists the documents you
opened last — however you opened them: a card, a link, a reload, search or
**Create** — and appears only once there are more documents than fit in the
first row of cards — before that it would show every card twice. On a phone
or a narrow window the strip is left out altogether, since the list is right below; it is also left out inside a
folder and in the one-column list, which already shows every document. A deleted document
waits in **Trash (_n_)** just above the list, which names it, the folder it was
in and when it went, with **Restore** beside each one. Use the
toolbar to search everything or move a document to a new path; to put a
document in a folder, use **Move to folder…** in its menu or drag it onto the
folder ([organize into folders](../how-to/organize-into-folders.md)). **Back to
documents** returns you to the folder the document was in.

**New** in that toolbar opens the same two choices — **Canvas** or **Markdown
note** — and creates one in whichever folder you are standing in. A kind
cannot be changed later, which is why you pick it by name rather than by
icon; everything else about a document is editable afterwards, so nothing
else is asked for. A new document starts at the path `untitled`, and until it
has a name the lists, its page heading and its title box all call it
**Untitled** (**Untitled 2** for `untitled-2`); the first time
you give it a name in its title, its path becomes that name (`untitled` to
`checkout-architecture`), and from then on the path stays put. If you already know what the document is called and where
it goes, **Name and folder…** in that menu takes both up front. Its **Path**
follows the **Name** as you type — `Q3 hiring plan` fills in `q3-hiring-plan`,
accents are spelled without their marks, and a name in a script the address
cannot spell gives `note` or `canvas` and the next free number — until you edit
the path yourself. The hint under it says what an address may hold (letters
a–z, digits and hyphens, `/` between folders), and a path it cannot hold is
said while you type it, not after **Create**. Leaving the form untouched
creates exactly what the plain entries would have.

On a phone, or any touch screen, **New** opens a sheet from the bottom edge
instead. Its first field is the name, with the keyboard already up; type it and
press **Canvas** or **Markdown note**, and the document is created under that
name at the path the name earns (`Meeting notes` becomes `meeting-notes`;
`概要` becomes `note`, or the next free `note-2`, `note-3` …).
Leave the name empty and it starts at `untitled` as above.

Two documents side by side in one folder cannot share a name: the sheet, the
**Name and folder…** form and **Rename…** each refuse a name another document
in the same folder already shows — ignoring case and surrounding spaces — and
say so beside the field before anything is saved. The same name in another
folder is fine.

Either way the new document opens straight away, ready to work in. The folder
you are standing in is part of the address — the URL carries a `?folder=`
while you are inside one — so coming back lands you where you were, a reload
keeps your place, and a link you paste to someone opens the folder you meant.
The column layout is not in the link: that is a per-browser preference, so
your choice is remembered here without being imposed on whoever you send it
to.

![The document browser for a workspace kept in this browser](../assets/browser-local-list.png)

A fresh canvas starts empty, with a one-line hint ("Double-click or press N to add a note", or "Tap + to add a note" on a touch screen) that disappears with the first node. Double-click empty canvas space to make a note
and start typing immediately (this works in Hand mode too, and never moves the
view), or open the **+** menu in the bottom dock: tap
an entry to place it in the middle of the view, or drag one onto the canvas
to drop it exactly where you want it. Notes added one after another from the
menu (or with `N`) line up in the order you made them — each to the right of
the last, starting a new row below when the row would leave the screen — with
32px between them. **Frame** makes a new, empty frame — to the right of the frames already there, when there are any — in a free
spot, with room above it for its name and the usual gap from the boxes around it when the view has room for one, and opens that name for typing; an empty frame is drawn with a faint tint
so it can be found. To frame nodes you have already made, select them,
right-click one and choose **Frame selection**, which also opens the new
frame's name. In **Select** mode, right-clicking
(long-pressing on touch) empty space offers the same creations, placed where
you pressed. On touch the menu is a sheet titled for what you pressed, dimmed behind, at most half the screen (it scrolls), and the canvas pans so the pressed object stays visible above it; tap the dimmed area to close it. Hand mode is navigation only, so it deliberately leaves the
right-click menu closed (a tap on a comment still opens its conversation:
comments are chrome, not content). The
browser UI also selects, moves, resizes, connects, and edits existing nodes,
and deletes the selected node with Delete/Backspace (disabled while you're
typing in its text editor, so Backspace edits text instead of deleting the
note). Reload the tab after any of these edits and the change is still
there — that's your canvas persisting to IndexedDB in your own browser, with
no server and no account.

A small status beside the document title tells you whether your edits are safe.
It reads **Saved** (quietly) once the last change has landed, **Saving…** if a
write takes longer than a moment, **Not saved — storage problem** when the
browser refuses a write or no write lands for several seconds while a change
waits to be saved, and **Offline — changes kept here** when a document
kept by the daemon cannot reach it: your edits stay in this browser and are sent
when the connection returns. On a phone it shrinks to an icon; hover or long-press
for the words. A problem is shown, and a screen reader told, only once it has
lasted a moment — one that clears by itself is never announced — and never on an
ordinary save.

If you used an early build of the browser app, its saved data may be in a format
this version no longer reads. Nothing is migrated, and nothing is shown as empty
or deleted: the page says why the data cannot be opened. A workspace written as
per-document records is refused on its own (other workspaces in this browser keep
working; start a new one); a whole browser database from an older version cannot
be opened at all, so clear this site's data in your browser settings to start
over. A single document saved in a retired form is named as such and is not
offered for deletion. Workspaces kept by the daemon are not affected.

**Where to go next:** want your AI agent (Claude Code, Codex, Gemini) to draw with
you, or durable canvases as files on disk? That's the **Local daemon** — see
[Quick install](../../README.md#quick-install). Curious how whiteboard scales from a
browser tab to a self-hosted team server? See [the runtime modes](../explanation/).

name: auditing-workspaces
description: Audit a whiteboard workspace's documents to find likely-stale or duplicate spatial canvases before creating new ones. Use when a workspace has been in heavy use and you want to check for clutter, or you want a quick sense of what a document actually contains before opening it.
---

# auditing-workspaces

List a workspace's documents (or find them by what they say with `wb_document_search`), then use `wb_canvas_snapshot` on the spatial ones (its `nodeCount`, and `layout: true` for how tidy it is) to judge which look empty
or abandoned. There is no server-side audit endpoint — this skill is a recipe for composing the
regular document tools toward that end, nothing more.

For the main drawing workflow, see the drawing-visuals skill in `skills/drawing-visuals/SKILL.md`.

---

## When To Use It

- When a workspace has been in heavy use and you want a sense of what is in it before adding more
- When you want to check for a likely-duplicate path before creating a document
- When you want to know whether a spatial document is worth opening without rendering it

---

## Execution Flow

### Step 1: List The Workspace's Documents

```js
wb_document_list({ workspaceId })
```

`workspaceId` is `default` unless the user names another workspace: the segment of the first workspace a data directory gets, and the one the web app opens first.

Returns `{ documents: [{ documentId, path, name?, kind?, updatedAt?, shadowed? }] }` — placement only, no content. An unknown
`workspaceId` is an error here, not an empty list, so a typo reads as a failure rather than "nothing
found."

### Step 1b: Search Instead Of Listing, When You Know What You Are Looking For

A duplicate or a stale copy is often easier to find by content than by path:

```js
wb_document_search({ workspaceId, query: "checkout flow" })                 // what documents say
wb_document_search({ workspaceId, tags: ["status:draft"], kind: "spatial" }) // a tag, a kind, or both, with no query
```

`query` is full-text over markdown bodies and canvas text (nodes, group labels, edge labels), plus
names and paths, and Japanese works without a dictionary. `tags` and `kind` filter and stand alone,
so "every document carrying this tag" is one call. Each result is `{ documentId, path, name, kind,
score, contexts }`, ranked; scores compare within one response only, and `limit` (default 10, at
most 50) is how many come back, so a long result is a reason to narrow, not proof it is complete.
Two results whose `contexts` read alike are near-duplicate candidates for Step 3.

### Step 2: Classify, Then Sample Each Document

Step 1's `kind` is the cheap classification, and it is `optional` for a real reason: a document
whose index row never recorded one has no `kind` in the listing. That absence is itself the
signal — it is the pre-kind case Step 3 asks about, spotted without reading anything.

Content still needs `wb_document_get`, but that is ONE call for up to 20 documents:

```js
wb_document_get({ workspaceId, documentIds: [a, b, c] })
// -> { documents: [...], failed: [...] }
// markdown -> { documentId, kind: "markdown", content: "...", frontmatter: {...} }  (the body, directly)
// spatial  -> { documentId, kind: "spatial", content: "..." }                        (full JSON Canvas payload)
// either kind also carries `threads` when anyone commented: each thread whole, with its status
// no recorded kind -> an entry in `failed` with the reason — it does not take the batch with it
```

`documents` comes back in the order asked for, minus anything in `failed`, so read `failed` rather
than assuming the two arrays line up.

**Read the kind before reading the content.** A spatial read refuses a document it knows to be
markdown rather than reporting its containers as empty, so it cannot silently answer "nothing
here" about a document full of prose — but it also cannot tell you the kind of a document you have
not identified yet. Step 1's `kind`, or `wb_document_get`'s, is what establishes that.

Once a document is KNOWN spatial (from `wb_document_get`'s `kind`, or because this session created
it), `wb_canvas_snapshot` is the cheap re-probe for later passes — node text, geometry and lock
state without the untruncated JSON Canvas payload:

```js
wb_canvas_snapshot({ workspaceId, documentId })               // what is on it
wb_canvas_snapshot({ workspaceId, documentId, layout: true })  // ...and whether it is tidy
```

A document with no recorded kind predates format tracking (`wb_document_get` reports it in
`failed` rather than guessing; a snapshot of it still answers, misleadingly, from the empty spatial
containers). The only way to give it a kind is
to write to it (a `wb_canvas_edit` call records `spatial`, a `document.set` op records `markdown`).

### Step 3: Judge Staleness

There is no true last-modified or last-accessed time exposed through these tools. The listing's
`updatedAt` is one replica's register stamp: it moves on a real content change here, but a merge
does not consult it (ADR-0027), so it is a hint and never proof a document is untouched. Judge
staleness structurally first:

| Signal | How To Check | Likely Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| empty spatial document | `kind` is `spatial` (Step 2) AND `wb_canvas_snapshot` reports `nodeCount: 0` | never drawn, or already redrawn elsewhere — candidate for a `document.delete` op. A zero `nodeCount` ALONE proves nothing for a document whose kind you have not established: the snapshot refuses a markdown document, but one with no recorded kind answers empty |
| near-duplicate path | two `wb_document_list` entries with similar `path`/`name` | probably one abandoned in favor of the other |
| old or missing `updatedAt` | `updatedAt` in the Step 1 listing, if present | a hint only — one replica's stamp, not a merge-proof clock; corroborate with a structural signal before proposing deletion |
| markdown document with an empty body | `content` is blank apart from frontmatter | scaffolded but never written |
| document with no recorded kind | no `kind` in the Step 1 listing, and a `failed` entry from `wb_document_get` | predates format tracking; needs deciding, not deleting on sight |

### Step 4: Write The Report

Keep the user-facing summary short and structured:

```text
## whiteboard audit report — workspace {workspaceId}

Documents: {N}
Empty or near-empty: {list of path -> documentId}
Likely-duplicate paths: {pairs}
No recorded kind: {list}

### Deletion candidates
- {path} ({documentId}): {reason}
```

Do **not** delete anything automatically. Always confirm with the user before calling
a `wb_workspace_edit` `document.delete` op.

---

## Notes

- `document.delete` fails if other documents sit below the target's path — deletion is refused
  rather than silently cascading, so report the blocker back to the user instead of retrying
  differently.
- Deletion is not recoverable through these tools beyond a document's own saved versions
  (`wb_version_list` / `wb_version_restore`) — the same history the History panel shows — and
  those do not survive the document itself being deleted.
- **What batches, and what does not.** `wb_document_get` takes up to 20 `documentIds`, so reading
  a workspace's content costs `ceil(N / 20)` calls rather than N. `wb_facet_set` and
  `wb_version_save` take up to 50 each, with the payload — the facets, the label — SHARED across
  every document named; that is what makes them cheap, and also what they are for. What still
  takes exactly one document is `wb_canvas_snapshot` and the per-document content verbs
  (`wb_canvas_edit`, `wb_body_edit`, `wb_thread_edit`), where each document's payload is its own
  and there is nothing to share. `wb_document_get`'s 20 is lower than the writes' 50 because it
  returns UNTRUNCATED content — for a very large workspace, classify from Step 1's `kind` and
  sample the content rather than reading every document whole.
